guides.title: How to check a property’s condition: the complete Australian guide
guides.summary: A calm, practical way to understand an Australian home, from its documents and physical condition to the work and costs that may lie ahead.

Start with the legal and property records that exist for the address. Every state runs seller disclosure its own way. sections.heading: Then read the building, and decide how hard
sections.markdown:
A building and timber-pest inspection puts eyes on the actual house: what could be seen, what could be reached, and what sat outside the scope. Decide what the property and transaction warrant, whether an existing report gives you reliance rights, and which unresolved signals need specialist follow-up. The checks below move from early triage to more specific investigation:

**The common checks, at a glance**

| Check | What it catches | When it's worth it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Section 32 / contract review | Legal, title, zoning, disclosure risk | Always |
| Desktop / pre-inspection read | Likely repair exposure, what to ask, what to inspect | Early, before spending on a physical inspection |
| Building & pest inspection | Visible defects, pests, moisture, structural signs | Before you commit, and before any unconditional offer |
| Specialist (structural, electrical) | A specific suspected defect | When an earlier check flags something |

Guides for each: [desktop and physical reports](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/desktop-vs-physical-report), [what an inspection costs](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/building-and-pest-inspection-cost), [whether one is worth it before auction](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/building-inspection-before-auction), and [which kind of condition report you need](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/what-is-a-property-condition-report). For damp, mould and indoor-environment questions, see [building biologist scope and cost](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/building-biologist-cost). Buying interstate? Read [NSW's contract for sale](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/reading-a-contract-for-sale-nsw) or [Queensland's Form 2](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/seller-disclosure-qld).

sections.markdown:
### Risk clusters by era

Risk clusters by construction and era. A 1970s brick veneer, a 1920s weatherboard and a 2015 apartment each create different inspection priorities. See [red flags by era](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/red-flags-by-era) and [the wall-crack guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/cracks-structural-or-cosmetic).

### Apartments add a financial dimension

An apartment is two purchases in one: the lot itself, and a share of a building run by its owners corporation. The physical inspection covers the unit; the owners-corporation records cover the building's finances and the special levies that can land on you after settlement. For apartments, read both: [buying an apartment](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/buying-an-apartment-strata).

guides.contentMarkdown:
# How to check a property’s condition: the complete Australian guide

A home becomes much easier to understand when you read three things together: what the documents say, what the building is showing you and what the likely work could cost. Start with the records you can get, use them to sharpen the inspection, then turn the findings into a short list of decisions and follow-up questions.

## Research note
The sequence below reflects official buyer guidance: read the contract and disclosure material early, then commission the physical and specialist checks the property warrants. See the [NSW inspection guidance](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/buying-and-selling-property/buying-property-nsw/inspecting-a-property/inspection-reports) and [Victoria's due-diligence checklist](https://www.consumer.vic.gov.au/housing/buying-and-selling-property/checklists/due-diligence).

## Opening
### Three views of the same home
- **Documents:** What the paperwork says the home is
- **Building:** What the building itself is telling you
- **Decision:** What it will cost, when, and what to ask next

_Read together, they show what you are buying and what is coming._

## The order to do things in
Working through it in sequence is cheaper and calmer than doing everything at once on a single property. A workable order: read whatever documents exist first (cheap or free), form a view of the building's likely exposure early, then spend on a physical inspection when it matters. If you are buying, settle your finance and price limit before any auction.

## Start with the available documents
Start with the legal and property records that exist for the address. Every state runs seller disclosure its own way. Victoria hands you a Section 32, NSW builds the disclosure into the contract itself, Queensland now requires a Form 2, and the rest each have arrangements of their own. Titles, searches, plans, permits and owners-corporation records can expose legal or shared-building issues outside a visual inspection. Have the contract and required disclosure reviewed for the property's jurisdiction.

See the dedicated guide: [how to read a Section 32 (Vendor's Statement)](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/reading-a-section-32).

## Then read the building, and decide how hard
A building and timber-pest inspection puts eyes on the actual house: what could be seen, what could be reached, and what sat outside the scope. Decide what the property and transaction warrant, whether an existing report gives you reliance rights, and which unresolved signals need specialist follow-up. The checks below move from early triage to more specific investigation:

**The common checks, at a glance**

| Check | What it catches | When it's worth it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Section 32 / contract review | Legal, title, zoning, disclosure risk | Always |
| Desktop / pre-inspection read | Likely repair exposure, what to ask, what to inspect | Early, before spending on a physical inspection |
| Building & pest inspection | Visible defects, pests, moisture, structural signs | Before you commit, and before any unconditional offer |
| Specialist (structural, electrical) | A specific suspected defect | When an earlier check flags something |

Guides for each: [desktop and physical reports](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/desktop-vs-physical-report), [what an inspection costs](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/building-and-pest-inspection-cost), [whether one is worth it before auction](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/building-inspection-before-auction), and [which kind of condition report you need](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/what-is-a-property-condition-report). For damp, mould and indoor-environment questions, see [building biologist scope and cost](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/building-biologist-cost). Buying interstate? Read [NSW's contract for sale](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/reading-a-contract-for-sale-nsw) or [Queensland's Form 2](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/seller-disclosure-qld).

## Match the checks to the property
### Risk clusters by era

Risk clusters by construction and era. A 1970s brick veneer, a 1920s weatherboard and a 2015 apartment each create different inspection priorities. See [red flags by era](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/red-flags-by-era) and [the wall-crack guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/cracks-structural-or-cosmetic).

### Apartments add a financial dimension

An apartment is two purchases in one: the lot itself, and a share of a building run by its owners corporation. The physical inspection covers the unit; the owners-corporation records cover the building's finances and the special levies that can land on you after settlement. For apartments, read both: [buying an apartment](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/buying-an-apartment-strata).

## If you are buying, your method changes your protections
How you buy matters as much as what you buy. A private-treaty purchase usually lets you make the offer conditional and gives a short cooling-off period; an **auction is generally unconditional, with no cooling-off to fall back on**, so every check gets finished before you bid. Know which you are in: [cooling-off periods by state](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/cooling-off-period-by-state) and [auction-day due diligence](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/auction-day-due-diligence).

## Continue the record through ownership
Keep the condition picture current through ownership. It helps plan repairs, supports insurance and prepares the evidence for a future sale. Continue with [what your home needs by decade](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/what-your-home-needs-by-decade), [the maintenance that prevents the big bills](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/the-maintenance-that-prevents-the-big-bills), and [keeping a record of your home](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/keeping-a-record-of-your-home).

> Note: Homechecker combines public signals, visible property evidence and supplied documents into an independent read of likely needs and worthwhile next checks. Keep it current as the property changes.

## Frequently asked questions
### What checks should I do before buying a house in Australia?
At minimum, arrange contract and disclosure review plus a building and pest inspection before an unconditional offer. A desktop read can triage earlier questions. Auction and private-treaty rules create different deadlines and protections.

### What order should I do the checks in?
Read the disclosure documents first, form an early view of the building’s likely exposure (a desktop read does this cheaply), then commission a physical inspection on the property you are serious about, and settle your finance and price limit before any auction.

### How much do pre-purchase checks cost?
It depends on the property, the state and the scope. Start with inexpensive steps such as documents and desktop triage, then commission the physical and specialist inspections the property warrants. See the building and pest inspection cost guide.

### Do I need a building inspection if the vendor provides one?
Read the report and its fine print: when it was done, what areas were reached, who inspected, whether they carry insurance, and whether you are allowed to rely on it. Commission your own inspection when those answers leave a material gap.

### How does condition evidence help during ownership?
It turns guesswork into a plan: what to maintain and when, what to tell the insurer, what a renovation will run into, and what a future buyer will ask. Keep it current as the house changes.

## Method
We took the official buyer guidance and arranged it in the order a buyer meets it: documents first, then the building, then the specialists, with a deep-dive waiting at each step.

## Limitations
General Australian guidance only. Contracts, statutes, policies, site conditions and professional scopes vary; obtain advice for the property and decision in front of you.

## Sources
- [Inspection reports before buying property](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/buying-and-selling-property/buying-property-nsw/inspecting-a-property/inspection-reports) — NSW Government; accessed 2026-07-19
- [Due diligence checklist for home buyers](https://www.consumer.vic.gov.au/housing/buying-and-selling-property/checklists/due-diligence) — Consumer Affairs Victoria; accessed 2026-07-19

guides.question: How do I read a Section 32 vendor's statement?
guides.title: How to read a Section 32 vendor's statement in Victoria
guides.summary: A Section 32 is evidence about the legal and administrative position of Victorian land, not a condition report on the building. Read it by asking what each record establishes, what it leaves unknown and what the property itself needs you to check next.
guides.answer: The seller must give the buyer a Section 32 vendor's statement before the buyer signs the contract. Start by confirming the seller, title, lot and plan, then work through financial matters, easements and covenants, planning controls, notices, building permits, owner-builder material, owners-corporation information, services and title evidence. The useful step is reconciliation: a permit can show that work was authorised, but not its present condition; an easement can show a legal right, but not how it affects the extension you want to build. Consumer Affairs Victoria expressly says a Section 32 does not tell you the condition of the buildings, whether they comply with building regulations or whether title measurements are accurate, so pair the legal bundle with physical inspection, survey, council or specialist evidence where the property raises those questions.
guides.methodology: Written against the current Sale of Land Act and Victoria’s own consumer guidance, and updated for the July 2026 Home Warranty changeover.
guides.limitations: This provides Victorian legal orientation. A Victorian conveyancer or solicitor should read the statement and contract before you sign anything.
guides.researchNote: Consumer Affairs Victoria says the seller must provide the Section 32 before the buyer signs and recommends legal review. The statement covers legal disclosure. Arrange a separate physical inspection for the building's condition. Read the [official Section 32 overview](https://www.consumer.vic.gov.au/housing/buying-and-selling-property/selling-property/conveyancing-and-contracts-for-sellers) alongside the contract.

cluster.label: Documents and state rules
cluster.blurb: Read the disclosure bundle for the right jurisdiction, then arrange the physical and specialist checks the property warrants.

sections.heading: Opening
sections.markdown:
### Read the land, then inspect the building
- **Title:** Who owns it, and what the title lets or forbids
- **Planning:** What the zone and overlays will let you do
- **Outside the statement:** The roof, the damp, the pests: none of it is in here

_The statement covers the land. Someone still has to look at the house._

sections.heading: Three documents, three different jobs
sections.markdown:
Section 32 of Victoria's [Sale of Land Act 1962](https://www.legislation.vic.gov.au/in-force/acts/sale-land-act-1962/173) requires prescribed information to be given to the buyer before the buyer signs the contract. [Consumer Affairs Victoria](https://www.consumer.vic.gov.au/housing/buying-and-selling-property/selling-property/conveyancing-and-contracts-for-sellers) describes the Section 32 as a legal document containing information about matters such as title, mortgages, covenants, easements, zoning and outgoings.

Keep three layers separate. The **Section 32** records prescribed facts about the land and transaction. The **contract** sets the terms of the deal. The **building inspection and other due diligence** investigate the physical property and questions outside the statutory statement. Reading them together is powerful; substituting one for another is not.

> Important: Consumer Affairs Victoria says the Section 32 does not include information about the condition of buildings, whether buildings comply with building regulations or whether measurements on the title are accurate. Those are separate due-diligence questions.

sections.heading: Use sections 32A to 32I as the contents map
sections.markdown:
**A working map of the statutory disclosure structure**

| Act section | Evidence area | Buyer question |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 32A | Financial matters, including rates, taxes, charges and other prescribed liabilities | What is payable, is the information current, and how will amounts be adjusted or borne? |
| 32B | Insurance details required in specified circumstances, including vendor insurance where risk does not remain with the vendor and statutory insurance cover for relevant residential building work | Which circumstance applies, what policy or statutory cover exists, and does it reconcile with the work, risk allocation and sale? |
| 32C | Land-use matters including easements, covenants and planning information | Where does each control or restriction apply and what does it mean for current use or future work? |
| 32D | Notices, orders, declarations, reports and proposals affecting the land | What triggered the item, what action remains and who carries the responsibility or cost? |
| 32E | Particulars of building permits issued in the preceding seven years | Do the permits line up with the additions, renovations and structures you can actually see? |
| 32F | Owners-corporation certificate and prescribed information where applicable | What do scheme boundaries, fees, funds, insurance, defects, disputes and future works say together? |
| 32G | Growth Areas Infrastructure Contribution information where applicable | Is there a current or deferred liability affecting the land or transaction? |
| 32H | Whether prescribed services are connected | Does the documentary position match the services the property appears to use, and what remains unknown about their condition or capacity? |
| 32I | Evidence of the vendor’s title to the land | Do the vendor, title reference, lot and plan match the property being offered? |

The statutory labels help you navigate the bundle, but they are only the first pass. The second pass is to translate each legal fact into its **practical implication for this address**.

sections.heading: Read the statement as evidence, not as conclusions
sections.markdown:
**What common Section 32 evidence can and cannot tell you**

| Evidence | What it can establish | What it cannot establish | What to do next |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Title and plan | The registered land, proprietor and interests shown on title | That fences, improvements and occupation align exactly with legal boundaries | Compare the plan with the site; raise discrepancies with the conveyancer and commission a survey where warranted. |
| Easement or covenant | A registered right or restriction affects the land | Whether your proposed extension, pool, driveway, drainage works or access strategy is acceptable | Locate it relative to the property and test the intended use or design against the legal restriction. |
| Planning zone or overlay | A planning control applies to the land | That a renovation, demolition, subdivision or change of use will be approved | Read the schedule/maps and obtain planning advice for the actual proposal. |
| Building permit particulars | A permit was issued for described work within the disclosure period | That the work was completed exactly as approved, is defect-free, meets every current requirement or remains in good condition | Ask for approved plans, occupancy/final evidence and compare them with the visible work and physical inspection. |
| Notice or order | A statutory or administrative issue has been recorded | That the cause is resolved or the required work has been completed satisfactorily | Obtain the underlying notice, response and completion evidence; inspect the affected area where physically relevant. |
| Service connection information | A prescribed service is recorded as connected or not connected | The age, capacity, safety, layout or condition of the service | Inspect or test the actual system where its age, performance or alteration matters. |
| Owners-corporation certificate | Prescribed scheme, fee, insurance and other information at a point in time | The complete history of common-property condition, defects, disputes or future capital demand | Read the register, recent minutes, budgets, maintenance plan, reports and proposed works as one evidence set. |

sections.heading: Map title restrictions against the physical home
sections.markdown:
Do not leave easements, covenants and other encumbrances as abstract lines in a legal document. Map them against the house, garage, deck, pool, retaining walls, access, drainage and any extension you may want to build. A sewer easement under open lawn is a different practical problem from the same easement running beneath a structure. If the title plan is hard to reconcile with what stands on the land, ask the conveyancer whether a licensed surveyor or further title work is warranted.

**Title questions that become building questions**

| Document signal | Physical question | Possible consequence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Easement through a side or rear setback | Is an existing or proposed structure over or near it? | Access, consent, relocation or design constraints may affect future work. |
| Restrictive covenant | Does the existing use or proposed design conflict with the restriction? | The covenant may constrain development even if the site physically accommodates it. |
| Plan dimensions that do not feel consistent with fences or improvements | Are occupation and legal boundaries aligned? | Survey/legal clarification may be needed before relying on the apparent usable land. |
| Shared or unusual access arrangement | How is vehicle/pedestrian access physically used and maintained? | Rights, maintenance responsibility and practical access can all matter. |

sections.heading: Planning controls tell you the rulebook, not the outcome
sections.markdown:
A zone establishes the broad planning framework. Overlays add controls for matters such as heritage, flooding, vegetation or bushfire. Their importance depends on the address and what you intend to do. An overlay is not automatically a defect or a reason not to buy; it is evidence that future work may need a different design, approval pathway, consultant input, material choice or budget. For the Victorian heritage pathway, continue with [living in a Heritage Overlay](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/living-in-a-heritage-overlay).

If renovation or redevelopment matters to the purchase decision, do not stop at the label shown in the Section 32. Read the relevant schedule and map, then test the actual proposal with the responsible authority or planning adviser.

sections.heading: A building permit is evidence of process, not a condition report
sections.markdown:
Section 32E requires particulars of building permits issued in the preceding seven years. This is one of the most useful bridges between the legal bundle and the physical property because it lets you compare the documented work with what is actually visible.

**How to reconcile recent building work**

| Question | Evidence to seek | What remains a physical question |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What was approved? | Building permit particulars, approved drawings and specifications where available | Whether the visible work matches the documented scope. |
| Was the work completed? | Occupancy permit, certificate of final inspection or other applicable completion evidence | Whether finishes, waterproofing, drainage, structure and services remain sound today. |
| Who carried it out? | Builder/owner-builder records, contracts, invoices and insurance/warranty material where applicable | Quality of workmanship and any defects not apparent from paperwork. |
| Has it changed since approval? | Later permits, plans, photos and owner records | Whether subsequent alterations created new approval or condition questions. |

A permit is not proof that a bathroom is currently watertight, a deck has no decay, a roof alteration is leak-free or an extension has no movement. It is one piece of evidence in a chain.

sections.heading: Owner-builder work deserves its own evidence chain
sections.markdown:
[Consumer Affairs Victoria says an owner builder selling within six years and six months of obtaining the Certificate of Final Inspection or Occupancy Permit must provide a defects inspection report that is no more than six months old](https://www.consumer.vic.gov.au/housing/building-and-renovating/checklists/owner-builders) for the relevant work, including extensions, renovations, garages and verandas. Insurance requirements can also apply depending on the work and circumstances.

Victoria's domestic-building insurance framework changed on 1 July 2026. The [Building and Plumbing Commission](https://www.bpc.vic.gov.au/home-owners/insurance-for-domestic-building-work/domestic-building-insurance-and-home-warranty) explains that existing Domestic Building Insurance continues for earlier cover while Home Warranty applies to new eligible domestic building work under the post-1 July 2026 regime. The [BPC also says](https://www.bpc.vic.gov.au/owner-builders/what-is-an-owner-builder) an owner-builder who wishes to sell applicable owner-built work within six years of completion may need a Home Warranty Notice of Cover and premium. For a purchase, have the conveyancer identify the work, completion date, builder status, applicable defects report, insurance or warranty evidence and any transition issue, then compare that documentary chain with the physical condition of the work.

sections.heading: For apartments, investigate the scheme as well as the lot
sections.markdown:
An apartment purchase is partly a purchase of the lot and partly an exposure to common property, shared services and collective decision-making. Use the owners-corporation information in the Section 32 as the entry point, not the finish line. [Consumer Affairs Victoria](https://www.consumer.vic.gov.au/housing/owners-corporations/finance-insurance-and-record-keeping/records) notes that Section 32 statements can be prepared many months before sale and recommends asking for a new owners-corporation certificate before settlement or inspecting the register and records, so freshness matters.

**What to reconcile for an owners-corporation property**

| Evidence set | What to look for | Capital question |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Plan of subdivision | Lot boundaries, car park/storage, common property and lot liability/entitlement | What do you actually own and what costs are shared? |
| Certificate and fees | Current fees, arrears, insurance and prescribed information | Is the present contribution consistent with the building’s obligations? |
| Minutes and register | Water ingress, façade, fire safety, lifts, services, disputes, consultant reports and recurring complaints | Are known problems becoming future works or special levies? |
| Maintenance plan and budgets | Planned works, reserves, timing and funding | Is there enough money for the work already visible on the horizon? |
| Defect/consultant reports | Scope, severity, responsibility, remediation status and unresolved recommendations | What risk or expenditure remains after purchase? |

Continue with [how to read owners-corporation records](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/reading-your-owners-corporation-report).

sections.heading: What the Section 32 does not tell you
sections.markdown:
Consumer Affairs Victoria is unusually clear about the boundary: the Section 32 does not include information about **building condition, building-regulation compliance or the accuracy of title measurements**. Those exclusions should shape your next steps.

**Important questions that sit outside the Section 32 itself**

| Question | Why the Section 32 is not enough | Evidence to use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What condition is the roof in? | A permit, title or planning document does not assess current roof covering, flashings, drainage or leaks. | Building inspection and specialist roofing advice where warranted. |

sections.heading: Mismatch is often where the useful work begins
sections.markdown:
A mismatch is not proof of a defect or legal problem. It is a signal that two evidence sources do not yet reconcile. That is exactly where a buyer should slow down.

**High-value mismatches to resolve before commitment**

| Mismatch | Question it creates | Who may help resolve it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Visible extension or deck but no obvious permit trail | When was it built, under what approval pathway and is completion evidence available? | Conveyancer, council/building records, building professional. |
| Permit description does not match the current layout | Was the work changed, superseded or partly completed? | Council/building records, approved plans, physical inspection. |

sections.heading: A fast review before your conveyancer
sections.markdown:
1. **Confirm identity:** seller, address, title, lot and plan.
2. **Mark every encumbrance:** easement, covenant, mortgage, caveat or other restriction and where it matters physically.
3. **Write down the planning controls:** zone, overlays and any question they create for your intended use or work.
4. **Extract every notice and recent permit:** identify the underlying issue, required action, work description and available completion evidence.
5. **Reconcile recent work with the building:** extensions, decks, wet areas, structural openings, garages, sheds and service alterations.
6. **For an apartment, read the scheme as a second asset:** plan, certificate, minutes, budgets, funds, insurance, defects and future works.
7. **Create the physical-condition gap list:** roof, subfloor, drainage, cracking, moisture, pests, electrical, plumbing and inaccessible areas.
8. **Send the whole bundle with your questions:** a conveyancer can give sharper advice when the property-specific mismatches and intended use are explicit.

# How to read a Section 32 vendor's statement in Victoria

The seller must give the buyer a Section 32 vendor's statement before the buyer signs the contract. Start by confirming the seller, title, lot and plan, then work through financial matters, easements and covenants, planning controls, notices, building permits, owner-builder material, owners-corporation information, services and title evidence. The useful step is reconciliation: a permit can show that work was authorised, but not its present condition; an easement can show a legal right, but not how it affects the extension you want to build. Consumer Affairs Victoria expressly says a Section 32 does not tell you the condition of the buildings, whether they comply with building regulations or whether title measurements are accurate, so pair the legal bundle with physical inspection, survey, council or specialist evidence where the property raises those questions.

## Research note
Consumer Affairs Victoria says the seller must provide the Section 32 before the buyer signs and recommends legal review. The statement covers legal disclosure. Arrange a separate physical inspection for the building's condition. Read the [official Section 32 overview](https://www.consumer.vic.gov.au/housing/buying-and-selling-property/selling-property/conveyancing-and-contracts-for-sellers) alongside the contract.

## Opening
### Read the land, then inspect the building
- **Title:** Who owns it, and what the title lets or forbids
- **Planning:** What the zone and overlays will let you do
- **Outside the statement:** The roof, the damp, the pests: none of it is in here

_The statement covers the land. Someone still has to look at the house._

## Three documents, three different jobs
Section 32 of Victoria's [Sale of Land Act 1962](https://www.legislation.vic.gov.au/in-force/acts/sale-land-act-1962/173) requires prescribed information to be given to the buyer before the buyer signs the contract. [Consumer Affairs Victoria](https://www.consumer.vic.gov.au/housing/buying-and-selling-property/selling-property/conveyancing-and-contracts-for-sellers) describes the Section 32 as a legal document containing information about matters such as title, mortgages, covenants, easements, zoning and outgoings.

Keep three layers separate. The **Section 32** records prescribed facts about the land and transaction. The **contract** sets the terms of the deal. The **building inspection and other due diligence** investigate the physical property and questions outside the statutory statement. Reading them together is powerful; substituting one for another is not.

> Important: Consumer Affairs Victoria says the Section 32 does not include information about the condition of buildings, whether buildings comply with building regulations or whether measurements on the title are accurate. Those are separate due-diligence questions.

## Use sections 32A to 32I as the contents map
**A working map of the statutory disclosure structure**

| Act section | Evidence area | Buyer question |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 32A | Financial matters, including rates, taxes, charges and other prescribed liabilities | What is payable, is the information current, and how will amounts be adjusted or borne? |
| 32B | Insurance details required in specified circumstances, including vendor insurance where risk does not remain with the vendor and statutory insurance cover for relevant residential building work | Which circumstance applies, what policy or statutory cover exists, and does it reconcile with the work, risk allocation and sale? |
| 32C | Land-use matters including easements, covenants and planning information | Where does each control or restriction apply and what does it mean for current use or future work? |
| 32D | Notices, orders, declarations, reports and proposals affecting the land | What triggered the item, what action remains and who carries the responsibility or cost? |
| 32E | Particulars of building permits issued in the preceding seven years | Do the permits line up with the additions, renovations and structures you can actually see? |
| 32F | Owners-corporation certificate and prescribed information where applicable | What do scheme boundaries, fees, funds, insurance, defects, disputes and future works say together? |
| 32G | Growth Areas Infrastructure Contribution information where applicable | Is there a current or deferred liability affecting the land or transaction? |
| 32H | Whether prescribed services are connected | Does the documentary position match the services the property appears to use, and what remains unknown about their condition or capacity? |
| 32I | Evidence of the vendor’s title to the land | Do the vendor, title reference, lot and plan match the property being offered? |

The statutory labels help you navigate the bundle, but they are only the first pass. The second pass is to translate each legal fact into its **practical implication for this address**.

## Read the statement as evidence, not as conclusions
**What common Section 32 evidence can and cannot tell you**

| Evidence | What it can establish | What it cannot establish | What to do next |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Title and plan | The registered land, proprietor and interests shown on title | That fences, improvements and occupation align exactly with legal boundaries | Compare the plan with the site; raise discrepancies with the conveyancer and commission a survey where warranted. |
| Easement or covenant | A registered right or restriction affects the land | Whether your proposed extension, pool, driveway, drainage works or access strategy is acceptable | Locate it relative to the property and test the intended use or design against the legal restriction. |
| Planning zone or overlay | A planning control applies to the land | That a renovation, demolition, subdivision or change of use will be approved | Read the schedule/maps and obtain planning advice for the actual proposal. |
| Building permit particulars | A permit was issued for described work within the disclosure period | That the work was completed exactly as approved, is defect-free, meets every current requirement or remains in good condition | Ask for approved plans, occupancy/final evidence and compare them with the visible work and physical inspection. |
| Notice or order | A statutory or administrative issue has been recorded | That the cause is resolved or the required work has been completed satisfactorily | Obtain the underlying notice, response and completion evidence; inspect the affected area where physically relevant. |
| Service connection information | A prescribed service is recorded as connected or not connected | The age, capacity, safety, layout or condition of the service | Inspect or test the actual system where its age, performance or alteration matters. |
| Owners-corporation certificate | Prescribed scheme, fee, insurance and other information at a point in time | The complete history of common-property condition, defects, disputes or future capital demand | Read the register, recent minutes, budgets, maintenance plan, reports and proposed works as one evidence set. |

## Map title restrictions against the physical home
Do not leave easements, covenants and other encumbrances as abstract lines in a legal document. Map them against the house, garage, deck, pool, retaining walls, access, drainage and any extension you may want to build. A sewer easement under open lawn is a different practical problem from the same easement running beneath a structure. If the title plan is hard to reconcile with what stands on the land, ask the conveyancer whether a licensed surveyor or further title work is warranted.

**Title questions that become building questions**

| Document signal | Physical question | Possible consequence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Easement through a side or rear setback | Is an existing or proposed structure over or near it? | Access, consent, relocation or design constraints may affect future work. |
| Restrictive covenant | Does the existing use or proposed design conflict with the restriction? | The covenant may constrain development even if the site physically accommodates it. |
| Plan dimensions that do not feel consistent with fences or improvements | Are occupation and legal boundaries aligned? | Survey/legal clarification may be needed before relying on the apparent usable land. |
| Shared or unusual access arrangement | How is vehicle/pedestrian access physically used and maintained? | Rights, maintenance responsibility and practical access can all matter. |

## Planning controls tell you the rulebook, not the outcome
A zone establishes the broad planning framework. Overlays add controls for matters such as heritage, flooding, vegetation or bushfire. Their importance depends on the address and what you intend to do. An overlay is not automatically a defect or a reason not to buy; it is evidence that future work may need a different design, approval pathway, consultant input, material choice or budget. For the Victorian heritage pathway, continue with [living in a Heritage Overlay](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/living-in-a-heritage-overlay).

If renovation or redevelopment matters to the purchase decision, do not stop at the label shown in the Section 32. Read the relevant schedule and map, then test the actual proposal with the responsible authority or planning adviser.

## A building permit is evidence of process, not a condition report
Section 32E requires particulars of building permits issued in the preceding seven years. This is one of the most useful bridges between the legal bundle and the physical property because it lets you compare the documented work with what is actually visible.

**How to reconcile recent building work**

| Question | Evidence to seek | What remains a physical question |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What was approved? | Building permit particulars, approved drawings and specifications where available | Whether the visible work matches the documented scope. |
| Was the work completed? | Occupancy permit, certificate of final inspection or other applicable completion evidence | Whether finishes, waterproofing, drainage, structure and services remain sound today. |
| Who carried it out? | Builder/owner-builder records, contracts, invoices and insurance/warranty material where applicable | Quality of workmanship and any defects not apparent from paperwork. |
| Has it changed since approval? | Later permits, plans, photos and owner records | Whether subsequent alterations created new approval or condition questions. |

A permit is not proof that a bathroom is currently watertight, a deck has no decay, a roof alteration is leak-free or an extension has no movement. It is one piece of evidence in a chain.

## Owner-builder work deserves its own evidence chain
[Consumer Affairs Victoria says an owner builder selling within six years and six months of obtaining the Certificate of Final Inspection or Occupancy Permit must provide a defects inspection report that is no more than six months old](https://www.consumer.vic.gov.au/housing/building-and-renovating/checklists/owner-builders) for the relevant work, including extensions, renovations, garages and verandas. Victoria's domestic-building insurance framework changed on 1 July 2026. The [Building and Plumbing Commission](https://www.bpc.vic.gov.au/home-owners/insurance-for-domestic-building-work/domestic-building-insurance-and-home-warranty) explains that existing Domestic Building Insurance continues for earlier cover while Home Warranty applies to new eligible domestic building work under the post-1 July 2026 regime. The [BPC also says](https://www.bpc.vic.gov.au/owner-builders/what-is-an-owner-builder) an owner-builder who wishes to sell applicable owner-built work within six years of completion may need a Home Warranty Notice of Cover and premium. For a purchase, have the conveyancer identify the work, completion date, builder status, applicable defects report, insurance or warranty evidence and any transition issue, then compare that documentary chain with the physical condition of the work.

## For apartments, investigate the scheme as well as the lot
An apartment purchase is partly a purchase of the lot and partly an exposure to common property, shared services and collective decision-making. Use the owners-corporation information in the Section 32 as the entry point, not the finish line. [Consumer Affairs Victoria](https://www.consumer.vic.gov.au/housing/owners-corporations/finance-insurance-and-record-keeping/records) notes that Section 32 statements can be prepared many months before sale and recommends asking for a new owners-corporation certificate before settlement or inspecting the register and records, so freshness matters.

**What to reconcile for an owners-corporation property**

| Evidence set | What to look for | Capital question |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Plan of subdivision | Lot boundaries, car park/storage, common property and lot liability/entitlement | What do you actually own and what costs are shared? |
| Certificate and fees | Current fees, arrears, insurance and prescribed information | Is the present contribution consistent with the building’s obligations? |
| Minutes and register | Water ingress, façade, fire safety, lifts, services, disputes, consultant reports and recurring complaints | Are known problems becoming future works or special levies? |
| Maintenance plan and budgets | Planned works, reserves, timing and funding | Is there enough money for the work already visible on the horizon? |
| Defect/consultant reports | Scope, severity, responsibility, remediation status and unresolved recommendations | What risk or expenditure remains after purchase? |

Continue with [how to read owners-corporation records](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/reading-your-owners-corporation-report).

## What the Section 32 does not tell you
Consumer Affairs Victoria is unusually clear about the boundary: the Section 32 does not include information about **building condition, building-regulation compliance or the accuracy of title measurements**. Those exclusions should shape your next steps.

**Important questions that sit outside the Section 32 itself**

sections.heading: Opening
sections.markdown:
### Read it before you exchange
- **Read early:** Ask for the contract the day the listing appears
- **Change before exchange:** Anything you want changed, agree it before exchange
- **Inspect separately:** The building gets its own inspection, on its own merits

_Exchange is the moment it becomes real. Arrive ready._

sections.heading: Get the contract while there is still time to act
sections.markdown:
Ask for the complete current contract as soon as you are seriously interested. [NSW's sales-contract requirements](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/property-professionals/working-as-an-agent/sales-contracts) require a proposed residential sale contract to be available before marketing. Send the whole bundle, including special conditions and attachments, to your NSW solicitor or licensed conveyancer. A front page and an agent's assurance are not enough to assess what you would agree to.

Begin with your intended use. Tell the reviewer if you need vacant possession, want to extend, rely on a parking space or intend to use a converted garage as a bedroom. A restriction that is manageable for one buyer may defeat another buyer's reason for purchasing. That context helps turn a document review into specific questions and proposed contract changes.

sections.heading: Read the attachments against the property you inspected
sections.markdown:
The required bundle depends on the title and property. [The regulator's checklist](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/property-professionals/working-as-an-agent/sales-contracts) covers title, drainage, planning and relevant title dealings, together with prescribed notices and additional off-the-plan documents. Have the reviewer check the applicable requirements rather than treating this overview as an exhaustive attachment checklist.

**A document is useful when it answers a property question**

| Material | What it helps establish | What to cross-check |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Title search and deposited or strata plan | The legal parcel, registered interests and lot arrangement | Address, apartment, parking, storage and the property shown in the marketing. |
| Easement, covenant or restriction instrument | The terms behind a short title notation | Who benefits, where it applies and how it affects the intended use or works. |
| Section 10.7 planning certificate | Prescribed planning information about the land | Certificate date, relevant controls and whether further council information is needed. |
| Drainage and service diagrams | Recorded private drainage or authority assets, depending on the diagram | Actual buildings, later additions and any proposed extension or pool. |
| Special conditions and front-page particulars | The negotiated obligations and commercial terms | Deposit, settlement, possession, inclusions, exclusions and altered remedies. |
| Property-specific material | Pool, strata, off-the-plan or other applicable disclosures | Which documents and exceptions apply to this particular transaction. |

Match the identifiers throughout the bundle. A street address can be familiar while a lot number, parking title or plan tells a different story. If a fence, garage or driveway appears inconsistent with the plan, ask whether survey evidence is needed. Neither an aerial image nor a quick measurement on a sales floor plan settles a legal boundary.

sections.heading: Understand what the 10.7 certificate can establish
sections.markdown:
[Service NSW distinguishes the section 10.7(2) certificate from the combined (2) and (5) certificate](https://www.service.nsw.gov.au/transaction/apply-online-for-a-planning-certificate). The former provides prescribed planning controls and constraints; the combined certificate adds relevant council-held advice. Ask whether that additional information would help with the proposed use or a particular uncertainty.

Read a planning notation as a prompt for its consequence. A flood notation might lead to questions about levels, design constraints and insurance; a heritage control might change an extension proposal. The certificate does not inspect the house or establish that every existing room and alteration was approved. Where the purchase depends on an extension or secondary dwelling, seek planning advice about that proposal before assuming it can proceed.

sections.heading: Separate private drains, authority assets and title rights
sections.markdown:
[Sydney Water explains that a sewer service diagram records private wastewater pipes](https://www.sydneywater.com.au/accounts-billing/managing-your-account/buying-and-selling-a-property/certificates-documents-diagrams.html), while other documents address its assets and approval to build over or near them. Use the relevant water authority outside its area. A line on a drainage diagram and an easement on title answer related but different questions.

Put the existing and proposed footprint beside the appropriate diagrams. If a later bathroom or extension is absent from an older record, seek clarification and the relevant approvals; that discrepancy is a question, not proof of unlawful work. A diagram also does not establish pipe condition, present depth or an accurate excavation location. Those may require a plumber, authority advice and further investigation.

sections.heading: Give special conditions the same attention as attachments
sections.markdown:
Ask the reviewer to explain how the actual contract handles settlement timing, late completion, access, inclusions, vacant possession or a tenancy, and known defects or unapproved work. If a verbal promise matters, such as removing rubbish, repairing a leak or leaving a particular appliance, have the agreed obligation recorded appropriately. Check that any negotiated amendments appear in the version that will be exchanged.

Finance pre-approval and a deposit payment do not by themselves give you a right to withdraw if funding fails. Ask what finance or inspection protection is actually agreed, what triggers it and when it expires. With strata, have proposed or resolved levies and settlement adjustments examined alongside the [scheme records](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/buying-an-apartment-strata). A satisfactory apartment inspection does not answer that allocation question.

sections.heading: Know which clock applies before exchange
sections.markdown:
[NSW's contracts guidance](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/buying-and-selling-property/buying-property-nsw/contracts-and-deposits) describes the usual residential cooling-off period: five business days after exchange, ending at 5 pm on the fifth business day after the exchange day. Off-the-plan contracts generally have ten business days. Cooling off is unavailable at auction and for exchange on the same day after the property is passed in.

A 66W certificate can waive cooling off; written agreement can also change the period. If you withdraw using ordinary cooling-off rights, the usual forfeiture is 0.25% of the price. Ask your representative to confirm the actual deadline and notice requirements. Complete the checks you need before waiving protection; a signed certificate does not establish that the property, finance or inspections are satisfactory.

sections.heading: A disclosure problem needs its own legal assessment
sections.markdown:
The [regulator identifies a possible 14-day rescission right for missing required documents](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/property-professionals/working-as-an-agent/sales-contracts). This is a separate issue from cooling off. Do not assume that every unsatisfactory answer, later defect or vendor-warranty allegation falls within the same right or deadline. If something appears missing or inconsistent after exchange, contact your representative immediately to assess the applicable ground, evidence, timing and notice.

A practical approach before exchange is to list each unresolved matter, the document or answer needed, who is obtaining it and the decision it affects. Some questions can be resolved by a replacement attachment; others need contract negotiation, a specialist report or a decision about accepting uncertainty. A generic request for 'all approvals' is less useful than identifying the particular rear room or garage conversion you need explained.

sections.heading: Check condition and approval history separately
sections.markdown:
[NSW's inspection guidance](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/buying-and-selling-property/buying-property-nsw/inspecting-a-property/inspection-reports) explains the role and limits of pre-purchase reports. Commission the physical and specialist checks the property warrants, early enough to use the results. A contract attachment does not establish a dry roof, sound concealed frame or functioning waterproofing. Likewise, a neat renovation and a favourable visual inspection do not settle its approval history.

For later work, compare available approved drawings, consent conditions and completion documentation with what is visible. Keep documentary and physical findings separate in the decision record. A [desktop read](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/desktop-vs-physical-report) can organise those questions but cannot certify boundaries, legal rights or concealed condition. Before settlement, raise any material discrepancy found at the final inspection promptly with your representative.

sections.heading: Worked example: the advertised third bedroom
sections.markdown:
**Illustrative reasoning example, not an inspected property.** A house is advertised with three bedrooms. One is a converted garage, while the available drainage and planning papers do not explain the conversion. The room looks finished and dry. Those observations establish its current presentation, not its lawful use, structural scope or service history.

Tell the legal reviewer that using this room as a bedroom is central to the purchase. Seek the relevant approval records and have its physical condition assessed within an agreed scope. Depending on the results, the next step might be clarification, specialist advice or a negotiated term. Neither 'the contract exists' nor 'the inspector liked the room' resolves both questions.

> Important: NSW legal orientation only. Your solicitor or licensed conveyancer should review the actual contract, property-specific documents and any waiver before exchange. Use the [Victorian](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/reading-a-section-32) or [Queensland](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/seller-disclosure-qld) guide for those jurisdictions.

# Buying in NSW: how to read the contract for sale

Read the NSW sale contract as a combination of legal terms, title and property-specific disclosure. Match its documents to the property and your intended use, resolve important gaps before exchange, and confirm the applicable cooling-off or waiver position. Physical condition, approval history and strata funding need their own evidence alongside the legal review.

## Research note
Checked against [NSW's regulator guidance](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/property-professionals/working-as-an-agent/sales-contracts), with planning and water-authority sources linked where they inform a specific document question. Legal review remains property- and contract-specific.

## Opening

- **Read early:** Ask for the contract the day the listing appears
- **Change before exchange:** Anything you want changed, agree it before exchange
- **Inspect separately:** The building gets its own inspection, on its own merits

## Get the contract while there is still time to act

A restriction that is manageable for one buyer may defeat another buyer's reason for purchasing. That context helps turn a document review into specific questions and proposed contract changes.

## Read the attachments against the property you inspected

| Material | What it helps establish | What to cross-check |
| --- | --- | --- |

If a fence, garage or driveway appears inconsistent with the plan, ask whether survey evidence is needed. ## Understand what the 10.7 certificate can establish

## Separate private drains, authority assets and title rights

## Give special conditions the same attention as attachments

Check that any negotiated amendments appear in the version that will be exchanged.

Ask what finance or inspection protection is actually agreed, what triggers it and when it expires. With strata, have proposed or resolved levies and settlement adjustments examined alongside the [scheme records](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/buying-an-apartment-strata). A satisfactory apartment inspection does not answer that allocation question.

## Know which clock applies before exchange

A 66W certificate can waive cooling off; written agreement can also change the period. If you withdraw using ordinary cooling-off rights, the usual forfeiture is 0.25% of the price. Ask your representative to confirm the actual deadline and notice requirements. ## A disclosure problem needs its own legal assessment

## Check condition and approval history separately

Before settlement, raise any material discrepancy found at the final inspection promptly with your representative.

## Worked example: the advertised third bedroom
**Illustrative reasoning example, not an inspected property.** A house is advertised with three bedrooms. One is a converted garage, while the available drainage and planning papers do not explain the conversion. The room looks finished and dry. Those observations establish its current presentation, not its lawful use, structural scope or service history.

Tell the legal reviewer that using this room as a bedroom is central to the purchase. Seek the relevant approval records and have its physical condition assessed within an agreed scope. Depending on the results, the next step might be clarification, specialist advice or a negotiated term. Neither 'the contract exists' nor 'the inspector liked the room' resolves both questions.

> Important: NSW legal orientation only. Your solicitor or licensed conveyancer should review the actual contract, property-specific documents and any waiver before exchange. Use the [Victorian](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/reading-a-section-32) or [Queensland](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/seller-disclosure-qld) guide for those jurisdictions.

## Frequently asked questions
### What documents must be attached to a contract for sale in NSW?
The applicable bundle includes title, planning, drainage and relevant title dealings and notices. Strata, pools and off-the-plan sales can need additional material. Have your representative check the property-specific requirements against the complete contract.

### What is a section 10.7 certificate?
A council planning certificate containing prescribed controls and constraints affecting the land. A combined (2) and (5) certificate includes additional advice. It does not inspect the building or prove approval of every existing alteration.

### Is there a cooling-off period when buying in NSW?
Usually five business days after exchange for residential purchases, or ten for off-the-plan contracts. Auction and same-day post-pass-in purchases are excluded, and a waiver or written agreement may change the position. Confirm the actual deadline with your representative.

### What is a section 66W certificate?
A certificate used to waive cooling-off protection, given through the appropriate legal process. It does not confirm the building, finance or disclosure is satisfactory. Obtain advice before providing it.

### Can I get out if disclosure documents are missing?
Missing required documents may create a 14-day rescission right. Its applicability, notice requirements and other potential rights need immediate legal assessment. Do not treat all disclosure or warranty problems as one rule.

### Does the contract tell me the building is sound?
No. Contract review, physical inspection and approval-history enquiries answer different questions. Use the findings together before committing.

### Does the sewer diagram prove an extension was approved?
No. Compare the appropriate drainage records with building and authority approvals. A diagram has a particular purpose and may not reflect later changes or current pipe condition.

### Should I rely on an agent’s promise about repairs?
Ask your representative to record any material agreed obligation in the contract and confirm it appears in the exchanged version.

### What should I ask if the purchase depends on a future extension?
Ask a planning professional about the intended proposal and have title restrictions, services and relevant controls reviewed. Existing zoning alone does not guarantee that design will be approved.

## Method
We read the contract through the buyer’s intended use, distinguish documentary disclosure from physical evidence and keep cooling-off and disclosure remedies separate.

## Limitations
This is NSW legal orientation. A licensed conveyancer or Australian legal practitioner should review amendments and certificates.

guides.question: What does Queensland's seller disclosure statement (Form 2) include?
guides.title: Queensland seller disclosure: how to read the Form 2
guides.summary: Queensland Form 2 puts prescribed facts about the property on the table before you sign. The useful work is understanding what those facts establish, what they leave unanswered and which building, flood, approval or body-corporate checks should follow.
guides.answer: Queensland's seller disclosure scheme applies to relevant contracts entered into from 1 August 2025. In most covered sales, the seller must give the buyer a completed Form 2 and the prescribed certificates that apply before the buyer signs; auctions have separate make-available rules before the hammer falls. Read the bundle as evidence, not as a complete property report: it can establish title, encumbrances, planning and specified notices, but Queensland Government guidance expressly says structural soundness, flooding history and previous building or development approvals are not generally required disclosures. Reconcile what the documents say with the actual property, then commission the checks that close the remaining gaps.
guides.methodology: Built from the Queensland Government’s own scheme guide and its current cooling-off guidance, written while the scheme is still new enough to surprise people.
guides.limitations: This is Queensland legal orientation. Whether a defective Form 2 lets you out depends on the Act, the defect and your circumstances, which is exactly the question for your solicitor.
guides.researchNote: Queensland's scheme applies to contracts entered from 1 August 2025. The official guide explains delivery timing, prescribed certificates, exclusions, the over-$10 million waiver and the buyer's conditional termination right: read the [seller disclosure scheme](https://www.qld.gov.au/housing/buying-owning-home/seller-disclosure-scheme) before relying on a Form 2.

sections.heading: Opening
sections.markdown:
### What the disclosure gives you
- **Statement:** What the seller must now tell you, in the approved form
- **Certificates:** Title, plan and the prescribed paperwork behind it
- **Buyer checks:** Condition, pests and flood are still yours to check

_A wrong Form 2 may open an exit. The statutory test decides._

sections.heading: The scheme in one page
sections.markdown:
Queensland's [Property Law Act 2023](https://www.legislation.qld.gov.au/view/whole/html/inforce/current/act-2023-027) introduced a mandatory pre-contract seller disclosure system from 1 August 2025. The [Queensland Government seller disclosure guide](https://www.qld.gov.au/housing/buying-owning-home/seller-disclosure-scheme) applies across many sales of houses, townhouses, units, commercial property and vacant land, subject to statutory exceptions. For a covered private sale, the seller must give the buyer the approved disclosure statement and applicable prescribed certificates before the buyer signs.

Think of the transaction as several evidence layers doing different jobs. The **contract** records the bargain. The **Form 2 and certificates** disclose prescribed legal and property information. A **building and pest inspection** investigates accessible physical condition. Flood, planning, approval, survey and specialist searches answer other questions. One layer should not be mistaken for another.

> Important: A completed Form 2 is not a certificate that the house is sound, flood-free, approved, compliant or free of concealed defects. It is a statutory disclosure document with a defined scope.

sections.heading: What is actually in the disclosure bundle
sections.markdown:
**Read the Form 2 and prescribed certificates as an evidence set**

| Evidence area | What you may receive or see | What to establish |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Property identity | Seller name, property address, lot and plan details | That the legal parcel, marketed property and contract all refer to the same land. |
| Title | Current title search and registered interests | Ownership and registered rights, restrictions, mortgages or other interests affecting the lot. |
| Plan | Registered survey plan | The legal parcel shape and plan reference; compare it with access, structures and the way the property is being used. |
| Encumbrances | Registered, unregistered and statutory encumbrance information required by the scheme | What rights or restrictions affect use, access, services or future works, and whether further documents are needed to understand them. |
| Occupation | Required tenancy or rooming-accommodation information where applicable | Whether occupation, possession and settlement expectations align. |
| Planning and environment | Zoning, specified transport/resumption notices, contaminated-land status, tree matters and heritage information | Whether a control, notice or register entry changes intended use, future work, cost or risk. |
| Buildings and structures | Pool information and specified notices under building, planning or related legislation | Whether a statutory issue, notice, certification requirement or continuing obligation needs investigation. |
| Community title | Community management statement and body-corporate certificate where prescribed | The scheme structure, by-laws, financial position, insurance and matters that should be checked in the broader body-corporate records. |

The [Property Law Regulation 2024](https://www.legislation.qld.gov.au/view/whole/html/inforce/current/sl-2024-0211) prescribes documents that can include a title search, registered survey plan and, where applicable, other notices and certificates. The Queensland Government's public summary also identifies pool-safety material and community-title documents among the certificates that may apply. The exact bundle depends on the property.

sections.heading: Read every fact twice: what it proves and what it does not
sections.markdown:
**The evidence-to-building bridge**

| Disclosure evidence | What it can establish | What it does not establish | Useful next question |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Title and plan | The registered parcel and interests shown on title | That fences, sheds, additions, driveways or services sit exactly where you assume | Does the legal plan reconcile with what is physically on the land, or is survey/legal clarification warranted? |
| Easement or other encumbrance | A legal right or restriction exists | Its practical effect on a proposed extension, pool, retaining wall, access route or drainage solution | Where does it sit relative to the building and intended works, and what consent or design constraint follows? |
| Zoning or heritage information | A planning control applies | That a proposed renovation is permitted, simple or inexpensive | Which overlays, schedules, local provisions or approvals control the work you have in mind? |
| Building or planning notice | A formal notice or statutory issue exists or has been issued | That the underlying physical issue is resolved or that the current building is satisfactory | What triggered the notice, what work was required, what evidence shows completion and what condition remains today? |
| Pool information or certificate | Specified pool-safety information is available | The broader condition of the pool, shell, equipment, paving, drainage or surrounding structures | Is there separate maintenance, structural or equipment expenditure to investigate? |
| Body-corporate certificate | Prescribed scheme and financial information at a point in time | The full history of defects, disputes, water ingress, maintenance decisions or future capital work | What do minutes, budgets, insurance, maintenance plans, reports and proposed levies show when read together? |

This is the central discipline: **do not turn the existence of a document into a conclusion the document does not support**. A permit is evidence of a permit. A title is evidence of registered title. A body-corporate certificate is evidence of prescribed scheme information. The physical building still needs its own evidence.

sections.heading: The condition gaps are deliberate
sections.markdown:
Queensland Government guidance expressly says the general disclosure requirements do not require the seller to include **structural soundness of the building, flooding history or previous building or development approvals**. Those omissions are not small print; for a buyer they define some of the most important work that still remains after the Form 2 arrives.

**What the Form 2 does not replace**

| Question left open | Why it matters | Evidence that can close the gap |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Is the building structurally sound? | Cracking, movement, footing performance and structural alterations can carry large cost and safety consequences. | Qualified building inspection; structural engineer where signs, history or proposed work justify it. |
| Is there termite or timber-pest activity? | Damage can be concealed and may affect framing, floors, roofs and external timber. | Qualified timber-pest inspection and targeted invasive investigation where recommended. |
| Is there moisture or waterproofing failure? | Leaks, damp and failed wet-area systems can create concealed damage and recurring repair costs. | Building inspection, moisture investigation and specialist assessment where evidence warrants it. |
| Has the property flooded? | Past flooding can affect future risk, insurance, resilience work and buyer tolerance. | Council/state hazard mapping, historical records, insurer enquiries and property-specific flood investigation. |
| Were additions or renovations approved? | A visually finished extension, deck, enclosure, retaining wall or wet area may still have approval or completion gaps. | Council/building approval search, permits, approved plans, final certificates and comparison with what exists. |
| Are services safe and serviceable? | Electrical, plumbing, drainage, hot-water and other systems can be old or altered without being described by disclosure. | Inspection, compliance records and licensed trade assessment where age, condition or alteration warrants it. |
| What is concealed or inaccessible? | Roofs, subfloors, wall cavities and covered finishes can hide defects. | Access-based inspection, specialist tests and explicit acceptance of residual uncertainty where access is impossible. |
| What will the home cost to own? | Legal disclosure does not produce a maintenance or capital forecast. | Condition evidence, component age, likely interventions, cost allowances and a longer-term ownership view. |

sections.heading: Reconcile the paperwork with the property you can see
sections.markdown:
The most useful questions often come from **mismatches**. Compare the Form 2, plan, title, listing photographs, floor plan, street imagery and inspection evidence. A mismatch does not prove wrongdoing or defect; it tells you where another piece of evidence is needed.

**Common mismatch patterns and what they should trigger**

| What you notice | Why the mismatch matters | Next evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The house has a rear extension, enclosed patio or large deck that is hard to reconcile with available records | The visible building may have changed materially from the documentary picture. | Approval history, plans, final/completion evidence and physical inspection of the altered area. |
| A driveway, shed, pool or retaining wall appears close to an easement or boundary | Legal rights and physical improvements may interact. | Plan/title review, survey if warranted, relevant approvals and legal advice on the encumbrance. |
| Marketing describes a bedroom, studio or self-contained area not obvious in records | Use, approval, services, fire separation or habitability questions may arise. | Council/approval search, approved plans and physical inspection. |
| There is evidence of recent repair but no clear explanation of the cause | A cosmetic repair can hide a recurring moisture, movement or maintenance issue. | Invoices, reports, before/after photos, warranty information and targeted inspection. |
| The disclosure identifies a notice or environmental/planning issue | The legal fact may have a direct cost, use or capital implication. | Obtain the underlying notice/report, identify required action, responsibility, timing and evidence of any completed work. |

sections.heading: For units, the scheme is a second property to investigate
sections.markdown:
For a unit or townhouse in a community titles scheme, do not stop at the body-corporate certificate. Read it as the doorway into a second asset: the shared building and common property. Reconcile the community management statement and certificate with minutes, budgets, sinking or capital funds, insurance, maintenance records, defect reports, disputes, planned works and proposed special levies. A financially healthy lot can still sit inside a building facing major common-property work, and a physically sound apartment can still carry scheme-level financial exposure.

Continue with [buying an apartment or strata property](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/buying-an-apartment-strata) and treat common-property condition, governance and money as one combined question.

sections.heading: Auction delivery is different
sections.markdown: For a sale by auction, the Queensland Government says the disclosure statement and prescribed certificates must be given or made available before the fall of the hammer. Do not confuse availability with adequate review time. Obtain the bundle early, have legal questions resolved before bidding and complete the physical and hazard checks that matter to your decision. Cooling-off is generally unavailable after a successful auction bid.

sections.heading: Exceptions do not make the evidence problem disappear
sections.markdown: The scheme contains statutory exceptions, including specified government or corporate buyers, related parties and particular statutory sales. The Queensland Government summary also describes an exception for a sale price over $10 million where the buyer waives disclosure. If an exception or waiver is said to apply, have the transaction's solicitor confirm the legal position. From a due-diligence perspective, less mandatory disclosure means the buyer may need to obtain more information independently, not less.

sections.heading: When a disclosure problem may affect the contract
sections.markdown:
The Queensland Government says a buyer may have a right to terminate before settlement where required disclosure was not given or was inaccurate or incomplete. For inaccurate or incomplete information, the published test includes materiality, the buyer's lack of prior knowledge and whether the buyer would have signed had the truth been known. The interaction with other legislation can change the consequence.

> Important: Do not use a guide or an AI summary to decide whether to terminate a contract. Delivery, timing, materiality, prior knowledge, statutory interaction and the contract facts matter. Have a Queensland solicitor assess the actual documents and circumstances immediately.

sections.heading: A practical buyer workflow
sections.markdown:
1. **Collect the whole transaction set:** Form 2, prescribed certificates, contract, title, plan and any listing or agent material you relied on.
2. **Confirm identity first:** seller, address, lot, plan and the land actually being marketed.
3. **Map rights and controls:** encumbrances, planning, heritage, notices, environmental entries, community-title obligations and any use restriction.
4. **Compare documents with the visible property:** extensions, decks, pools, sheds, retaining walls, access, services and signs of recent work or repair.
5. **Write a gap list:** structure, pests, moisture, flood, approval history, services, boundaries, common-property condition and anything concealed or inaccessible.
6. **Assign each gap to the right evidence source:** conveyancer/solicitor, council, surveyor, building inspector, engineer, pest inspector, body corporate, insurer or another specialist.
7. **Resolve mismatches before commitment where possible:** especially before an auction, an unconditional contract or expiry of a contractual due-diligence right.
8. **Keep the evidence together:** the value is not in any single document but in the reconciled picture they create of the property.
