# Queensland seller disclosure: how to read the Form 2

Queensland's seller disclosure scheme applies to relevant contracts entered into from 1 August 2025. In most covered sales, the seller must give the buyer a completed Form 2 and the prescribed certificates that apply before the buyer signs; auctions have separate make-available rules before the hammer falls. Read the bundle as evidence, not as a complete property report: it can establish title, encumbrances, planning and specified notices, but Queensland Government guidance expressly says structural soundness, flooding history and previous building or development approvals are not generally required disclosures. Reconcile what the documents say with the actual property, then commission the checks that close the remaining gaps.

## Research note
Queensland's scheme applies to contracts entered from 1 August 2025. The official guide explains delivery timing, prescribed certificates, exclusions, the over-$10 million waiver and the buyer's conditional termination right: read the [seller disclosure scheme](https://www.qld.gov.au/housing/buying-owning-home/seller-disclosure-scheme) before relying on a Form 2.

## Opening
### What the disclosure gives you
- **Statement:** What the seller must now tell you, in the approved form
- **Certificates:** Title, plan and the prescribed paperwork behind it
- **Buyer checks:** Condition, pests and flood are still yours to check

_A wrong Form 2 may open an exit. The statutory test decides._

## The scheme in one page
Queensland's [Property Law Act 2023](https://www.legislation.qld.gov.au/view/whole/html/inforce/current/act-2023-027) introduced a mandatory pre-contract seller disclosure system from 1 August 2025. The [Queensland Government seller disclosure guide](https://www.qld.gov.au/housing/buying-owning-home/seller-disclosure-scheme) applies across many sales of houses, townhouses, units, commercial property and vacant land, subject to statutory exceptions. For a covered private sale, the seller must give the buyer the approved disclosure statement and applicable prescribed certificates before the buyer signs.

Think of the transaction as several evidence layers doing different jobs. The **contract** records the bargain. The **Form 2 and certificates** disclose prescribed legal and property information. A **building and pest inspection** investigates accessible physical condition. Flood, planning, approval, survey and specialist searches answer other questions. One layer should not be mistaken for another.

> Important: A completed Form 2 is not a certificate that the house is sound, flood-free, approved, compliant or free of concealed defects. It is a statutory disclosure document with a defined scope.

## What is actually in the disclosure bundle
**Read the Form 2 and prescribed certificates as an evidence set**

| Evidence area | What you may receive or see | What to establish |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Property identity | Seller name, property address, lot and plan details | That the legal parcel, marketed property and contract all refer to the same land. |
| Title | Current title search and registered interests | Ownership and registered rights, restrictions, mortgages or other interests affecting the lot. |
| Plan | Registered survey plan | The legal parcel shape and plan reference; compare it with access, structures and the way the property is being used. |
| Encumbrances | Registered, unregistered and statutory encumbrance information required by the scheme | What rights or restrictions affect use, access, services or future works, and whether further documents are needed to understand them. |
| Occupation | Required tenancy or rooming-accommodation information where applicable | Whether occupation, possession and settlement expectations align. |
| Planning and environment | Zoning, specified transport/resumption notices, contaminated-land status, tree matters and heritage information | Whether a control, notice or register entry changes intended use, future work, cost or risk. |
| Buildings and structures | Pool information and specified notices under building, planning or related legislation | Whether a statutory issue, notice, certification requirement or continuing obligation needs investigation. |
| Community title | Community management statement and body-corporate certificate where prescribed | The scheme structure, by-laws, financial position, insurance and matters that should be checked in the broader body-corporate records. |

The [Property Law Regulation 2024](https://www.legislation.qld.gov.au/view/whole/html/inforce/current/sl-2024-0211) prescribes documents that can include a title search, registered survey plan and, where applicable, other notices and certificates. ## Read every fact twice: what it proves and what it does not
**The evidence-to-building bridge**

| Disclosure evidence | What it can establish | What it does not establish | Useful next question |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Title and plan | The registered parcel and interests shown on title | That fences, sheds, additions, driveways or services sit exactly where you assume | Does the legal plan reconcile with what is physically on the land, or is survey/legal clarification warranted? |

| Zoning or heritage information | A planning control applies | That a proposed renovation is permitted, simple or inexpensive | Which overlays, schedules, local provisions or approvals control the work you have in mind? |
| Building or planning notice | A formal notice or statutory issue exists or has been issued | That the underlying physical issue is resolved or that the current building is satisfactory | What triggered the notice, what work was required, what evidence shows completion and what condition remains today? |
| Pool information or certificate | Specified pool-safety information is available | The broader condition of the pool, shell, equipment, paving, drainage or surrounding structures | Is there separate maintenance, structural or equipment expenditure to investigate? |
| Body-corporate certificate | Prescribed scheme and financial information at a point in time | The full history of defects, disputes, water ingress, maintenance decisions or future capital work | What do minutes, budgets, insurance, maintenance plans, reports and proposed levies show when read together? |

| What is concealed or inaccessible? | Roofs, subfloors, wall cavities and covered finishes can hide defects. | Access-based inspection, specialist tests and explicit acceptance of residual uncertainty where access is impossible. |

## Reconcile the paperwork with the property you can see

| A driveway, shed, pool or retaining wall appears close to an easement or boundary | Legal rights and physical improvements may interact. | Plan/title review, survey if warranted, relevant approvals and legal advice on the encumbrance. |
| Marketing describes a bedroom, studio or self-contained area not obvious in records | Use, approval, services, fire separation or habitability questions may arise. | Council/approval search, approved plans and physical inspection. |
| There is evidence of recent repair but no clear explanation of the cause | A cosmetic repair can hide a recurring moisture, movement or maintenance issue. | Invoices, reports, before/after photos, warranty information and targeted inspection. |
| The disclosure identifies a notice or environmental/planning issue | The legal fact may have a direct cost, use or capital implication. | Obtain the underlying notice/report, identify required action, responsibility, timing and evidence of any completed work. |

## For units, the scheme is a second property to investigate
For a unit or townhouse in a community titles scheme, do not stop at the body-corporate certificate. Read it as the doorway into a second asset: the shared building and common property. Reconcile the community management statement and certificate with minutes, budgets, sinking or capital funds, insurance, maintenance records, defect reports, disputes, planned works and proposed special levies. Continue with [buying an apartment or strata property](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/buying-an-apartment-strata) and treat common-property condition, governance and money as one combined question.

## Auction delivery is different
For a sale by auction, the Queensland Government says the disclosure statement and prescribed certificates must be given or made available before the fall of the hammer. Do not confuse availability with adequate review time. Obtain the bundle early, have legal questions resolved before bidding and complete the physical and hazard checks that matter to your decision. If an exception or waiver is said to apply, have the transaction's solicitor confirm the legal position. From a due-diligence perspective, less mandatory disclosure means the buyer may need to obtain more information independently, not less.

## A practical buyer workflow
1. **Collect the whole transaction set:** Form 2, prescribed certificates, contract, title, plan and any listing or agent material you relied on.
2. **Confirm identity first:** seller, address, lot, plan and the land actually being marketed.
3. **Map rights and controls:** encumbrances, planning, heritage, notices, environmental entries, community-title obligations and any use restriction.

guides.question: Is a building inspection worth it before auction?
guides.title: Is a building inspection worth it before auction?
guides.summary: If the condition of the home could change your bid, inspect it before auction day. You need enough time to understand the report, ask questions and follow up anything serious.
guides.answer: Arrange an inspection whenever the condition of the building could change your decision or maximum bid. Do it early enough to understand the important findings and any areas the inspector could not reach. # Is a building inspection worth it before auction?

Arrange an inspection whenever the condition of the building could change your decision or maximum bid. Do it early enough to understand the important findings and any areas the inspector could not reach. If the seller supplies a report, check who commissioned it, when it was done, what was accessed, whether the inspector carries professional indemnity insurance and whether you have a right to rely on it.

## Research note
[Victorian buyer guidance](https://www.consumer.vic.gov.au/housing/buying-and-selling-property/buying-property/inspect-properties-before-you-buy) supports professional inspection before signing; [NSW auction guidance](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/buying-and-selling-property/buying-property-nsw/buying-property-at-an-auction) explains its cooling-off exclusion. ## Opening

- **Scope:** What was assessed and what remains inaccessible

- **Follow-up:** Resolve material questions with the appropriate professional before commitment

A [desktop review](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/desktop-vs-physical-report) may help organise the shortlist where the available evidence warrants it; it is an optional service, not a prerequisite or a substitute for necessary investigation.

## Work backwards from the decision, not the report delivery

> Note: Keep the report with later repairs, monitoring and photographs. That record helps the next property decision start from current evidence.

> Important: Complete the full auction plan: contract review, agreed changes, property-specific finance, deposit arrangements and a hard limit. Use [auction-day due diligence](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/auction-day-due-diligence) as the checklist.

## Frequently asked questions
### Is a building inspection worth it before auction?
Usually, yes, if the condition of the building could change your bid. The report gives you findings to act on, shows which areas could not be reached and leaves time for specialist advice before the contract becomes binding.

### Can I get out of an auction purchase if the building has problems?
Auction sales are generally unconditional and cooling-off is usually unavailable. Complete inspection and contract checks before bidding.

### What does a building and pest inspection cover?
It is a visual, non-invasive assessment of the agreed accessible areas and timber-pest scope. The report should record concealed and inaccessible areas as limitations.

### When should I book the inspection before an auction?
As soon as the property becomes serious, leaving time to read the report, clarify limitations and obtain specialist follow-up before bidding.

### Should I trust the building report the agent gives me?
Check date, scope, access, qualifications, insurance and your contractual right to rely on it. Commission more work where those answers leave material gaps.

### How do I reduce inspection spend on properties I may not win?
Check the property, likely price, intended use and existing evidence before commissioning further work. A desktop review may help organise a shortlist, but it is optional. An inspection that supports a decision not to buy still has value.

### Is a report delivered the night before auction early enough?

## Method

## Limitations

guides.summary: Dated provider prices give a starting point. Compare the tax basis, property scope, report and follow-up before deciding what the inspection will actually cost.

Obtain an address-specific total and check access, timber-pest scope, written reporting and follow-up.

guides.limitations: Every quote reflects a particular property, access and scope. Use the examples as bearings, then get the current inclusions, insurance and timing in writing.

### What the inspection fee includes
- **Access:** Does the fee cover the roof space, the subfloor, the sheds?
- **Report:** Building and timber pests, in writing, with photos, on time
- **Assurance:** Qualified, insured, and answering the phone afterwards

_A low fee can reflect a narrow job._

sections.markdown:
Four provider price pages were checked on 7 September 2026. The Adelaide price page could not be reconfirmed, so that earlier observation is identified separately. Treat each figure as a dated offer for a particular service, not a guaranteed quote for your property.

**Named provider examples, with check dates and scope limits**

| City | Published example | Scope and check status |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sydney | [$655 including GST](https://csibuilding.com.au/prices/) | CSI combined building and pest price; checked 7 September 2026 |
| Melbourne | [$500 plus GST](https://buildinginspectorsmelbourne.au/pricing/) | Residential house building and pest; checked 7 September 2026 |
| Brisbane | [$500 plus GST](https://buildingandpestinspectorsbrisbane.com.au/pricing/) | Residential house building and pest; checked 7 September 2026 |
| Adelaide | [$580 plus GST, historical only](https://aejbuildinginspections.com.au/prices/) | July 19 observation retained for context; page unavailable for verification on 7 September. Obtain a current quote. |
| Perth | [$499 plus GST](https://pierus.com.au/services/) | Combined inspection up to 4 bedrooms / 2 bathrooms; extra-fee items listed; checked 7 September 2026 |

Ask for the fee at your actual address, because almost everything about a house can move it: the size, the storeys, the subfloor, the roof voids, the sheds, the age, the drive to get there, and how urgently you need the answer.

The [NSW Government advises buyers to check qualifications, professional indemnity insurance and report inclusions](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/buying-and-selling-property/buying-property-nsw/inspecting-a-property/inspection-reports).

sections.heading: The quote decoder
sections.markdown:
**Ask every inspector to answer the same fields**

| Field | What to ask | Why the answer changes value |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Commissioning and reliance | Is the report addressed to me, and may I rely on it? | Reliance rights depend on the engagement terms |
| Building scope | Which structures and areas are included? | Garage, outbuildings, retaining walls, balconies and site may be excluded or limited |
| Timber-pest scope | Is a separate timber-pest inspection included, and to what scope? | Pest assessment needs an explicit scope |
| Access | Roof exterior, roof space, subfloor and restricted rooms, what is safely accessible? | Inaccessible areas remain blind spots |
| Methods | Visual inspection plus which meters or tools, used for what defined purpose? | Tools need access and defined interpretation |
| Report | Written report, photographs, significant items, limitations and delivery time? | A written report creates the decision record |
| Professional standing | Relevant qualification, state registration if applicable and professional indemnity insurance? | Requirements vary by state; insurance and competence need verification |
| Follow-up | Can I speak with the inspector, and is a reinspection available? | Clarification and changed access can matter before commitment |

sections.heading: What moves the quote
sections.markdown:
- **Property form and size:** apartment lot, freestanding house, multi-level home, acreage, ancillary structures.
- **Access and safety:** low subfloor, roof pitch, locked or stored areas, height, confined spaces and weather.
- **Construction complexity:** mixed eras, additions, retaining structures, balconies, unusual materials or multiple roof voids.
- **Scope:** building only, timber pests, pool, invasive testing, specialist diagnostics or strata records are separate questions.
- **Timing and travel:** urgent auction turnaround, remote call-out, return visit and report deadline.

The quote should reflect the actual accessible scope. For apartments, combine the lot inspection with a [strata or owners-corporation records inspection](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/reading-your-owners-corporation-report).

sections.heading: Understand the inspection limits
sections.markdown:
A conventional pre-purchase inspection is generally visual and non-invasive within the agreed scope and safe access. It does not ordinarily remove fixed finishes or establish every concealed condition. Service testing, compliance questions and repair pricing need explicit scope. Read the report’s limitations and the question behind any recommendation for further work.

Ask the inspector to name the agreed Australian Standard and scope in the engagement, then check that the report matches it. Standards documents themselves may require paid access.

sections.heading: Vendor reports: test the rights as well as the content
sections.markdown: For a vendor-supplied report, check its date, scope, access, commissioning party, inspector, professional indemnity insurance and purchaser-reliance or assignment terms. Commission your own inspection or specialist advice when reliance is absent, key areas were inaccessible or your concern sits outside scope.

sections.heading: Allow for specialist follow-up
sections.markdown: A good inspector states the limits of their scope clearly. Structural movement goes to an engineer, wiring to a licensed electrician, drainage to a plumber, suspect materials to a competent assessor, and air-quality questions to a defined indoor-environment scope. Leave time before the auction or the cooling-off deadline for that follow-up to happen.

sections.heading: Choose the inspector you can rely on

# Building and pest inspection cost in Australia: 2026 examples

Provider prices checked on 7 September 2026 were $499 plus GST in Perth, $500 plus GST in Melbourne and Brisbane, and $655 including GST in Sydney. These are individual service examples, not city averages. The earlier Adelaide example was not reconfirmed. Obtain an address-specific total and check access, timber-pest scope, written reporting and follow-up.

## Research note
Four provider pages were checked on 7 September 2026; the Adelaide July observation is explicitly historical because its pricing page could not be reconfirmed. Provider advertising supports prices and stated inclusions only. The fictional quotation example demonstrates arithmetic and scope, not an average market fee.

## Opening
### What the inspection fee includes
- **Access:** Does the fee cover the roof space, the subfloor, the sheds?
- **Report:** Building and timber pests, in writing, with photos, on time
- **Assurance:** Qualified, insured, and answering the phone afterwards

_A low fee can reflect a narrow job._

## Published price examples from five cities
Four provider price pages were checked on 7 September 2026. The Adelaide price page could not be reconfirmed, so that earlier observation is identified separately. Treat each figure as a dated offer for a particular service, not a guaranteed quote for your property.

**Named provider examples, with check dates and scope limits**

| City | Published example | Scope and check status |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sydney | [$655 including GST](https://csibuilding.com.au/prices/) | CSI combined building and pest price; checked 7 September 2026 |
| Melbourne | [$500 plus GST](https://buildinginspectorsmelbourne.au/pricing/) | Residential house building and pest; checked 7 September 2026 |
| Brisbane | [$500 plus GST](https://buildingandpestinspectorsbrisbane.com.au/pricing/) | Residential house building and pest; checked 7 September 2026 |
| Adelaide | [$580 plus GST, historical only](https://aejbuildinginspections.com.au/prices/) | July 19 observation retained for context; page unavailable for verification on 7 September. Obtain a current quote. |
| Perth | [$499 plus GST](https://pierus.com.au/services/) | Combined inspection up to 4 bedrooms / 2 bathrooms; extra-fee items listed; checked 7 September 2026 |

Ask for the fee at your actual address, because almost everything about a house can move it: the size, the storeys, the subfloor, the roof voids, the sheds, the age, the drive to get there, and how urgently you need the answer.

The [NSW Government advises buyers to check qualifications, professional indemnity insurance and report inclusions](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/buying-and-selling-property/buying-property-nsw/inspecting-a-property/inspection-reports).

## The quote decoder
**Ask every inspector to answer the same fields**

| Field | What to ask | Why the answer changes value |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Commissioning and reliance | Is the report addressed to me, and may I rely on it? | Reliance rights depend on the engagement terms |
| Building scope | Which structures and areas are included? | Garage, outbuildings, retaining walls, balconies and site may be excluded or limited |
| Timber-pest scope | Is a separate timber-pest inspection included, and to what scope? | Pest assessment needs an explicit scope |
| Access | Roof exterior, roof space, subfloor and restricted rooms, what is safely accessible? | Inaccessible areas remain blind spots |
| Methods | Visual inspection plus which meters or tools, used for what defined purpose? | Tools need access and defined interpretation |
| Report | Written report, photographs, significant items, limitations and delivery time? | A written report creates the decision record |
| Professional standing | Relevant qualification, state registration if applicable and professional indemnity insurance? | Requirements vary by state; insurance and competence need verification |
| Follow-up | Can I speak with the inspector, and is a reinspection available? | Clarification and changed access can matter before commitment |

## What moves the quote
- **Property form and size:** apartment lot, freestanding house, multi-level home, acreage, ancillary structures.
- **Access and safety:** low subfloor, roof pitch, locked or stored areas, height, confined spaces and weather.
- **Construction complexity:** mixed eras, additions, retaining structures, balconies, unusual materials or multiple roof voids.
- **Scope:** building only, timber pests, pool, invasive testing, specialist diagnostics or strata records are separate questions.
- **Timing and travel:** urgent auction turnaround, remote call-out, return visit and report deadline.

The quote should reflect the actual accessible scope. For apartments, combine the lot inspection with a [strata or owners-corporation records inspection](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/reading-your-owners-corporation-report).

## Understand the inspection limits
A conventional pre-purchase inspection is generally visual and non-invasive within the agreed scope and safe access. It does not ordinarily remove fixed finishes or establish every concealed condition. Service testing, compliance questions and repair pricing need explicit scope. Read the report’s limitations and the question behind any recommendation for further work.

Ask the inspector to name the agreed Australian Standard and scope in the engagement, then check that the report matches it. Standards documents themselves may require paid access.

## Vendor reports: test the rights as well as the content
For a vendor-supplied report, check its date, scope, access, commissioning party, inspector, professional indemnity insurance and purchaser-reliance or assignment terms. Commission your own inspection or specialist advice when reliance is absent, key areas were inaccessible or your concern sits outside scope.

## Allow for specialist follow-up
A good inspector states the limits of their scope clearly. Structural movement goes to an engineer, wiring to a licensed electrician, drainage to a plumber, suspect materials to a competent assessor, and air-quality questions to a defined indoor-environment scope. Leave time before the auction or the cooling-off deadline for that follow-up to happen.

## Choose the inspector you can rely on
A clear scope, good access and a useful conversation after the report can be worth far more than a small saving on the fee. Write down any blind spots before you commit. For an auction, use the [five-gate due-diligence plan](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/auction-day-due-diligence); for early triage, read about [desktop and physical report scopes](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/desktop-vs-physical-report).

## Put every quote on the same payment basis
Compare the total payable for the same service before comparing the headline fee. Keep GST treatment, travel, additional structures, urgency and report delivery explicit. A residential-house price may not cover a detached studio, a separate garage or all the roof voids created by additions. Ask whether each item is included, excluded or priced only after the property is reviewed.

A 'from' price is an entry point, not a ceiling. A fixed quote still needs a defined scope and an explanation of what happens if the inspection cannot proceed as planned. Record who can authorise an extra visit or specialist service and the charge, estimate or approval process that applies. Silence about an item should remain a question rather than becoming an assumed inclusion.

**Three different parts of the inspection budget**

| Budget item | What to obtain | What it does not establish |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Agreed base service | Address-specific scope, total payable and delivery arrangements | That every inaccessible or specialist question can be answered |
| Possible additional work | Trigger, rate or quote process, and your authority before commitment | That the extra service will necessarily be required |
| Work to the building | A separate, defined repair scope and appropriate quotation | That the inspection fee includes treatment or repair |

## Budget for the unanswered question, not every possible test
An inspection can correctly identify a material issue without resolving its cause or repair extent. Reserve room in the programme for relevant follow-up, but do not order every available add-on simply because it appears on a price list. Ask what decision the additional service will change and whether suitable access exists. A drain camera, structural opinion and timber-pest assessment answer different questions.

Likewise, a lower-cost copy of an existing report may be useful where its date, coverage and reliance terms match your need. It may leave the same inaccessible area unexamined. Compare the remaining evidence gap and cost of closing it, not just the cost of obtaining a PDF. [The condition-report guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/what-is-a-property-condition-report) separates report purpose and reliance from appearance and length.

## One provider per city is not a city average
These observations show prices offered by named providers for specified services. They do not establish the typical fee in each city, relative quality or a reliable national range. Some providers may share pricing structures or related businesses, so matching figures should not be treated as independent market confirmation. Do not infer that Sydney is more expensive than Melbourne from this sample alone.

For an apartment, the lot inspection and the investigation of shared-building issues are different scopes. Scheme records, access to common property and specialist work may involve separate costs. For a large or altered house, multiple construction systems can matter more than bedroom count. Explain the property to each provider using the same brief, then use [the inspector-selection guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/how-to-choose-a-building-and-pest-inspector) to assess competence and the quality of the proposed service.

## Worked example: the lower headline fee costs more to finish
**Illustrative reasoning example, not an inspected property.** Two fictional quotes cover the same initial building-and-pest visit. Quote A is $500 plus GST, with a $100 plus GST return visit if stored goods block the subfloor. Quote B is $650 including GST and includes one agreed return visit. All other inclusions are assumed equal for this illustration.

The initial totals are $550 and $650. If the stated return visit is needed, A becomes $660 and B remains $650. If access is available at the first visit, A remains cheaper. Confirm the access arrangements and exact return-visit terms rather than assuming either scenario.

Price still does not settle the choice. Verify who attends, what can safely be assessed and when the result will arrive. Neither quote promises a conclusive inspection behind every fixed finish. This comparison identifies a cost dependency; it does not rank the fictional providers' competence.

A useful inspection budget records what you are buying now, what might be commissioned later and the unresolved condition that could change the next decision.

> Important: Licensing and registration differ by state. Confirm qualifications, insurance, engagement terms, access, standard, pest scope and delivery before booking.

## Frequently asked questions
### How much does a building and pest inspection cost?
Provider prices checked on 7 September 2026 were $499 plus GST in Perth, $500 plus GST in Melbourne and Brisbane, and $655 including GST in Sydney. These are individual service examples, not city averages. The earlier Adelaide example was not reconfirmed. Obtain an address-specific total and check access, timber-pest scope, written reporting and follow-up.

### Why do inspection prices vary?
Property size, storeys, age, safe roof and subfloor access, outbuildings, timber-pest scope, travel, urgency, report depth and follow-up all affect the fee.

### Is the cheapest inspection a bad one?
A low fee can still buy a useful inspection. Trace the price back to the scope: what was accessed, whether pests are included, what the written report covers, the inspector’s qualifications and insurance, and whether they will take your call afterwards.

### Does a building inspection include termites?
Timber-pest assessment needs an explicit scope. Ask how its findings and limitations will be reported.

### Is a vendor-supplied report useful?
Check date, scope, access, inspector, insurance and your purchaser-reliance or assignment rights. Commission more work where those terms leave material gaps.

### Does an apartment inspection cover the whole building?
A typical inspection focuses on the lot and accessible areas. Use the registered plan and scheme records for common-property condition, funding, insurance, defects and works.

### What extra inspections might be needed?
Only those prompted by material evidence or the property: for example structural engineering, electrical, plumbing/drainage, hazardous material, pool or indoor-environment work.

### Are the city examples average market prices?
No. They are dated observations from named providers with different scopes. They should not be used to rank cities or providers or to infer a national average.

### Should I compare prices including GST?
Compare the total payable on the same basis and ask the provider to confirm any unclear tax treatment. Keep travel, extra structures and follow-up charges visible.

### Does the inspection fee include repairing defects or termite treatment?
Only if expressly included in a separate agreed scope. Inspection, further diagnosis, treatment and building repairs are different services.

## Method
A dated provider-price sample and scope comparison, not a national average or provider endorsement. The guide distinguishes confirmed prices, historic observations, taxes, inclusions and contingent follow-up.

## Limitations
Every quote reflects a particular property, access and scope. Use the examples as bearings, then get the current inclusions, insurance and timing in writing.

## Sources

- [Pricing](https://buildinginspectorsmelbourne.au/pricing/) — Building Inspectors Melbourne; accessed 2026-09-07
- [Pricing](https://buildingandpestinspectorsbrisbane.com.au/pricing/) — Building and Pest Inspectors Brisbane; accessed 2026-09-07

cluster.label: How to buy
cluster.blurb: Sequence the checks, understand their limits and be ready before your offer becomes binding.

sections.heading: Opening
sections.markdown:
### Choose the person and the scope together
- **Person:** Relevant experience, standing and independence
- **Scope:** Structures, pests, access, exclusions and standard
- **Report:** Clear findings, visible limits and human follow-up

_The written agreement should match the home and the decision._

sections.heading: Start with the home in front of you
sections.markdown:
Tell each inspector the address, property type, approximate age, storeys, construction, outbuildings, auction or contract deadline and any known access issue. Mention the specific concern that brought you to them, such as cracking, a low subfloor, a flat roof, a balcony leak or termite history.

The aim is a comparable written scope. A person who is excellent with new detached homes may have a different body of experience from someone who regularly reads period houses, apartments, retaining structures or complex additions.

sections.heading: Qualifications and licensing vary by state
sections.markdown:
Ask what qualification and experience support this particular inspection. The [NSW Government recommends a suitably qualified person](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/buying-and-selling-property/buying-property-nsw/inspecting-a-property/inspection-reports), giving a licensed builder, surveyor or architect as examples, and advises checking professional indemnity insurance.

Queensland has a specific [QBCC completed residential building inspection licence class](https://www.qbcc.qld.gov.au/licences/apply-licence/available-licence/inspectors-certifiers/completed-residential-building). Requirements elsewhere differ, so check the relevant state regulator and confirm that the person attending, as well as the contracting business, has the standing needed for the agreed work.

Building and timber-pest work can involve different competencies and authorisations. Ask who performs each part, what licence or qualification applies and whether the findings will appear in one report or separate reports.

sections.heading: Ask for the engagement agreement before booking
sections.markdown:
The agreement should identify the client, property, inspection type, included structures, access basis, exclusions, fee, timing, report format and the terms governing reliance. The [AS 4349.1-2007 pre-purchase inspection standard](https://store.standards.org.au/product/as-4349-1-2007) provides a national framework for residential building inspections. Ask which standard and edition the service uses and how the agreed scope relates to it.

**Use the same questions for every quote**

| Question | A useful answer should identify |
| --- | --- |
| Who will attend? | The individual inspector, relevant experience and the business responsible for the report |
| What is included? | Dwelling, site, garage, outbuildings, retaining walls, balconies and agreed timber-pest scope |
| What access is attempted? | Roof exterior, roof space, subfloor, internal rooms and conditions that may prevent safe access |
| What is excluded? | Services, concealed areas, compliance, estimates and specialist matters outside scope |
| What will I receive? | Written report, photographs, significant findings, limitations, recommendations and delivery time |
| Can I ask questions? | A direct conversation with the inspector and a process for written clarification or reinspection |
| What protects the engagement? | Professional indemnity insurance, complaint process and clear reliance terms |

sections.heading: Independence should be easy to explain
sections.markdown:
Ask who recommended the inspector, who pays them and whether they have a financial relationship with the agent, vendor, report marketplace, repairer or pest-treatment provider. A referral can still lead to capable work; a clear answer lets you understand the relationship.

Consumer Affairs Victoria advises buyers to use an inspection service with professional indemnity insurance and to be cautious with a report offered by the seller or agent. Read the [Victorian inspection guidance](https://www.consumer.vic.gov.au/housing/buying-and-selling-property/buying-property/inspect-properties-before-you-buy) before deciding whether a supplied report meets your needs.

sections.heading: Read a sample report
sections.markdown:
A sample reveals how the inspector thinks and communicates. Look for property-specific observations, useful photographs, precise locations, plainly stated access limits and recommendations that identify the next kind of expertise. A template can provide structure; the finished report should still feel like someone paid close attention to this home.

- **Clear significance:** the reader can tell what deserves attention first.
- **Visible limitations:** inaccessible areas are easy to find and understand.
- **Traceable photographs:** images have locations and connect to written findings.
- **Proportionate recommendations:** the next step answers a defined question.
- **Human follow-up:** the inspector is available to explain material findings.

sections.heading: Access often matters more than gadgets
sections.markdown:
Ask what safe-access conditions are needed for the roof exterior, roof space and subfloor, and who will arrange keys, hatches or permission. Tools such as moisture meters and thermal cameras can support defined observations. Their value depends on access, method, conditions and interpretation.

If a critical area is inaccessible on the day, ask about a return visit and its fee. Read the resulting limitation carefully using the [guide to building and pest reports](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/how-to-read-a-building-and-pest-report).

sections.heading: Choose the scope before comparing price
sections.markdown:
Put the quotes beside one another only after the inclusions line up. A lower price may reflect a smaller property, narrower access, building-only work, fewer structures, limited photographs or no follow-up. The [inspection-cost guide and quote decoder](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/building-and-pest-inspection-cost) provides current examples and a comparison framework.

Ask about cancellation, urgent turnaround, travel, reinspection and specialist follow-up fees. For an auction, leave enough time to read the report and act on it with the [pre-auction inspection guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/building-inspection-before-auction).

sections.heading: A short selection checklist
sections.markdown:
1. Write a short property and deadline brief.
2. Confirm the individual inspector and relevant experience.
3. Verify state licensing or registration where it applies.
4. Confirm professional indemnity insurance in writing.
5. Compare building, timber-pest, structures and access scope.
6. Read the engagement agreement and a sample report.
7. Confirm report timing, follow-up and reinspection arrangements.

sections.heading: Test the sample report with one difficult finding
sections.markdown:
Choose one item in the sample and follow it from photograph to conclusion to recommendation. Can you locate it? Does the description distinguish visible damage from its suspected cause? Does the recommendation identify the unanswered question? If the report says 'seek specialist advice', ask what sort of advice and what the reader would need to learn from it. Long reports and many photographs can still leave that chain incomplete.

Try a limitation as well. If the subfloor was inaccessible, does the report explain its significance for that property rather than burying the statement in standard text? A useful conversation is: 'What would you tell me if this happened at my house?' You are assessing how the inspector handles incomplete evidence, not asking them to diagnose a property they have not visited.

**Listen to how the provider answers**

| Question to ask | An answer worth exploring | An answer needing clarification |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What if the roof space cannot be accessed? | Explains safe-access requirements, reporting and possible follow-up | Says the equipment will find everything anyway |
| What does this moisture finding establish? | Separates observation, interpretation and further investigation | Names a hidden failure without explaining the evidence |
| Who deals with a combined building and pest finding? | Identifies responsible practitioners and how their reports connect | Cannot say who performs the pest work |

guides.contentMarkdown:
# How to choose a building and pest inspector: the questions worth asking

Choose the inspector whose experience suits the property and whose written scope clearly covers the areas, structures and timber-pest work you need. Confirm independence, professional indemnity insurance, relevant state licensing, safe-access expectations, the report standard and whether you can speak with the inspector afterwards.

## Research note
The linked NSW, Victorian and Queensland sources ground the practitioner and scope checks. The AS 4349.1 catalogue identifies the cited inspection framework; this is not a licensed full-text standards audit. The sample-report questions and fictional comparison are original editorial tools, not a provider ranking.

## Opening
### Choose the person and the scope together
- **Person:** Relevant experience, standing and independence
- **Scope:** Structures, pests, access, exclusions and standard
- **Report:** Clear findings, visible limits and human follow-up

_The written agreement should match the home and the decision._

## Start with the home in front of you
Tell each inspector the address, property type, approximate age, storeys, construction, outbuildings, auction or contract deadline and any known access issue. Mention the specific concern that brought you to them, such as cracking, a low subfloor, a flat roof, a balcony leak or termite history.

The aim is a comparable written scope. A person who is excellent with new detached homes may have a different body of experience from someone who regularly reads period houses, apartments, retaining structures or complex additions.

## Qualifications and licensing vary by state
Ask what qualification and experience support this particular inspection. The [NSW Government recommends a suitably qualified person](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/buying-and-selling-property/buying-property-nsw/inspecting-a-property/inspection-reports), giving a licensed builder, surveyor or architect as examples, and advises checking professional indemnity insurance.

Queensland has a specific [QBCC completed residential building inspection licence class](https://www.qbcc.qld.gov.au/licences/apply-licence/available-licence/inspectors-certifiers/completed-residential-building). Requirements elsewhere differ, so check the relevant state regulator and confirm that the person attending, as well as the contracting business, has the standing needed for the agreed work.

Building and timber-pest work can involve different competencies and authorisations. Ask who performs each part, what licence or qualification applies and whether the findings will appear in one report or separate reports.

## Ask for the engagement agreement before booking
The agreement should identify the client, property, inspection type, included structures, access basis, exclusions, fee, timing, report format and the terms governing reliance. The [AS 4349.1-2007 pre-purchase inspection standard](https://store.standards.org.au/product/as-4349-1-2007) provides a national framework for residential building inspections. Ask which standard and edition the service uses and how the agreed scope relates to it.

**Use the same questions for every quote**

| Question | A useful answer should identify |
| --- | --- |
| Who will attend? | The individual inspector, relevant experience and the business responsible for the report |
| What is included? | Dwelling, site, garage, outbuildings, retaining walls, balconies and agreed timber-pest scope |
| What access is attempted? | Roof exterior, roof space, subfloor, internal rooms and conditions that may prevent safe access |
| What is excluded? | Services, concealed areas, compliance, estimates and specialist matters outside scope |
| What will I receive? | Written report, photographs, significant findings, limitations, recommendations and delivery time |
| Can I ask questions? | A direct conversation with the inspector and a process for written clarification or reinspection |
| What protects the engagement? | Professional indemnity insurance, complaint process and clear reliance terms |

## Independence should be easy to explain
Ask who recommended the inspector, who pays them and whether they have a financial relationship with the agent, vendor, report marketplace, repairer or pest-treatment provider. A referral can still lead to capable work; a clear answer lets you understand the relationship.

Consumer Affairs Victoria advises buyers to use an inspection service with professional indemnity insurance and to be cautious with a report offered by the seller or agent. Read the [Victorian inspection guidance](https://www.consumer.vic.gov.au/housing/buying-and-selling-property/buying-property/inspect-properties-before-you-buy) before deciding whether a supplied report meets your needs.

## Read a sample report
A sample reveals how the inspector thinks and communicates. Look for property-specific observations, useful photographs, precise locations, plainly stated access limits and recommendations that identify the next kind of expertise. A template can provide structure; the finished report should still feel like someone paid close attention to this home.

- **Clear significance:** the reader can tell what deserves attention first.
- **Visible limitations:** inaccessible areas are easy to find and understand.
- **Traceable photographs:** images have locations and connect to written findings.
- **Proportionate recommendations:** the next step answers a defined question.
- **Human follow-up:** the inspector is available to explain material findings.

## Access often matters more than gadgets
Ask what safe-access conditions are needed for the roof exterior, roof space and subfloor, and who will arrange keys, hatches or permission. Tools such as moisture meters and thermal cameras can support defined observations. Their value depends on access, method, conditions and interpretation.

If a critical area is inaccessible on the day, ask about a return visit and its fee. Read the resulting limitation carefully using the [guide to building and pest reports](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/how-to-read-a-building-and-pest-report).

## Choose the scope before comparing price
Put the quotes beside one another only after the inclusions line up. A lower price may reflect a smaller property, narrower access, building-only work, fewer structures, limited photographs or no follow-up. The [inspection-cost guide and quote decoder](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/building-and-pest-inspection-cost) provides current examples and a comparison framework.

Ask about cancellation, urgent turnaround, travel, reinspection and specialist follow-up fees. For an auction, leave enough time to read the report and act on it with the [pre-auction inspection guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/building-inspection-before-auction).

## A short selection checklist
1. Write a short property and deadline brief.
2. Confirm the individual inspector and relevant experience.
3. Verify state licensing or registration where it applies.
4. Confirm professional indemnity insurance in writing.
5. Compare building, timber-pest, structures and access scope.
6. Read the engagement agreement and a sample report.
7. Confirm report timing, follow-up and reinspection arrangements.

## Test the sample report with one difficult finding
Choose one item in the sample and follow it from photograph to conclusion to recommendation. Can you locate it? Does the description distinguish visible damage from its suspected cause? Does the recommendation identify the unanswered question? If the report says 'seek specialist advice', ask what sort of advice and what the reader would need to learn from it. Long reports and many photographs can still leave that chain incomplete.

Try a limitation as well. If the subfloor was inaccessible, does the report explain its significance for that property rather than burying the statement in standard text? A useful conversation is: 'What would you tell me if this happened at my house?' You are assessing how the inspector handles incomplete evidence, not asking them to diagnose a property they have not visited.

**Listen to how the provider answers**

| Question to ask | An answer worth exploring | An answer needing clarification |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What if the roof space cannot be accessed? | Explains safe-access requirements, reporting and possible follow-up | Says the equipment will find everything anyway |
| What does this moisture finding establish? | Separates observation, interpretation and further investigation | Names a hidden failure without explaining the evidence |
| Who deals with a combined building and pest finding? | Identifies responsible practitioners and how their reports connect | Cannot say who performs the pest work |
| How do I clarify a material issue before my deadline? | Identifies a person, response arrangements and limits | Promises a fast PDF without access to the author |

## Know who takes responsibility for the work
A familiar brand may arrange a local subcontractor. That arrangement can work well, but identify the business you contract with, the person attending and the author responsible for each report. Ask how a substitution would be handled if the named inspector becomes unavailable. The experience you selected should belong to the person doing the relevant work, or be supported by a clear supervision arrangement.

Check insurance evidence against the service and contracting party. Professional indemnity and public liability address different kinds of exposure; a document headed 'insured' may not answer your question about professional advice. Ask the provider or insurer to clarify material uncertainty. Insurance is a protection to investigate, not a guarantee that every missed defect, excluded service or later loss will be covered.

## Match the appointment to the building’s difficult parts
An older house with several additions may need careful reading of interfaces and changing construction. A relatively new apartment may raise common-property questions beyond a lot inspection. A sloping site may make retaining structures and drainage central to the brief. Ask about relevant experience and the boundaries of the service. A competent general inspector can identify a need for other expertise; they do not have to claim they can personally resolve every specialist issue.

If a particular symptom already dominates the decision, ask whether a general inspection plus targeted work is appropriate or whether the specialist should be involved first. Specify who will coordinate the findings. A combined booking is convenient only if it includes the actual services and leaves you with clear responsibility for the result.

## Avoid turning the selection into a competition for certainty
The most reassuring sales answer may be the least useful professional answer. A promise to identify every leak or confirm all structural adequacy goes beyond what a limited visual visit can establish. Conversely, limitations do not excuse vague observations about areas that were examined. Look for precision on both sides: confidence about what was observed and candour about what was not established.

Tools should have a purpose in the agreed service. Ask which question a proposed tool helps answer, under what conditions and how the result will be interpreted. Do not buy the number of devices on the equipment list. Equally, do not demand unsafe access or unapproved opening simply to make the inspection feel thorough. The quality of the method is its fit to the question and the permission available.

## Worked example: two quotes for a house with a low subfloor
**Illustrative reasoning example, not an inspected property.** Two providers quote for an interwar house. One highlights thermal imaging and same-day delivery. The other asks for the subfloor access dimensions, requests the previous pest report and proposes a call after inspection. Both advertise building and pest services.

The second response identifies useful questions, but does not alone establish competence or make it the automatic choice. Ask both for the attending practitioners, actual building and pest scope, insurance, access method and a sample report. Establish what each would do if the critical area remained inaccessible.

If one service expressly excludes the relevant subfloor and the other proposes an appropriate safe assessment, the quotes are for different evidence. If neither can access it, a lower price or faster turnaround will not close the gap. Choose the appointment that best addresses the property question, and plan separately for what it cannot establish.

Before confirming the booking, write back the agreed scope, access arrangements, report deadline and follow-up contact. That brief is a practical record of what you selected, not just what the advertisement appeared to promise.

> Note: The best appointment is the one that gives a careful inspector enough scope, access and time to answer the questions this particular home raises.

> Important: Verify licence and insurance details with the relevant regulator or insurer where they are material. Business names, licence classes and personnel can change.

## Frequently asked questions
### What qualifications should a building inspector have?
Look for qualifications and experience relevant to the property and inspection scope. Government guidance recommends a suitably qualified professional, and state licensing requirements differ. Verify the person attending, their role and their insurance.

### Do building inspectors need a licence in Australia?
Requirements vary by state and by the work performed. Queensland has a completed residential building inspection licence class. Check the regulator for the property location and the separate requirements applying to timber-pest work.

### Should a building inspector have professional indemnity insurance?
Yes. NSW and Victorian buyer guidance both recommend checking professional indemnity insurance. Ask for current evidence and confirm which person and business the policy covers.

### Should I use the building inspector recommended by the agent?
Ask about the relationship, scope, commissioning party and your reliance rights. Review the inspector on their qualifications, insurance, independence, access and report quality.

### Does a building inspection include a pest inspection?
Only when timber-pest work is expressly included. Confirm who performs it, their relevant authorisation, the standard or scope used and how the findings will be delivered.

### Is thermal imaging essential in a building inspection?
It can support a defined investigation under suitable conditions. It does not see through every surface or replace access, experience and careful interpretation.

### How many quotes should I compare?
Enough to understand the available scope and fee for the property. Use the same written questions so you can compare access, inclusions, experience, insurance, report quality and follow-up fairly.

### Does a well-known inspection brand guarantee the person attending?
Confirm the actual inspector, relevant experience, contracting business and arrangements for any substitution or subcontracting. Review the scope and responsibility in writing.

### Is public liability insurance the same as professional indemnity?
No. Ask for the insurance relevant to the inspection and professional advice, and clarify the covered person, business and service. A generic insurance statement is insufficient.

### Should I choose the inspector who promises the most certainty?
Prefer precise explanations of observations, access, scope and limits. A limited visual inspection cannot guarantee that every concealed defect or specialist issue will be found.

## Method
A service-selection guide distinguishing practitioner competence, contracting responsibility, scope, access and useful judgement. Its fictional comparison tests the quality of answers rather than ranking tools or providers.

## Limitations
Licensing, registration and timber-pest requirements vary by jurisdiction and service. Verify the individual, business, licence class and insurance for the property and work commissioned.

## Sources
- [Inspection reports before buying property](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/buying-and-selling-property/buying-property-nsw/inspecting-a-property/inspection-reports) — NSW Government; accessed 2026-07-19

guides.question: How do I read a building and pest inspection report?
guides.title: How to read a building and pest inspection report, and what to do next
guides.summary: A calm, practical way to read the findings, limitations and recommendations in a pre-purchase report, then decide which questions need answering before you commit.
guides.answer: Start with the inspection scope and access limitations, then read the significant findings alongside the photographs and recommendations. Sort each unresolved issue by consequence, urgency and the person qualified to investigate it. A long defect list can include routine maintenance; one short limitation can hide a much larger uncertainty.
guides.methodology: We turn the report into a decision register, resolve scope and wording differences, and match any follow-up evidence to the original finding rather than treating an overall summary as clearance.
guides.limitations: General reading guidance only. The report, engagement terms, property evidence, contract and advice from the relevant professional control the decision.
guides.researchNote: Read each finding within the agreed scope and access. [NSW's inspection guidance](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/buying-and-selling-property/buying-property-nsw/inspecting-a-property/inspection-reports) identifies the role of separate checks. The report's definitions and any written clarification govern how its conclusions should be understood.

cluster.label: How to buy
cluster.blurb: Sequence the checks, understand their limits and be ready before your offer becomes binding.

sections.heading: Opening
sections.markdown:
### Findings and blind spots belong together
- **Observed:** What the inspector saw and where
- **Unresolved:** What access or scope could not settle
- **Next question:** Who can answer it before your deadline

_One material unknown can matter more than a long maintenance list._

sections.heading: Before the defect list, check the report itself
sections.markdown:
Confirm the property address, inspection date, weather, commissioning party, inspector and agreed scope. Check whether the report is addressed to you or gives you a documented right to rely on it. A useful report should make clear what was inspected, what could not be inspected and what kind of inspection was performed.

The [Australian Standard AS 4349.1-2007](https://store.standards.org.au/product/as-4349-1-2007) sets requirements for pre-purchase inspections of residential buildings. Read the report's own agreement and definitions as well, since the engagement may identify exclusions, additional services and property-specific limits.

sections.heading: Read it in five passes
sections.markdown:
1. **Scope:** which buildings, structures and inspection types were included?
2. **Access:** which roof, roof-space, subfloor, room, outbuilding or external area could not be reached?
3. **Significant findings:** which observations affect safety, structure, weatherproofing, timber pests or use?
4. **Recommendations:** which findings need clarification, monitoring, repair advice or a specialist?
5. **Decision:** what must be understood before the contract, cooling-off deadline or auction?

This order matters because findings and blind spots describe different risks. A visible leak is a finding. A roof space hidden by unsafe or restricted access is an unresolved area. Give both a place in the decision.

sections.heading: What common report language is telling you
sections.markdown:
**Translate the label into the next useful question**

| Report language | What it usually tells you | What to ask |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Major or significant defect | The inspector considers the consequence material within the report definition | What is the observed evidence, likely consequence and recommended next investigation? |
| Minor defect | A defect that may be localised, serviceable or less consequential | Does it need maintenance, monitoring or repair, and could several minor items share one cause? |
| Safety hazard | A condition the report identifies as presenting a safety concern | What immediate precaution and appropriately qualified trade or professional are recommended? |
| Further investigation | The observation cannot be resolved within the inspection scope | Who should investigate, what question should they answer and when is the answer needed? |
| Inaccessible or obstructed | The inspector could not observe a relevant area | Can access be arranged before commitment, and what uncertainty remains if it cannot? |
| Monitor | Change over time may be important | What should be measured or photographed, at what interval, and what change triggers escalation? |

Treat the report's definitions as controlling for that document. Ask the inspector to explain any label that changes your decision. The photograph shows an observation; the surrounding text should explain its location, context and significance.

sections.heading: Turn the report into a decision register
sections.markdown:
Create one line for every material finding and limitation. Record the location, evidence, consequence, open question, next person, deadline and any cost information you have. This keeps a worrying report readable and stops an important blind spot disappearing beneath a long maintenance list.

**A simple triage for unresolved findings**

| Signal | Useful next step |
| --- | --- |
| Movement with distortion, sticking openings or changing cracks | Ask whether a structural engineer should assess cause and significance; use the [wall-crack guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/cracks-structural-or-cosmetic) to organise the observations |
| Moisture, staining, mould or damaged finishes | Identify the water source and extent before pricing cosmetic work; follow the [moisture pathway](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/damp-and-moisture-in-your-home) |
| Active timber pests or evidence of damage | Clarify the timber-pest scope, activity, affected areas and recommended extent assessment |
| Suspect electrical, gas, plumbing or drainage condition | Use the appropriately licensed trade for that service and a clearly defined question |
| Roof space, subfloor or outbuilding not inspected | Seek safe access, a return inspection or a conscious allowance for the unresolved area |
| Possible asbestos or another hazardous material | Avoid disturbing it and use an appropriately competent assessor where identification affects the decision or planned work |

sections.heading: A report is a visual record with boundaries
sections.markdown:
A conventional pre-purchase inspection is generally visual and non-invasive over safely accessible areas. It does not open walls or prove the condition of every concealed element. Building condition, timber pests, electrical safety, plumbing, drainage, hazardous materials, approvals and legal rights may sit in different scopes.

The [NSW Government's buyer guidance](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/buying-and-selling-property/buying-property-nsw/inspecting-a-property/inspection-reports) describes building, pest and strata reports as separate checks and recommends using a suitably qualified, insured professional. Use each report for its commissioned purpose and let its findings identify the next question.

sections.heading: Call the inspector while the inspection is fresh
sections.markdown:
- Which three findings deserve my attention first, and why?
- Which areas were inaccessible or only partly visible?
- Did any observations suggest one shared cause?
- Which recommendations should be completed before I commit?
- Which specialist should I brief, and what question should I ask?
- Would safe access or further documents change your view?

Write the answers into your decision register. If the response materially changes the written report, ask whether the inspector can confirm the clarification in writing.

sections.heading: Repairs and costs need a defined scope
sections.markdown:
A repair number becomes useful once the cause, extent and intended remedy are reasonably clear. Ask whether a figure in the report is an estimate, an allowance or a contractor quotation. Keep urgent safety work, investigation costs, near-term repairs and ordinary maintenance in separate lines.

For the inspection fee and inclusions, see the [2026 inspection-cost examples and quote decoder](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/building-and-pest-inspection-cost). If you are still appointing someone, use the [inspector selection guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/how-to-choose-a-building-and-pest-inspector).

sections.heading: Use the right deadline
sections.markdown: Your useful deadline comes from the transaction: before signing, before a cooling-off period expires, or before bidding. Share material findings with your conveyancer or solicitor where they affect contract conditions, disclosure, settlement or the decision to proceed. At auction, work through the [five-gate due-diligence plan](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/auction-day-due-diligence) early enough to obtain specialist follow-up.

sections.heading: Resolve apparent contradictions before averaging the verdicts
sections.markdown:
A summary might describe the home as generally serviceable while a later page records inaccessible roof framing or recommends an engineer. These can coexist: one describes the accessible overall condition, while the other preserves a specific unresolved question. Read the summary with every material limitation rather than using it to cancel them.

If two reports differ, compare the dates, weather, access and commissioned scopes before deciding that one is wrong. A dry-day inspection and a visit after heavy rain can produce different moisture evidence. Ask each author to explain the specific difference. A buyer needs the open question resolved; an informal vote between report conclusions does not achieve that.

sections.heading: Separate pest activity, damage and management history
sections.markdown:
The [QBCC termite guidance](https://www.qbcc.qld.gov.au/home-owner-hub/maintain-protect/protect-against-termites) explains why a management system still needs inspection and maintenance. A treatment notice records a measure at a particular time. It does not establish the present condition of every timber. Read the pest report for accessible evidence, activity status, damage, conducive conditions and the areas it could not inspect.

'No active termites observed' and 'no damage' are different statements. Historical damage can need assessment even where no current activity is seen; restricted access limits what can be concluded about both. Ask whether further access, treatment advice or assessment of affected timber is recommended. Avoid disturbing suspected activity before obtaining the pest professional's advice.

sections.heading: Read a seller’s repair response against the original question
sections.markdown:
If the report identified a stain and recommended investigation, an invoice for repainting does not answer the source question. If an electrician attended, ask which circuit or item was tested and what was remedied. Match the response to the finding's location and scope, and seek written clarification or an agreed reinspection where it matters to the purchase.

A short follow-up can materially narrow uncertainty without pretending to reopen the whole report. Useful wording identifies the original item, the new document or inspection, what conclusion changed and what remains excluded. Give the legal representative that clarification if it affects an agreed condition or deadline.

sections.heading: Worked example: a reassuring summary with an inaccessible subfloor
sections.markdown:
**Illustrative reasoning example, not an inspected property.** A report describes a postwar home as generally serviceable, lists old staining near a bathroom and says stored goods prevented inspection of the rear subfloor. The summary does not establish the condition of the concealed floor framing. The seller offers to repaint before settlement.

Ask the inspector whether safe access and targeted follow-up can resolve the moisture and framing questions. If access reveals a documented historic leak with sound accessible timber, the uncertainty narrows. If access remains blocked, it remains an uninspected area. The buyer can consider that position with their advisers, but the repaint should not be recorded as closure of the original recommendation.

> Note: A good report does not make the decision for you. It gives you a dated set of observations, limitations and next questions so you can make the decision with your eyes open.

> Important: Urgent safety concerns and evidence of active water, pest activity or movement deserve prompt, property-specific advice. Avoid disturbing suspected hazardous material.

faqs.question: What should I read first in a building inspection report?
faqs.answer: Read the scope and access limitations first, followed by the significant findings and recommendations. This shows both what the inspector observed and what remains unknown.

faqs.question: What does a major defect mean in a building inspection report?
faqs.answer: Use the definition in the report and engagement agreement. Ask the inspector to explain the observed evidence, likely consequence and recommended next investigation for every major or significant item.

faqs.question: Should I worry about a long list of minor defects?
faqs.answer: Look for shared causes, active deterioration and accumulated cost. Many minor items can be manageable, while repeated moisture or movement signals may justify closer investigation.

faqs.question: What if the roof space or subfloor was inaccessible?
faqs.answer: Ask whether safe access and a return inspection can be arranged. If access remains unavailable, record the area as unresolved and decide how that uncertainty affects the purchase.

faqs.question: Can a building inspector quote repair costs?
faqs.answer: That depends on the agreed service and the inspector. Establish whether any figure is an estimate, allowance or contractor quotation, and seek a defined scope before relying on it.

faqs.question: Who should investigate a structural concern?
faqs.answer: Ask the inspector whether the observed issue warrants assessment by a suitably qualified structural engineer and what specific question the engineer should answer.

faqs.question: Can I rely on a report supplied by the vendor or agent?
faqs.answer: Check its date, scope, access, commissioning party, inspector, insurance and written purchaser-reliance or assignment terms. Commission your own work when those answers leave an important gap.

faqs.question: What if the summary sounds reassuring but a later page recommends investigation?
faqs.answer: Read both together. An overall description does not cancel a specific unresolved finding or access limitation. Ask the inspector what needs resolving before your decision.

faqs.question: Does no active termite evidence mean no timber damage?
faqs.answer: No. Activity, damage, management history and inaccessible areas are separate matters. Read the pest report’s exact findings and recommendations for each.

faqs.question: Does a repair invoice close a report recommendation?
faqs.answer: Only if its scope and supporting evidence answer the original question. A finish repair does not necessarily establish that the underlying cause was investigated and remedied.
