sections.heading: Opening
sections.markdown:
### Let the era sharpen your questions
- **Start:** The build date and construction open the questions
- **Look closer:** Plans, invoices, alterations and what you can see
- **Settle it:** An inspection, or a specialist, settles it for this house

_The era points; the evidence decides._

sections.heading: Treat the era as a hypothesis, not a diagnosis
sections.markdown:
A construction date can narrow the list of questions, but it cannot tell you the condition of the home in front of you. A 1930s house may have a new roof, rewired services and a 1990s bathroom. A 1970s house may have a 2018 extension. A 2012 apartment may have years of façade or waterproofing history sitting in the owners-corporation records. The useful question is not simply **how old is the building?** It is **which parts belong to which era, and how are those parts performing now?**

The Australian Government's [YourHome buying guidance](https://www.yourhome.gov.au/buy-build-renovate/buying-existing-house) makes the same distinction in practical terms: building and pest inspections are used to identify structural, damp, drainage, waterproofing and termite issues, while the property records and installed systems add the history that a visual inspection cannot supply.

> Note: A useful era clue should change the evidence you seek, the professional you engage or the decision you make. If it changes none of those things, it is probably just trivia.

sections.heading: The era matrix
sections.markdown:
_[Illustration: Five detailed Australian house models progressing from a pre-1920s home through interwar, postwar, 1980s to 1990s and contemporary construction. Each era leaves its own clues in the roof, walls, footings, services and later alterations. The table below turns those clues into inspection questions.]_

**Where to begin, and which guide to open next**

| Era / form | First useful questions | Follow the evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pre-1920s | What supports the walls and floors? Where does moisture enter? Which services and finishes are later? | [Period homes](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/period-homes-pre-1920s) → [moisture pathways](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/damp-and-moisture-in-your-home) → footing, roof and repair records. |
| 1920s–40s | Does the original house meet an extension on different supports? Are low walls damp? Which alterations changed drainage? | [Interwar homes](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/interwar-homes-1920s-40s) → [timber fabric](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/weatherboard-homes) or [masonry construction](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/brick-veneer-vs-double-brick). |
| 1950s–70s | What is the wall system? What was replaced? Will proposed work disturb suspect materials? | [Postwar homes](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/postwar-homes-1950s-70s) → [renovation sequence](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/planning-a-renovation) → material and service evidence. |
| 1980s–90s | Which wet areas, roof details and services are original? Is the recent work cosmetic or a documented renewal? | [1980s–90s homes](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/homes-1980s-90s) → [movement](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/cracks-structural-or-cosmetic) or [damp investigation](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/damp-and-moisture-in-your-home). |
| 2000s onward, house | Do approval and completion records match the home? What happens at roof, window, balcony and ground junctions? | [Modern homes](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/modern-homes-2000s-on) → drainage, defect history and repair evidence. |
| Apartment or shared scheme, any era | What is shared, what is already known about the building, and how will work be paid for? | [Apartment due diligence](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/buying-an-apartment-strata) → [scheme records](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/reading-your-owners-corporation-report) → technical reports and funding. |

sections.heading: Read four timelines, not one build year
sections.markdown:
**The four timelines that usually matter**

| Timeline | What to establish | Why it changes the inspection |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Original construction | Footings, wall system, roof form, floor system, openings and original services where known | This establishes the base construction and the era-linked questions that remain relevant. |
| Major alterations | Extensions, enclosed verandas, wall removal, re-roofing, window replacement, façade work and structural changes | Later work may be built under a different code era, may hide original fabric and can create junctions where water or movement concentrates. |
| Wet areas and services | Bathroom, laundry, kitchen, wiring, switchboard, plumbing, hot water, heating/cooling and solar upgrade dates | These systems often age independently of the shell. The house age is a poor proxy for their current age. |
| Repairs and defects | Leaks, cracking, termite treatment, underpinning/restumping, roof repairs, drainage works, cladding or waterproofing rectification | A repair can be reassuring only when the cause, scope, completion and present performance are understood. |

This is why a renovated older home can be harder to read than an untouched one. Renovation can solve genuine defects, but it can also hide interfaces, remove visible clues and mix materials from several periods. Keep asking **what changed, when, why and with what evidence?**

sections.heading: Cross-era red flags that deserve evidence
sections.markdown:
### Water that is not being shed, drained or dried

Across every era, water is one of the highest-value things to follow. Look at the whole path: roof covering, flashings, gutters, downpipes, surface falls, openings, wall cavities, wet areas, subfloor and plumbing. The Australian Government's [repairs and maintenance guidance](https://www.yourhome.gov.au/buy-build-renovate/repairs-and-maintenance) specifically treats leaks, blocked drainage, failed flashings, damp and shower waterproofing as issues that can create larger building damage if the cause is not addressed. Use [the damp guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/damp-and-moisture-in-your-home) to separate source, path and damage.

### Movement without a timeline

Cracks are more useful when read with direction, width, associated distortion, footing type, drainage, trees, soil and change over time. A repaired crack with no explanation is not the same evidence as a diagnosed cause with monitoring and completed structural work. Use [the crack triage](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/cracks-structural-or-cosmetic) and escalate progressive or consequential movement to the appropriate professional.

### Timber-pest risk hidden by finishes or landscaping

Termites are not an 'old house' problem. Risk changes with region, construction, subfloor clearance, moisture, slab edges, service penetrations, landscaping and the condition of any management system. YourHome recommends a building and pest inspection before buying in termite-risk areas, while [QBCC guidance](https://www.qbcc.qld.gov.au/home-owner-hub/maintain-protect/protect-against-termites) shows why later landscaping, paths and renovations can undermine a termite-management system. Ask what system exists, how it has been maintained and what the latest inspection found.

### Services whose age is being guessed from the house

Do not infer wiring, plumbing or hot-water age from the build date. Look for switchboard changes, invoices, certificates and alterations, then use licensed inspection where the system matters to safety, capacity or budget. This becomes especially important where solar, battery, electric-vehicle charging or electrification has increased demand on an older electrical installation.

sections.heading: Hazards with useful date screens
sections.markdown:
### Asbestos-containing materials

The [national householders' guide](https://www.newaste.org.au/asbestos/assets/asbestos-guide-for-householders.pdf) says houses built or renovated before 1990 may contain asbestos products. The [NSW asbestos timeline](https://www.asbestos.nsw.gov.au/safety/safety-in-the-home/when-was-asbestos-banned-in-australia) records the national ban from 31 December 2003. The date is a screening trigger, not a material diagnosis: follow [ASSEA’s asbestos-in-the-home guidance](https://www.asbestossafety.gov.au/about-asbestos/finding-asbestos/home) to identify suspect material before drilling, sanding, cutting or demolition and follow the licensing and disposal rules for the material, amount and jurisdiction.

### Lead in older paint

Older paint, especially pre-1970s layers, may contain much higher lead concentrations than modern coatings. Before sanding, scraping or heat stripping, follow the [Australian Government Lead Alert](https://www.agriculture.gov.au/sites/default/files/documents/lead-paint-fifth-edition.pdf), test where appropriate and use lead-safe controls.

sections.heading: Later energy upgrades can create their own questions
sections.markdown: Insulation, draught sealing, replacement glazing and cladding upgrades can improve comfort, but the work has to suit the existing building. [YourHome's condensation guidance](https://www.yourhome.gov.au/passive-design/condensation) explains that moisture risk depends on temperature, humidity, ventilation and the way roof and wall assemblies dry. For an older home, ask what insulation and membranes were actually installed, whether roof-space electrical clearances were respected, and whether a retrofit changed ventilation or moisture behaviour.

sections.heading: Regional variation can outweigh decade
sections.markdown: A decade does not erase climate or site. Tropical elevated houses, cyclone-region homes, coastal masonry, alpine roofs, bushfire construction and southern clay-soil suburbs demand different questions. Add the location to every era profile: climate, wind exposure, termites, flood and bushfire context, soil, salt, vegetation and site drainage. The most useful era guide is one that gets narrower after you add the address, not one that pretends every 1960s house behaves the same.

sections.heading: Use an evidence hierarchy
sections.markdown:
1. **Start with what is actually visible:** material, crack, stain, distortion, clearance, repair, meter box, roof line or other observable clue.
2. **Then find the record:** permit, plan, invoice, certificate, warranty, previous report, pest notice, insurance correspondence or dated photo.
3. **Test the current condition:** a historical document does not prove that a system still performs today.
4. **Use the right discipline:** building inspector, engineer, electrician, plumber, pest professional, hygienist, strata specialist or lawyer where the question leaves general building guidance.
5. **Keep unknowns explicit:** inaccessible roof spaces, concealed membranes, buried drainage and undocumented alterations remain unknown until better evidence appears.

sections.heading: Worked example: a 1970s brick home with cracking and damp
sections.markdown:
**Illustrative reasoning example, not an inspected property.** A listing shows stepped brick cracking near a window, a low internal stain and recent garden paving. Begin by recording those three observations separately. Do not jump from “1970s” to “failing foundations”, or assume that the stain and crack share a cause.

Next establish whether the wall is veneer or loadbearing, whether the stain responds to rain or plumbing use, and whether the paving changed levels or water disposal. Photographs predating the paving and a suitable physical inspection could strengthen or weaken a connection. If the crack is progressing with floor or opening distortion, an engineer becomes more relevant. If a local leak explains the stain, price that defined scope rather than an assumed whole-house repair.

> Note: Keep the conclusion at the level the evidence supports: observed, reported, inferred or confirmed. “Not visible in the available photographs” does not mean “absent”.

sections.heading: Turn a red flag into a decision
sections.markdown:
**A red flag is useful when it changes the next step**

| Clue | Useful next question | Possible decision effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Suspect pre-1990 sheet material | What is it, where else is it present and will planned work disturb it? | Material identification, removal scope, renovation sequencing and budget. |
| Crack with sticking doors or floor distortion | Is movement active, what footing/site factors are involved and what would an engineer need to see? | Specialist investigation, repair allowance, monitoring or purchase condition. |
| Bathroom with staining below | Is the source plumbing, junctions, drainage or waterproofing, and when was the room renewed? | Moisture investigation, invasive testing if justified, repair scope or contingency. |
| Termite history | Was activity eradicated, what damage was repaired and how is the management system maintained? | Pest/structural follow-up, access improvements, ongoing inspection plan. |
| Undocumented extension | What approvals, structural changes, services and waterproofing sit behind the visible work? | Council/legal review, specialist checks, valuation of uncertainty and future renovation constraints. |
| Apartment defect in minutes | Is it lot or common property, diagnosed or suspected, funded or unfunded, resolved or ongoing? | Records review, special-levy exposure, insurance/warranty questions and purchase decision. |

For a purchase, translate the era questions into the brief for a [physical inspection](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/building-inspection-before-auction). For ownership planning, use [what your home needs by decade](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/what-your-home-needs-by-decade). Then move into the specific construction guides rather than trying to make one era label carry the whole decision.

> Important: Do not use an era guide to diagnose a defect, certify compliance or set a repair scope. It is a way to ask better questions and seek better evidence.

faqs.question: Which era of house has the most problems?
faqs.answer: There is no reliable ranking. Construction, region, alterations, maintenance and current condition matter more than decade alone. The era is useful because it changes the questions you ask.

faqs.question: What is the asbestos screening date?
faqs.answer: Homes built or renovated before 1990 may contain asbestos-containing materials. All uses were prohibited nationally from 31 December 2003. The date is a screening trigger; material identification is still required before disturbance.

faqs.question: Does an old home definitely have lead paint?
faqs.answer: No. Older coatings are a higher-priority screen, especially pre-1970s layers. Testing establishes presence and concentration. Use lead-safe methods before disturbance.

faqs.question: Can build year tell me how old the wiring or plumbing is?
faqs.answer: No. Services may be renewed, extended or mixed across several eras. Use records and licensed inspection to establish what is installed, how it was altered and whether it suits current use.

faqs.question: Are termites mainly a problem in older houses?
faqs.answer: No. Termite risk depends on location, moisture, access, construction details and the management system. Newer slab-on-ground homes can also be vulnerable if barriers, slab edges, penetrations or inspection zones are compromised.

faqs.question: Does a renovation remove the risks of an older era?
faqs.answer: Not automatically. Renovation can solve issues, but it can also retain concealed original fabric, introduce new junctions or mix several construction periods. Establish what was actually renewed and what stayed.

faqs.question: What should I check in a modern apartment?
faqs.answer: Read both the lot and the shared building: registered plan, common-property defects, external walls and cladding, waterproofing, fire systems, developer/warranty pathways, insurance, minutes, planned works and funding.

faqs.question: Should I compare a home with current building-code requirements?
faqs.answer: Current requirements can help explain good building principles, but an older building is not automatically defective because it differs from today’s code. Compliance questions depend on the approvals and rules that applied to the work at the relevant time.

Which alterations changed drainage? | [Interwar homes](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/interwar-homes-1920s-40s) → [timber fabric](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/weatherboard-homes) or [masonry construction](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/brick-veneer-vs-double-brick). |
| 1950s–70s | What is the wall system? What was replaced? Will proposed work disturb suspect materials? | [Postwar homes](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/postwar-homes-1950s-70s) → [renovation sequence](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/planning-a-renovation) → material and service evidence. |
| 1980s–90s | Which wet areas, roof details and services are original? Is the recent work cosmetic or a documented renewal? | [1980s–90s homes](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/homes-1980s-90s) → [movement](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/cracks-structural-or-cosmetic) or [damp investigation](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/damp-and-moisture-in-your-home). |
| 2000s onward, house | Do approval and completion records match the home? What happens at roof, window, balcony and ground junctions? | [Modern homes](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/modern-homes-2000s-on) → drainage, defect history and repair evidence. |
| Apartment or shared scheme, any era | What is shared, what is already known about the building, and how will work be paid for? | [Apartment due diligence](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/buying-an-apartment-strata) → [scheme records](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/reading-your-owners-corporation-report) → technical reports and funding. |

## Read four timelines, not one build year
**The four timelines that usually matter**

| Timeline | What to establish | Why it changes the inspection |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Original construction | Footings, wall system, roof form, floor system, openings and original services where known | This establishes the base construction and the era-linked questions that remain relevant. |
| Major alterations | Extensions, enclosed verandas, wall removal, re-roofing, window replacement, façade work and structural changes | Later work may be built under a different code era, may hide original fabric and can create junctions where water or movement concentrates. |
| Wet areas and services | Bathroom, laundry, kitchen, wiring, switchboard, plumbing, hot water, heating/cooling and solar upgrade dates | These systems often age independently of the shell. The house age is a poor proxy for their current age. |
| Repairs and defects | Leaks, cracking, termite treatment, underpinning/restumping, roof repairs, drainage works, cladding or waterproofing rectification | A repair can be reassuring only when the cause, scope, completion and present performance are understood. |

This is why a renovated older home can be harder to read than an untouched one. Renovation can solve genuine defects, but it can also hide interfaces, remove visible clues and mix materials from several periods. Keep asking **what changed, when, why and with what evidence?**

## Cross-era red flags that deserve evidence
### Water that is not being shed, drained or dried

Across every era, water is one of the highest-value things to follow. Look at the whole path: roof covering, flashings, gutters, downpipes, surface falls, openings, wall cavities, wet areas, subfloor and plumbing. The Australian Government's [repairs and maintenance guidance](https://www.yourhome.gov.au/buy-build-renovate/repairs-and-maintenance) specifically treats leaks, blocked drainage, failed flashings, damp and shower waterproofing as issues that can create larger building damage if the cause is not addressed. Use [the damp guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/damp-and-moisture-in-your-home) to separate source, path and damage.

### Movement without a timeline

Cracks are more useful when read with direction, width, associated distortion, footing type, drainage, trees, soil and change over time. A repaired crack with no explanation is not the same evidence as a diagnosed cause with monitoring and completed structural work. Use [the crack triage](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/cracks-structural-or-cosmetic) and escalate progressive or consequential movement to the appropriate professional.

### Timber-pest risk hidden by finishes or landscaping

Termites are not an 'old house' problem. Risk changes with region, construction, subfloor clearance, moisture, slab edges, service penetrations, landscaping and the condition of any management system. YourHome recommends a building and pest inspection before buying in termite-risk areas, while [QBCC guidance](https://www.qbcc.qld.gov.au/home-owner-hub/maintain-protect/protect-against-termites) shows why later landscaping, paths and renovations can undermine a termite-management system. Ask what system exists, how it has been maintained and what the latest inspection found.

### Services whose age is being guessed from the house

Do not infer wiring, plumbing or hot-water age from the build date. Look for switchboard changes, invoices, certificates and alterations, then use licensed inspection where the system matters to safety, capacity or budget. This becomes especially important where solar, battery, electric-vehicle charging or electrification has increased demand on an older electrical installation.

## Hazards with useful date screens
### Asbestos-containing materials

The [national householders' guide](https://www.newaste.org.au/asbestos/assets/asbestos-guide-for-householders.pdf) says houses built or renovated before 1990 may contain asbestos products. The [NSW asbestos timeline](https://www.asbestos.nsw.gov.au/safety/safety-in-the-home/when-was-asbestos-banned-in-australia) records the national ban from 31 December 2003. The date is a screening trigger, not a material diagnosis: follow [ASSEA’s asbestos-in-the-home guidance](https://www.asbestossafety.gov.au/about-asbestos/finding-asbestos/home) to identify suspect material before drilling, sanding, cutting or demolition and follow the licensing and disposal rules for the material, amount and jurisdiction.

### Lead in older paint

Older paint, especially pre-1970s layers, may contain much higher lead concentrations than modern coatings. Before sanding, scraping or heat stripping, follow the [Australian Government Lead Alert](https://www.agriculture.gov.au/sites/default/files/documents/lead-paint-fifth-edition.pdf), test where appropriate and use lead-safe controls.

## Later energy upgrades can create their own questions
Insulation, draught sealing, replacement glazing and cladding upgrades can improve comfort, but the work has to suit the existing building. [YourHome's condensation guidance](https://www.yourhome.gov.au/passive-design/condensation) explains that moisture risk depends on temperature, humidity, ventilation and the way roof and wall assemblies dry. For an older home, ask what insulation and membranes were actually installed, whether roof-space electrical clearances were respected, and whether a retrofit changed ventilation or moisture behaviour.

## Regional variation can outweigh decade
A decade does not erase climate or site. Tropical elevated houses, cyclone-region homes, coastal masonry, alpine roofs, bushfire construction and southern clay-soil suburbs demand different questions. Add the location to every era profile: climate, wind exposure, termites, flood and bushfire context, soil, salt, vegetation and site drainage. The most useful era guide is one that gets narrower after you add the address, not one that pretends every 1960s house behaves the same.

## Use an evidence hierarchy
1. **Start with what is actually visible:** material, crack, stain, distortion, clearance, repair, meter box, roof line or other observable clue.
2. **Then find the record:** permit, plan, invoice, certificate, warranty, previous report, pest notice, insurance correspondence or dated photo.
3. **Test the current condition:** a historical document does not prove that a system still performs today.
4. **Use the right discipline:** building inspector, engineer, electrician, plumber, pest professional, hygienist, strata specialist or lawyer where the question leaves general building guidance.
5. **Keep unknowns explicit:** inaccessible roof spaces, concealed membranes, buried drainage and undocumented alterations remain unknown until better evidence appears.

## Worked example: a 1970s brick home with cracking and damp
**Illustrative reasoning example, not an inspected property.** A listing shows stepped brick cracking near a window, a low internal stain and recent garden paving. Begin by recording those three observations separately. Do not jump from “1970s” to “failing foundations”, or assume that the stain and crack share a cause.

Next establish whether the wall is veneer or loadbearing, whether the stain responds to rain or plumbing use, and whether the paving changed levels or water disposal. Photographs predating the paving and a suitable physical inspection could strengthen or weaken a connection. If the crack is progressing with floor or opening distortion, an engineer becomes more relevant. If a local leak explains the stain, price that defined scope rather than an assumed whole-house repair.

> Note: Keep the conclusion at the level the evidence supports: observed, reported, inferred or confirmed. “Not visible in the available photographs” does not mean “absent”.

## Turn a red flag into a decision
**A red flag is useful when it changes the next step**

| Clue | Useful next question | Possible decision effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Suspect pre-1990 sheet material | What is it, where else is it present and will planned work disturb it? | Material identification, removal scope, renovation sequencing and budget. |
| Crack with sticking doors or floor distortion | Is movement active, what footing/site factors are involved and what would an engineer need to see? | Specialist investigation, repair allowance, monitoring or purchase condition. |
| Bathroom with staining below | Is the source plumbing, junctions, drainage or waterproofing, and when was the room renewed? | Moisture investigation, invasive testing if justified, repair scope or contingency. |
| Termite history | Was activity eradicated, what damage was repaired and how is the management system maintained? | Pest/structural follow-up, access improvements, ongoing inspection plan. |
| Undocumented extension | What approvals, structural changes, services and waterproofing sit behind the visible work? | Council/legal review, specialist checks, valuation of uncertainty and future renovation constraints. |
| Apartment defect in minutes | Is it lot or common property, diagnosed or suspected, funded or unfunded, resolved or ongoing? | Records review, special-levy exposure, insurance/warranty questions and purchase decision. |

For a purchase, translate the era questions into the brief for a [physical inspection](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/building-inspection-before-auction). For ownership planning, use [what your home needs by decade](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/what-your-home-needs-by-decade). Then move into the specific construction guides rather than trying to make one era label carry the whole decision.

> Important: Do not use an era guide to diagnose a defect, certify compliance or set a repair scope. It is a way to ask better questions and seek better evidence.

## Frequently asked questions
### Which era of house has the most problems?
There is no reliable ranking. Construction, region, alterations, maintenance and current condition matter more than decade alone. The era is useful because it changes the questions you ask.

### What is the asbestos screening date?
Homes built or renovated before 1990 may contain asbestos-containing materials. All uses were prohibited nationally from 31 December 2003. The date is a screening trigger; material identification is still required before disturbance.

### Does an old home definitely have lead paint?
No. Older coatings are a higher-priority screen, especially pre-1970s layers. Testing establishes presence and concentration. Use lead-safe methods before disturbance.

### Can build year tell me how old the wiring or plumbing is?
No. Services may be renewed, extended or mixed across several eras. Use records and licensed inspection to establish what is installed, how it was altered and whether it suits current use.

### Are termites mainly a problem in older houses?
No. Termite risk depends on location, moisture, access, construction details and the management system. Newer slab-on-ground homes can also be vulnerable if barriers, slab edges, penetrations or inspection zones are compromised.

### Does a renovation remove the risks of an older era?
Not automatically. Renovation can solve issues, but it can also retain concealed original fabric, introduce new junctions or mix several construction periods. Establish what was actually renewed and what stayed.

### What should I check in a modern apartment?
Read both the lot and the shared building: registered plan, common-property defects, external walls and cladding, waterproofing, fire systems, developer/warranty pathways, insurance, minutes, planned works and funding.

### Should I compare a home with current building-code requirements?
Current requirements can help explain good building principles, but an older building is not automatically defective because it differs from today’s code. Compliance questions depend on the approvals and rules that applied to the work at the relevant time.

## Method
We treat the build date as a first-pass risk map, then test four separate timelines: original construction, later alterations, services/wet areas and defect/repair history.

## Limitations
Construction practice varies by region, building type, climate and alteration history. An era profile cannot diagnose a defect or establish compliance; confirm materials, condition and service age through property-specific evidence.

### Read the whole pattern

- **Context:** What is around it: openings, floors, drainage, the soil
- **Change:** Whether it is growing. Date it, measure it, come back.

_Read growth, width, direction, distortion and location together. Escalate concerning movement._

sections.heading: Use width as one observation in a larger pattern
sections.markdown:
Measure the crack where it is safely accessible, then identify what is cracked: paint, plaster, render, mortar, brick or another structural material. Those are different observations. A narrow crack in a consequential location can need investigation, while a wider gap might be an intended joint. No width alone certifies safety, cause or repair cost.

[QBCC's subsidence guidance](https://qbcc.qld.gov.au/home-owner-hub/maintain-protect/protect-against-subsidence) considers cracking alongside bulging walls, distorted openings, drainage and changes around the building. This guide uses that contextual approach. The table below is Homechecker's practical triage, not a reproduction of an Australian Standard's damage categories or a compliance test.

**Choose the next step from the whole observation**

| What is observed | What needs establishing | Proportionate response |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fine surface crack without known distortion | Material, age of finish and whether the crack is stable | Record it and clarify with the inspector if the cause or history is uncertain. |
| Crack recurring through repairs or accompanied by sticking openings | Whether the movement is active and which elements move together | Arrange assessment; obtain repair history and dated observations. |
| Stepped masonry cracking or cracking near an opening | Wall system, support above the opening, joints and associated distortion | A building inspection can identify the need for structural engineering advice. |
| Sudden displacement, bulging, loose masonry or loss of support | Immediate stability and safe access | Keep away from potentially unstable areas and obtain urgent professional assistance. |

sections.heading: Read the crack and its surroundings together
sections.markdown:
_[Illustration: Architectural material study showing a fine plaster hairline, a diagonal crack from a window corner and stepped cracking along masonry joints. Record the material, pattern and surrounding distortion. A photograph supports an observation, not a diagnosis of its cause.]_

Use a wider photograph to show the room or elevation, a middle-distance view to locate the crack around an opening or junction, and a close view with a scale. Note whether the line follows a finish joint, mortar joints or passes through units. Keep its location identifiable so another person can compare the same place later.

Look for associated changes: a door that has recently begun binding, a gap at an extension junction, a displaced sill or a floor that appears uneven. Report what changed and when. A long-standing sloping floor and a new sticking door are not interchangeable evidence. Do not force an opening or enter an unstable area to complete a checklist.

sections.heading: The wall system changes the question
sections.markdown:
In brick veneer, the visible masonry and the internal frame have different roles. In cavity or solid masonry, a cracked wall may also carry building loads. [YourHome identifies these different masonry arrangements](https://www.yourhome.gov.au/materials/brickwork-and-blockwork). Confirm the actual construction, including later additions, before deciding what the visible crack might affect.

An internal lining crack can occur over a joint without establishing damage in the structure behind it. Equally, a clean internal face does not prove the outer masonry is adequately supported or restrained. Ask what was accessible on both sides and what remained concealed. The [wall-system guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/brick-veneer-vs-double-brick) develops the load-path and moisture questions.

sections.heading: Several mechanisms can produce similar-looking cracks
sections.markdown:
### Footing movement is one possibility

Ground moisture changes, drainage problems and changes around footings can be relevant. [YourHome discusses reactive soils, settlement and drainage among possible causes](https://www.yourhome.gov.au/buy-build-renovate/repairs-and-maintenance). A site classification or suburb's reputation does not diagnose the movement in one home. Ask for the actual footing arrangement, any geotechnical information and the condition evidence.

sections.heading: Separate local components from wider movement
sections.markdown:
A crack near a window raises questions about the opening support and local masonry as well as the foundations. A crack at an addition raises questions about the junction between construction phases. Repeated cracks in a finish raise questions about the substrate, joint and repair method. Keep plausible explanations separate until the inspection provides evidence to connect them.

Do not prescribe tree removal, underpinning or drainage excavation from a photograph. [QBCC warns that planting and removing trees can both affect footings](https://qbcc.qld.gov.au/home-owner-hub/maintain-protect/protect-against-subsidence). A response intended to help can change the moisture regime again. Engineering, arboricultural or drainage advice may be needed together where those factors are implicated.

sections.heading: Use time carefully; do not postpone a necessary assessment
sections.markdown:
Dated repeat observations can show whether a crack has changed, but monitoring is useful only when the situation is suitable for it. Ask the professional what to record, how often and what change should trigger action. One photograph labelled 'old crack' supplies no measured history. Fresh filler or paint can make comparison harder without proving that anyone intended to conceal a problem.

Keep a fixed location and a consistent measurement method. Record repair dates, significant rainfall, drainage works and changes to nearby trees or structures. A crack that opens and closes seasonally still needs its effects understood; seasonal behaviour is not automatically harmless. Short monitoring during a house purchase may not span the conditions that matter. If the decision deadline arrives first, the uncertainty remains explicit.

sections.heading: Brief the professional with a question they can answer
sections.markdown:
A competent building inspector can record the accessible pattern and recommend specialist follow-up. Ask a structural engineer to assess significance and likely mechanism where structural movement, support or stability is in question. The engineer may need floor levels, access, drawings, soil information or service testing. A conclusion can be provisional if that evidence is unavailable.

**A useful crack-assessment brief**

| Provide | Ask |
| --- | --- |
| Location, photographs, measurements and change history | Which elements are affected and what evidence supports the proposed explanation? |
| Plans, alteration dates and previous repairs | Does the repair address the cause, the damage or only the finish? |
| Known drainage, tree or service changes | What further test would change the assessment or repair scope? |
| Purchase or renovation deadline | What can be concluded now, and what uncertainty cannot be resolved in time? |

sections.heading: Price the established scope and its remaining uncertainty
sections.markdown:
Crack filling, local masonry repair, opening-support work and footing intervention solve different problems. A quote for one should not be used as a budget for another. Ask whether the estimate includes investigation, cause treatment, access, associated services and reinstatement. If further opening-up may change the scope, record that dependency rather than hiding it in a single reassuring number.

Review previous work the same way. 'Underpinned' or 'restumped' needs a location, date, design and scope. A repair to one corner is not evidence that every footing was renewed. Compare the documented area with today's symptoms and use the [interwar guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/interwar-homes-1920s-40s) where mixed supports or later additions complicate the picture.

sections.heading: Worked example: repaired cracking at an extension
sections.markdown:
**Illustrative reasoning example, not an inspected property.** A 1960s home has new paint over a stepped crack at a rear extension and a door that binds. The seller provides an invoice for local brickwork repair two years earlier. Record the repaired area, the present crack and the binding door separately; the invoice does not establish the cause or prove that the repair failed structurally.

Compare earlier photographs, establish the original and extension supports, and brief an assessment of the junction and associated distortion. A stable joint with an unsuitable finish repair leads to a different scope from continuing movement with support damage. Until the evidence distinguishes those possibilities, neither a filler allowance nor an underpinning budget is a confirmed answer.

> Important: Sudden movement, unstable masonry or loss of support needs urgent attention. Keep clear of the affected area. For a purchase, complete necessary investigation before commitment using the [report-reading guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/how-to-read-a-building-and-pest-report).

faqs.question: When should I investigate a wall crack?
faqs.answer: Seek assessment when it is changing, recurring through repairs, accompanied by distortion or water entry, or affects a potentially structural element. Sudden movement or unstable material needs urgent attention.

faqs.question: Are cracks a dealbreaker when buying?
faqs.answer: That depends on the assessed consequence, repair scope and uncertainty. Obtain the relevant investigation early enough to inform the purchase rather than deciding from a crack photograph alone.

faqs.question: How wide does a crack need to be to worry?
faqs.answer: There is no universal safe width. Read width with the material, location, distortion and history. A narrow crack can matter in a critical location, and a gap can also be an intended joint.

faqs.question: What causes structural cracks?
faqs.answer: Possible mechanisms include footing or ground movement, local support problems, alterations and material behaviour. Similar patterns can have different causes; the building and site need assessment.

faqs.question: Should I get an engineer or is a building inspection enough?
faqs.answer: A building inspector can record accessible concerns and recommend follow-up. An appropriately qualified structural engineer assesses structural significance and repair needs where indicated, sometimes with further tests or specialist input.

faqs.question: Is a hairline crack anything to worry about?
faqs.answer: It may be a minor finish issue, but its location, behaviour and associated signs still matter. Hairline width alone does not certify safety or establish the cause.

faqs.question: Does a crack that moves seasonally mean the house is safe?
faqs.answer: No. Seasonal behaviour is useful history, but the extent and consequences of that movement still need interpretation.

faqs.question: Does underpinning history mean the problem is solved?
faqs.answer: Ask for the design, location, scope and follow-up evidence. Work to one area does not establish the condition of every footing or explain a different current symptom.

Do not prescribe tree removal, underpinning or drainage excavation from a photograph. [QBCC warns that planting and removing trees can both affect footings](https://qbcc.qld.gov.au/home-owner-hub/maintain-protect/protect-against-subsidence). A response intended to help can change the moisture regime again. Engineering, arboricultural or drainage advice may be needed together where those factors are implicated.

## Use time carefully; do not postpone a necessary assessment
Dated repeat observations can show whether a crack has changed, but monitoring is useful only when the situation is suitable for it. Ask the professional what to record, how often and what change should trigger action. One photograph labelled 'old crack' supplies no measured history. Fresh filler or paint can make comparison harder without proving that anyone intended to conceal a problem.

Keep a fixed location and a consistent measurement method. Record repair dates, significant rainfall, drainage works and changes to nearby trees or structures. A crack that opens and closes seasonally still needs its effects understood; seasonal behaviour is not automatically harmless. Short monitoring during a house purchase may not span the conditions that matter. If the decision deadline arrives first, the uncertainty remains explicit.

## Brief the professional with a question they can answer
A competent building inspector can record the accessible pattern and recommend specialist follow-up. Ask a structural engineer to assess significance and likely mechanism where structural movement, support or stability is in question. The engineer may need floor levels, access, drawings, soil information or service testing. A conclusion can be provisional if that evidence is unavailable.

**A useful crack-assessment brief**

| Provide | Ask |
| --- | --- |
| Location, photographs, measurements and change history | Which elements are affected and what evidence supports the proposed explanation? |
| Plans, alteration dates and previous repairs | Does the repair address the cause, the damage or only the finish? |
| Known drainage, tree or service changes | What further test would change the assessment or repair scope? |
| Purchase or renovation deadline | What can be concluded now, and what uncertainty cannot be resolved in time? |

## Price the established scope and its remaining uncertainty
Crack filling, local masonry repair, opening-support work and footing intervention solve different problems. A quote for one should not be used as a budget for another. Ask whether the estimate includes investigation, cause treatment, access, associated services and reinstatement. If further opening-up may change the scope, record that dependency rather than hiding it in a single reassuring number.

Review previous work the same way. 'Underpinned' or 'restumped' needs a location, date, design and scope. A repair to one corner is not evidence that every footing was renewed. Compare the documented area with today's symptoms and use the [interwar guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/interwar-homes-1920s-40s) where mixed supports or later additions complicate the picture.

## Worked example: repaired cracking at an extension
**Illustrative reasoning example, not an inspected property.** A 1960s home has new paint over a stepped crack at a rear extension and a door that binds. The seller provides an invoice for local brickwork repair two years earlier. Record the repaired area, the present crack and the binding door separately; the invoice does not establish the cause or prove that the repair failed structurally.

Compare earlier photographs, establish the original and extension supports, and brief an assessment of the junction and associated distortion. A stable joint with an unsuitable finish repair leads to a different scope from continuing movement with support damage. Until the evidence distinguishes those possibilities, neither a filler allowance nor an underpinning budget is a confirmed answer.

> Important: Sudden movement, unstable masonry or loss of support needs urgent attention. Keep clear of the affected area. For a purchase, complete necessary investigation before commitment using the [report-reading guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/how-to-read-a-building-and-pest-report).

## Frequently asked questions
### When should I investigate a wall crack?
Seek assessment when it is changing, recurring through repairs, accompanied by distortion or water entry, or affects a potentially structural element. Sudden movement or unstable material needs urgent attention.

### Are cracks a dealbreaker when buying?
That depends on the assessed consequence, repair scope and uncertainty. Obtain the relevant investigation early enough to inform the purchase rather than deciding from a crack photograph alone.

### How wide does a crack need to be to worry?
There is no universal safe width. Read width with the material, location, distortion and history. A narrow crack can matter in a critical location, and a gap can also be an intended joint.

### What causes structural cracks?
Possible mechanisms include footing or ground movement, local support problems, alterations and material behaviour. Similar patterns can have different causes; the building and site need assessment.

### Should I get an engineer or is a building inspection enough?
A building inspector can record accessible concerns and recommend follow-up. An appropriately qualified structural engineer assesses structural significance and repair needs where indicated, sometimes with further tests or specialist input.

### Is a hairline crack anything to worry about?
It may be a minor finish issue, but its location, behaviour and associated signs still matter. Hairline width alone does not certify safety or establish the cause.

### Does a crack that moves seasonally mean the house is safe?
No. Seasonal behaviour is useful history, but the extent and consequences of that movement still need interpretation.

### Does underpinning history mean the problem is solved?
Ask for the design, location, scope and follow-up evidence. Work to one area does not establish the condition of every footing or explain a different current symptom.

## Method
We record the visible pattern, distinguish possible mechanisms and identify the evidence needed before a structural conclusion or repair scope. The triage table is editorial guidance, not a standard classification.

## Limitations
A structural engineer can diagnose the significance and cause for the building in front of them. Visible progression or movement affecting doors, floors and openings deserves professional investigation.

sections.heading: Opening
sections.markdown:
### You are joining the building too
- **Lot:** Your four walls: condition, services, alterations
- **Common property:** Everyone’s walls: the fabric and systems the plan makes shared
- **Scheme:** The scheme: its money, its minutes, its decisions

_Start with the registered plan, then read it with the legislation and scheme records._

sections.heading: Read the lot and the scheme together
sections.markdown:
The registered plan and state law define the lot/common-property boundary. Inspect the lot, understand owner alterations, and read scheme records for shared fabric, services, finances, insurance, disputes and decisions. Use the [shared-building risk guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/strata-risks-for-owners) to connect each issue to its boundary, decision maker and funding path. Check:

- **Maintenance / sinking fund balance:** is there enough set aside for the building’s age and the works it will need?
- **Special levies:** any raised recently, or foreshadowed in the meeting minutes?
- **Quarterly fees:** the ongoing cost, and the trend. Are they rising, and why?
- **Insurance:** what does the scheme policy insure, for what declared value, with which excesses, exclusions, claims and valuation basis?
- **Disputes & defects:** litigation, building-defect claims, or major works on the horizon.
- **By-laws / rules:** restrictions on pets, renovations or short-term letting that may affect how you use or rent the apartment.

sections.heading: Where to find it
sections.markdown: Available documents and disclosure routes differ by state. In Victoria, relevant owners-corporation information forms part of the [Section 32 process](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/reading-a-section-32); elsewhere, certificates, searches or records inspections take different forms. Commission the appropriate search early enough to review minutes, financials, maintenance plans, insurance, defects, disputes, notices and correspondence. Missing or thin records are a substantive evidence gap worth investigating.

sections.heading: The funding gap is the tell
sections.markdown: A fund balance has meaning only beside the building's forecast and known works, levy income, arrears, liabilities and timing. A low balance may be appropriate after completed work or inadequate for imminent work; a high balance may still be insufficient for a large program. Liability for a special levy can turn on the resolution, instalment due dates, state law, disclosure, contract and settlement adjustments. Have the legal representative map each known or proposed amount to this contract.

sections.heading: Then check the building itself
sections.markdown:
Use scheme records for boundaries, decisions, funding, insurance and known projects. Use a physical inspection for the lot and accessible common areas. Three recurring apartment questions deserve attention:

### Waterproofing and balcony membranes

Failed waterproofing in bathrooms and balconies is a recurring apartment defect category. Repair can cross common property and multiple lots, with costs funded through the scheme.

### Combustible cladding

Where external cladding is a concern, obtain the material assessment, any authority notices, rectification scope and completion evidence. Appearance and build decade cannot establish the product or the building's fire-safety position. Follow the issue through the records, including funding and unresolved stages.

### Builder defects

Newer buildings carry the risk of original builder defects, waterproofing, fire separation, structural and services issues that emerge in the first years. The minutes will often show whether defects have been identified, pursued, and resolved, or are still in dispute. See [red flags by era](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/red-flags-by-era) for what newer buildings tend to hide.

sections.heading: Start with what you are actually buying
sections.markdown:
Match the contract's lot numbers with the apartment, parking space and storage you were shown. A space may be a separate lot, part of the apartment lot, common property subject to exclusive-use rights or something governed by another arrangement. Ask the legal reviewer to show you the basis for its use and any conditions. Paint on a parking bay and an agent's description do not establish title.

[NSW's buyer guidance](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/strata/buying-a-strata-property) recommends reviewing titling information, by-laws and scheme records. For a building with shared facilities, ask whether more than one owners corporation or management arrangement is involved. A mixed retail/residential building can have costs and decisions outside the apartment scheme's familiar quarterly levy.

sections.heading: Read the sequence of a defect through the records
sections.markdown:
**Follow an issue beyond the first mention**

| Stage | What to request | What remains open |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Complaint or observation | Location, dates, photographs and correspondence | The cause and affected extent may still be unknown. |
| Investigation | Actual technical report, scope and access limitations | An assessment can recommend more investigation rather than a final repair. |
| Decision | Resolution, accepted scope and approvals | Voting for work does not show it is fully funded or complete. |
| Delivery | Contract, progress records and variations | A paid invoice alone does not establish performance. |
| Close-out | Completion evidence, follow-up reports and recurrence history | Check whether related stages or other areas remain outstanding. |

A search report summarises the material made available on a particular date. If it mentions an engineer's report but does not include it, obtain the report. If a later meeting was pending, ask for the decision. Where minutes say 'resolved', establish whether that means the motion was passed, the dispute was settled or the physical defect was repaired. Those are different outcomes for a buyer.

sections.heading: Compare the cash with the work and its timing
sections.markdown:
Read the works forecast against actual cash, approved contributions, arrears, committed expenditure and the latest quotations. A forecast prepared before a newly discovered defect may no longer describe the building's needs. [NSW's finance guidance](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/strata/living/levies-finances-insurance) distinguishes day-to-day expenditure from capital works and explains how contributions fund the scheme. Other states use different terminology and requirements.

An illustrative calculation helps expose the questions. Suppose a scheme has $120,000 available for a quoted $300,000 project, with no other funding committed: the apparent gap is $180,000. That is not yet your personal levy. Confirm whether the quoted scope is complete, whether the cash is already committed elsewhere, what future contributions or borrowing are approved and which lawful allocation applies to your lot. Do not divide by the number of apartments and treat the result as a liability.

sections.heading: Read shared services and insurance as ongoing obligations
sections.markdown:
Lifts, central hot water, pumps, ventilation, fire systems and embedded utilities create operating and renewal obligations even where the building looks tidy. Ask about service contracts, recent breakdowns, replacement proposals and the effect of outages on your apartment. A low-rise walk-up and a tower with multiple lifts have different cost structures; the comparison needs the assets as well as the levy.

Obtain the current insurance schedule and relevant policy terms, valuation information, excesses and records of claims or restrictions. Ask how known defects and completed rectification have been communicated to the insurer. A certificate showing that insurance exists does not settle whether a particular event would be covered or what you would pay. Cross-check material uncertainties with the insurer or broker using [the condition and insurance guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/home-condition-and-insurance).

sections.heading: State rules and your intended use change the review
sections.markdown:
In Victoria, follow the owners-corporation disclosure within the [Section 32 process](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/reading-a-section-32). In NSW, a section 184 certificate provides specified scheme information, while a records search gives access to a broader history; one is not a substitute for every document in the other. In Queensland, use [the current seller-disclosure guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/seller-disclosure-qld) and ask which body-corporate certificate and records apply. Have the legal reviewer identify the exact route for the property rather than assuming the same bundle is mandatory nationally.

Tell that reviewer what you intend to do: keep a pet, change flooring, renovate a bathroom, install air conditioning, charge an electric vehicle or let the apartment. Ask for the relevant rules, approvals and any maintenance responsibility transferred by an earlier alteration. An attractive renovated bathroom can carry a documentation question even when there is no visible defect.

sections.heading: Worked example: low levies and an unfunded roof proposal
sections.markdown:
**Illustrative reasoning example, not an inspected property.** A 1980s walk-up has modest levies and a dry apartment on inspection day. Recent minutes discuss roof replacement but the search report contains no final quote. The fund balance looks healthy in isolation. Neither the dry room nor the cash balance establishes whether the proposed work is affordable.

Obtain the roof assessment, updated scope, financial commitments and later resolutions. The outcome could be a staged repair already funded, a major renewal requiring new contributions, or an unresolved proposal. Ask your legal representative how any resolved levy is dealt with in this contract. Keep the physical scope, scheme funding and sale allocation as three connected but separate conclusions.

> Note: Read the apartment, the shared building and the scheme together. A records inspection, legal review and physical inspection each answer a different part of the purchase.

Terminology, boundaries, disclosure and liability differ by state and registered plan. Obtain state-specific strata and legal advice.

sections.heading: Opening
sections.markdown:
### Tell the story of your home clearly
- **Describe:** Describe it straight: construction, occupancy, works, hazards
- **Insure:** Know what it is insured for, and what the fine print excludes
- **Document:** Keep dated evidence before anything goes wrong

_The policy wording has the final word. Make sure you have read it._

sections.heading: Start with two different questions
sections.markdown:
Building condition and insurance overlap, but they are not the same subject. A building assessment asks **what is this asset, what condition is it in and what may it need?** Insurance asks **what risks has this insurer agreed to cover, on what terms, for what amount and subject to what exclusions, limits and conditions?** Good decisions require both questions to be answered separately before they are brought together.

[Moneysmart](https://moneysmart.gov.au/home-insurance/choosing-home-insurance) recommends comparing the definition of the building, insured events, exclusions, limits, excesses and optional covers in the actual policy. It also recommends an insurance amount that reflects the cost to rebuild the home rather than its market value.

> Important: A crack, leak, old roof or renovation does not by itself tell you whether an insurer will offer cover, change the premium or pay a future claim. Those are policy- and fact-specific insurance questions. Building evidence helps describe the risk; the insurer and policy determine the insurance response.

sections.heading: How the physical home enters an insurance decision
sections.markdown:
When quoting or underwriting, an insurer may ask about the address, construction, roof material, year built, occupancy, use, renovations, security, claims history, local hazards or other property characteristics. Different insurers ask different questions and have different underwriting appetites. The practical rule is simple: **describe the actual property accurately and answer the questions asked**.

For consumer insurance contracts, the [Insurance Contracts Act 1984](https://www.legislation.gov.au/C2004A02944/2024-03-01/text) imposes a duty to take reasonable care not to make a misrepresentation to the insurer. That is more precise than a vague instruction to volunteer everything you can think of: read the insurer's questions carefully, answer them accurately and ask the insurer or broker if you are unsure how a property feature should be described.

sections.heading: Six insurance questions every building raises
sections.markdown:
**Where building evidence fits into the insurance decision**

| Question | Useful property evidence | What actually controls the answer |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Will this insurer offer cover? | Address, use, construction, age, alterations, hazard context, condition information and claims history where asked | The insurer’s underwriting criteria and the answers given. |
| What counts as the insured building? | Plans, building description, fixtures, outbuildings, pools, solar and other improvements | The policy definition of home/building and the schedule. |
| Which events are covered? | Property hazard context and the risks you want protected | The insured-event definitions, optional covers, exclusions, limits and endorsements. |
| How much should the building be insured for? | Dimensions, construction, finishes, slope/access, demolition and rebuild complexity | The chosen cover basis, calculator/professional estimate, policy limits and any additional or extended cover. |
| What existing condition or maintenance matters? | Inspection reports, dated photos, maintenance history and known defects | The insurer’s questions, policy wording, exclusions, conditions and the facts of any later claim. |
| What evidence would support a future claim? | Baseline photos, invoices, permits, reports, repair history and event records | Cause of loss, what the policy covers, evidence of pre-loss condition and the insurer’s assessment. |

sections.heading: Separate four things that are often blurred together
sections.markdown:
**Condition is not the same thing as an insured event**

| Concept | What it means in building terms | Insurance question to ask |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Existing condition | The state of the building before the event: age, cracking, corrosion, deterioration, prior damage, defects or repairs. | Did the insurer ask about it, and how does the policy treat pre-existing damage or condition? |
| Maintenance / gradual deterioration | Work or degradation that develops through use, weathering, wear, blocked drainage, sealant failure, corrosion or similar processes. | What maintenance, wear, deterioration or gradual-damage exclusions/conditions apply? |
| Insured event | A defined occurrence such as storm, fire, flood or another event listed by the policy. | Does the policy cover this event at this address, and how is the event defined? |
| Resulting damage | Damage that follows an event or condition, sometimes involving several causes at once. | Which part of the damage is attributed to a covered event, which part to excluded condition/deterioration, and what evidence supports that causation? |

The difficult claim is often not about whether damage exists; it is about **why it happened**. A roof may be old and a storm may also occur. A pipe may fail and surrounding materials may already have long-term moisture damage. The policy response turns on the facts, causation and wording, which is why dated condition records can be so useful.

sections.heading: Read building systems through an insurance lens, carefully
sections.markdown:
**Physical evidence that may justify an insurance question**

| Building area | Condition evidence to understand | Why it may matter | What not to assume |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Roof and rainwater goods | Age/material, corrosion, broken tiles/sheets, flashings, gutters, downpipes, prior leaks | Weather resistance, maintenance history and the condition present before any future storm or water event | An old roof is not automatically uninsurable and a leak is not automatically an insured loss. |
| Drainage and site water | Surface falls, ponding, blocked drains, low points, retaining walls and discharge paths | Water entry and storm performance can involve both event severity and property condition | Site drainage observations do not determine flood/storm coverage. Read the policy definitions. |
| Cracking and movement | Location, width, pattern, history, distortion and prior repair | Pre-existing movement can be important context if later damage occurs | A crack does not establish cause, structural significance or insurance response. |
| Wet areas and moisture | Failed sealants, grout, membranes, plumbing leaks, damp staining and repair history | Long-term leakage and sudden events can look similar after damage has spread | Visible moisture does not establish whether the cause is covered. |
| Electrical systems | Age, alterations, visible defects, switchboard and available certificates | Safety, property description and renovation history may matter to underwriting questions | A building assessment is not an electrical safety certificate. Use a licensed electrician where needed. |
| Plumbing and hot water | Pipe materials, age, leaks, corrosion, heater age/location and repair history | A later escape-of-liquid claim may turn on event and causation evidence | Old plumbing is not itself proof of a future claim outcome. |
| Timber and pests | Termite evidence, decay, subfloor moisture and previous treatment | Existing damage may be relevant to condition and maintenance rather than a later insured event | Do not infer pest absence from a clean-looking room or general inspection. |
| Renovations and additions | What changed, when, by whom, approvals, certificates and before/after records | Alterations can change value, occupancy, construction and the building description | Approval evidence does not prove present condition; missing paperwork does not by itself determine cover. |
| Pools, solar and outbuildings | Presence, type, age, structures, equipment and attachment to the property | They may be treated differently under the policy definition of building or optional cover | Do not assume every improvement is covered in the same way. Check the policy. |

sections.heading: Before you buy, test insurability as part of due diligence
sections.markdown:
If insurance availability, exclusions or price would affect your decision to buy, obtain an **address-specific quote before you commit**. This is particularly sensible where the property has unusual construction, extensive renovation, heritage fabric, unresolved defects, significant flood/bushfire/cyclone exposure or another feature you already know may require explanation.

1. **Describe the property accurately:** construction, roof, use, occupancy, renovations, pools, solar, outbuildings and other details the insurer asks about.
2. **Ask about the risks that matter at this address:** especially flood, bushfire, cyclone, storm, actions of the sea or other locally relevant hazards.
3. **Read the PDS and Key Facts Sheet:** do not compare premium alone; compare event definitions, exclusions, limits, excesses and optional covers.
4. **Check the rebuild basis:** make sure the insured amount reflects reconstruction rather than purchase price or land value.
5. **Raise known unusual features or unresolved questions:** ask the insurer or licensed broker how they want the property described and keep important answers in writing.

sections.heading: Describe the actual home, not a generic version of it
sections.markdown:
A surprising amount of insurance quality starts with an accurate property description. Construction type, roof material, year built, occupancy, business use, short-term letting, security, renovations, pools, solar systems, outbuildings and past losses can all be relevant if the insurer asks about them. If you do not know whether the walls are brick veneer, double brick, lightweight cladding or another system, use plans, reports or qualified assessment rather than guessing.

The same applies to alterations. A property advertised as renovated may contain work from several different periods. Keep permits, plans, invoices, certificates and photographs where available so the description of the home can be anchored to evidence rather than memory.

sections.heading: Read exclusions and conditions against the building you actually own
sections.markdown:
Policies cover defined risks and also contain exclusions, limits and conditions. [Moneysmart](https://moneysmart.gov.au/home-insurance/choosing-home-insurance) recommends checking what is and is not covered in the PDS. Depending on the policy, wording can address matters such as wear, gradual deterioration, defects, vermin, ground movement, water damage, maintenance, vacancy or unoccupied periods. The wording varies, so a generic list is never a substitute for the actual policy.

The right question is not 'does insurance cover leaks?' or 'does insurance cover cracks?' in the abstract. Ask: **what caused this damage, what event does the policy define, what exclusions or conditions apply, and what evidence establishes the timeline and cause?**

sections.heading: Set the rebuild basis from the building, not the property price
sections.markdown:
Home building insurance is about repairing or rebuilding the insured structure, not replacing the land or reproducing the market price. [Moneysmart warns that underinsurance can leave a household unable to meet the full rebuild cost](https://moneysmart.gov.au/home-insurance/home-underinsurance) and recommends reviewing cover as costs and the property change.

**Inputs that can move a rebuild estimate**

| Input | Why it matters to reconstruction |
| --- | --- |
| Floor area and building form | More area, levels, complex geometry and attached structures change quantities and access. |
| Construction and finishes | Masonry, lightweight systems, heritage fabric, custom joinery and higher-grade finishes can carry different replacement costs. |
| Site access and slope | Restricted access, steep sites, retaining and difficult demolition can materially change rebuild logistics. |
| Demolition and debris removal | A total-loss rebuild often includes work before new construction can begin. |
| Professional and statutory costs | Design, engineering, approvals and other professional/statutory inputs may be relevant depending on the loss and policy. |
| Code and standard changes | Reconstruction may need to satisfy requirements different from those applying when the original building was built. |
| Pools, garages, decks, solar and other structures | Whether and how these are included depends on the policy definition and selected cover. |
| Cost escalation after a disaster | Demand, labour and material constraints can change actual reconstruction cost; check whether the policy provides any additional/extended cover. |

Use a detailed insurer or industry calculator and keep the inputs. Consider a professional rebuild estimate for heritage, high-value, unusual, extensively altered or otherwise complex buildings.

sections.heading: Hazard risk and building condition are different layers
sections.markdown:
Flood, storm, bushfire, cyclone and other natural hazards are address-specific exposures. Building condition influences how a home may perform, but hazard exposure is not established by a building inspection alone. [Moneysmart's storm, flood and fire guidance](https://moneysmart.gov.au/home-insurance/storm-flood-and-fire-insurance) recommends checking local hazard information and the policy definition of the event.

**Keep hazard, resilience and insurance separate but connected**

| Layer | Question |
| --- | --- |
| Hazard | Can flood, bushfire, cyclone, storm surge or another event affect this address, and at what severity/frequency? |
| Building vulnerability | How might the actual roof, openings, drainage, floor level, materials or surrounding site respond? |
| Resilience | What practical work could reduce damage or improve recovery? |
| Insurance | Does this policy cover the relevant event, at what excess/limit and subject to what definition or exclusion? |

sections.heading: Renovations change both the asset and the insurance story
sections.markdown:
Renovations can change occupancy, security, construction, services, value and the period during which parts of a home are open or incomplete. Before significant work begins, tell the insurer or broker what is planned and ask whether the policy continues unchanged, requires an endorsement or excludes/limits part of the construction period. Do the same for extended vacancy, short-term letting, business use or another change where the policy asks you to notify the insurer.

After work is complete, update the rebuild amount and property description where necessary. Keep contracts, approved plans, permits, certificates, warranties, invoices and before/during/after photographs. Those records can explain both **what changed** and **what existed before a later loss**.

sections.heading: Build an evidence stack before you ever need to claim
sections.markdown:
- **Identity and construction:** plans, specifications, property description, dimensions and major construction details.
- **Baseline condition:** dated exterior, roof-from-ground, room, wet-area, service and improvement photographs; inspection reports where available.
- **Maintenance:** invoices, service records, cleaning/clearing records where material, repair recommendations and evidence that identified work was completed.
- **Renovations:** contracts, permits, plans, certificates, warranties, product details and before/during/after photographs.
- **Monitoring:** crack measurements, moisture investigations, leak history, pest treatment and other time-series evidence where a condition is being watched.
- **Insurance:** proposal answers, schedules, PDS versions, Key Facts Sheets, endorsements, renewal notices and important written answers from the insurer or broker.
- **Loss:** photographs before clean-up where safe, emergency-work invoices, damaged-item evidence, weather/event information and a contemporaneous timeline of what occurred.

These records do not guarantee a claim. They improve the evidence available to establish what the building was, what work had been done, what condition existed beforehand and how the loss unfolded. Continue with [keeping a record of your home](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/keeping-a-record-of-your-home).

sections.heading: When a claim happens, preserve cause and timeline
sections.markdown:
If damage occurs, protect people and prevent further loss where it is safe to do so, then follow the insurer's claim instructions. [Moneysmart's claims guidance](https://moneysmart.gov.au/home-insurance/how-to-make-a-home-insurance-claim) recommends reviewing the policy and keeping records through the claims process. Photographs before clean-up, emergency invoices, dates, communications and any expert reports can help distinguish the event itself from pre-existing or progressive condition.

> Important: The policy schedule, PDS, Key Facts Sheet, endorsements, insurer questions, applicable insurance law and the facts of the loss determine cover. For property-specific insurance advice, confirm the position with the insurer or a licensed insurance broker; for a disputed claim, obtain appropriate specialist or legal advice.

faqs.question: Does my home's condition affect my insurance premium?
faqs.answer: It can be relevant to underwriting where the insurer asks about condition or related property characteristics, but there is no universal formula. Location, hazard, construction, use, claims history, rebuild cost and insurer appetite can all affect the quote.

faqs.question: Do I have to tell my insurer about every defect?
faqs.answer: For consumer insurance, the legal duty is to take reasonable care not to make a misrepresentation. Answer the insurer’s questions accurately and ask the insurer or broker if you are unsure how a known property feature should be described. Policy notification obligations can also apply after cover starts.

faqs.question: Does an old roof mean storm damage will not be covered?
faqs.answer: Not automatically. The outcome depends on the policy wording and the facts, including the cause of damage and any relevant exclusions or conditions. Evidence of the roof’s pre-loss condition can be important.

faqs.question: Does insurance cover gradual leaks or failed waterproofing?
faqs.answer: Policies differ and causation matters. Check the actual event definitions, water-damage cover, exclusions for wear/gradual deterioration/defects and any maintenance conditions. Do not rely on a generic answer.

faqs.question: Will maintenance lower my premium?
faqs.answer: It may or may not affect price depending on the insurer and measure. The more reliable benefit is reducing avoidable damage and maintaining evidence that the property has been looked after. Ask the insurer before spending money for an assumed premium benefit.

faqs.question: Does a condition report guarantee a claim will be paid?
faqs.answer: No. A report can establish useful evidence about pre-loss condition and timing. The cause, policy wording, exclusions, limits and insurer assessment determine the claim.

faqs.question: Should I get an insurance quote before buying?
faqs.answer: Yes where insurance availability, price or exclusions could affect the purchase decision, particularly for hazard-exposed, heritage, unusual, extensively renovated or defect-affected properties.

faqs.question: Is the rebuild cost the same as the purchase price?
faqs.answer: No. The purchase price includes land and market factors. Building insurance should be based on the cost to repair or rebuild the insured structure and applicable associated costs under the policy.

faqs.question: How do I avoid underinsurance?
faqs.answer: Use a detailed rebuild calculator or professional estimate where appropriate, keep the property inputs accurate, update the amount after renovations and review it regularly as construction costs change.

faqs.question: Should I tell the insurer before renovating?
faqs.answer: For significant work, ask the insurer or broker before work starts whether the proposed renovation changes cover, requires an endorsement or creates a construction-period limitation. Keep the answer and the project records.

faqs.question: What records are most useful after a claim?
faqs.answer: Dated pre-loss photos, maintenance and repair records, renovation documents, policy records, photographs of the damage before clean-up where safe, emergency invoices, communications and a clear event timeline can all help establish what happened.
