guides.contentMarkdown:
# Period homes (pre-1920s): what to expect and what they need

With a pre-1920s home, start below the floor and at the base of the walls. Identify the actual footing, floor and wall systems, check subfloor clearance and ventilation, drainage, low-wall moisture and salt, then follow water up through roofs, chimneys and openings. After that, map the service upgrades, wet areas, extensions and repairs that may be decades younger than the original shell. Treat older coatings and pre-1990 alterations as material-identification questions before disturbance, and check any heritage controls separately from physical condition.

## Research note
Pre-1920s homes need a fabric-first reading: actual footings and floor, subfloor clearance, older masonry and moisture, roof/chimney junctions, timber and pest access, then the services and renovations layered in later. National YourHome guidance supports the moisture, termite, maintenance and existing-home checks; the multi-agency [salt attack and rising damp guide](https://cdn.environment.sa.gov.au/environment/docs/saltdamp_techguide.pdf) adds specialist context for historic masonry and compatible repair.

## Opening
### Read it from the ground up
- **Stand:** Footings, floor and subfloor showing how the house is supported today
- **Dry:** Drainage, older masonry, roof and chimneys showing how water moves
- **Layers:** Services, wet areas and additions proving which parts are actually younger

_Old fabric is not a defect. Unexplained movement, moisture or incompatible repair is the question._

## Style is the label; construction is the evidence
Pre-1920s housing includes terraces, cottages and villas, freestanding masonry houses, timber-framed homes and many regional forms. Victorian, Edwardian and Federation are useful style labels, but they do not tell you whether the building sits on timber stumps, masonry piers, strip footings or a later mixed foundation, nor whether the walls are solid masonry, framed and clad, rendered, altered or partly rebuilt.

That distinction matters because the same visible symptom can mean different things in different assemblies. Floor slope in a raised timber house sends you toward stumps, bearers, joists, moisture and termite evidence. Low-wall deterioration in older masonry sends you toward ground levels, drainage, damp-proofing, salts and repair compatibility. A rear extension may sit on a completely different footing system from the original front rooms.

> Note: Do not inspect a 'Victorian house'. Inspect this footing system, this wall system, this roof, this subfloor and every later layer attached to them.

## A century-old house is usually several houses layered together
**Separate the original shell from the work that followed**

| Layer | What to establish | Common evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Original shell | Footings, floor, walls, roof structure, chimneys and original openings | Subfloor/roof access, visible materials, plans where available and building inspection |
| Early alterations | Enclosed verandas, lean-tos, fireplaces removed, reroofing, early plumbing or electrical work | Changes in materials, floor levels, roof lines, old permits or plans and service evidence |
| Mid-century work | Bathrooms, kitchens, sheet materials, services and additions installed decades after the original build | Material identification, invoices/records where they survive, physical junctions and pre-1990 hazard screening |
| Recent renovation | Restumping, rewiring, replumbing, roofing, insulation, wet areas, extensions and cosmetic work | Invoices, permits/certificates where applicable, photographs, warranties and present condition |
| Repair history | Damp treatment, termite work, cracking, drainage changes and recurring leaks | Reports, scopes, before/after photos, monitoring and evidence that the cause was resolved |

A renovated period home should therefore make you ask a more precise question, not fewer questions: **which systems were actually renewed, and what remained behind the new finishes?** A new kitchen does not date the subfloor. New paint does not date the roof plumbing. A restumping invoice does not tell you the condition of every bearer, joist or masonry wall.

## Start at ground level: footings, floor and subfloor
Raised timber floors are common in many period homes, but not universal. Identify whether the property uses timber or concrete stumps, masonry piers, strip footings, suspended floors or later concrete additions. Then look for differential floor levels, sticking doors, distorted openings, cracks, decayed timber, improvised packing, evidence of earlier restumping or underpinning and changes where old and new construction meet.

Subfloor moisture deserves particular attention. [YourHome's maintenance guidance](https://www.yourhome.gov.au/buy-build-renovate/repairs-and-maintenance) identifies poor subfloor ventilation or clearance, leaking pipes, obstructed vents and excess ground moisture as sources of underfloor and wall-cavity moisture. Garden beds, mulch, additions and later paving can quietly reduce the clearance or ventilation an older house once relied on.

**Ground-level clues and the questions they should trigger**

| Clue | Possible pathways | Evidence to seek |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sloping or springy floor | Footing movement, stump/pier deterioration, bearer/joist issue, local decay or historic settlement | Subfloor inspection, floor-level pattern, timber condition and movement history |
| Blocked or buried vents | Reduced subfloor drying, later landscaping or paving, addition built over original ventilation | Clearance around vents, subfloor humidity/moisture evidence and drainage route |
| Garden beds or paving against walls | Bridged damp-proofing, splashback, reduced inspection access and higher local moisture | Damp-proof course where visible, ground levels, moisture/salt pattern and stormwater behaviour |
| Cracks at old/new junction | Different footing systems, differential movement, poor connection or simple finish cracking | Plan/alteration date, crack pattern, distortion, monitoring and structural advice where indicated |
| Timber close to soil | Decay and termite access risk | Clearance, pest evidence, moisture source and professional pest inspection |

## Older masonry needs a moisture diagnosis before a cosmetic repair
Low-wall staining, fretting, blistered paint or salt deposits are not one diagnosis. Moisture can arrive from capillary rise, a bridged or deteriorated damp-proof course, roof or plumbing leaks, hard paving and poor drainage, garden irrigation, condensation or an old event that left salts behind. The first task is to identify the source and pathway, not to choose a coating.

The multi-agency [Salt attack and rising damp technical guide](https://cdn.environment.sa.gov.au/environment/docs/saltdamp_techguide.pdf) for historic and older buildings warns that hard cement repairs can be incompatible with older lime-based masonry and can shift moisture and salt damage into the surrounding brick or stone. Heritage Victoria likewise publishes specific guidance on lime mortars, repointing and rising damp. That does not mean every pre-1920 wall needs lime work. It means the existing masonry and mortar should be identified before repointing, rendering or sealing it.

If the damp pattern is significant, recurring or structurally consequential, use [the damp and moisture guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/damp-and-moisture-in-your-home) to separate rain, ground, plumbing and condensation pathways and bring in the appropriate specialist before destructive treatment.

## Roof, chimneys and rainwater are a connected system
Period roofs may include slate, terracotta, corrugated metal or later replacement coverings. What matters is not only the field of the roof but the junctions: valleys, flashings, parapets, chimney abutments, penetrations, gutters, downpipes and where the water goes after it leaves the roof. A sound-looking roof can still leak at one poorly maintained junction.

Chimneys deserve their own line in the inspection. Check masonry condition, mortar, flashings, caps and whether redundant fireplaces or flues have been altered. Water entry at a chimney can present as ceiling or wall staining well away from the obvious external defect. Heritage Victoria's maintenance material puts structural soundness and watertightness ahead of cosmetic conservation, which is the right sequence for a buyer too.

## Timber, openings and termites: keep access visible
Older timber floors, bearers, joists, weatherboards, joinery and roof framing can remain serviceable for very long periods when they stay dry and ventilated. The inspection question is therefore less about age than **moisture, pest access, section loss, movement and previous repair**. Look closely where timber meets masonry, soil, leaking wet areas or poorly ventilated subfloors.

YourHome recommends termite inspection before purchase in most Australian regions and identifies inadequate subfloor clearance and ventilation, moisture, buried timber and compromised barriers as risk factors. Later decks, paths, extensions and garden work can create new access routes around an old house. A past termite treatment is useful history; it is not a substitute for current inspection access and current evidence.

## Services often tell a different age story from the building
A pre-1920s address can contain several generations of wiring, switchboards, water pipes, sewer connections, gas work, hot-water systems and heating/cooling. Establish what is installed now and what the claimed upgrade actually covered. 'Rewired' might mean a full replacement or a much narrower job. 'Replumbed' might refer only to water supply and say nothing about drains.

Before adding insulation to an existing home, [YourHome recommends a licensed electrician assess the wiring and electrical fittings](https://www.yourhome.gov.au/passive-design/insulation), specifically noting that older homes can contain damaged or outdated wiring and other hazards. That is a good model for all service upgrades: understand the existing system before covering, extending or loading it.

## Wet areas and additions belong to their own era
Most period homes have bathrooms, kitchens and laundries that are much younger than the original shell. Read each wet area by its renovation date and current moisture evidence. Look for loose finishes, swelling, failed sealants, staining, leaks below and junctions where newer waterproofing meets older floors or walls. Current NCC guidance can explain modern waterproofing principles, but it should not be used as a retrospective declaration about whether historic work complied when carried out.

Extensions need the same separation. Compare footing and floor systems, roof lines, drainage, wall materials and movement at the junction. A masonry front and lightweight rear addition can behave differently under the same seasonal conditions. Plans, permits and invoices can help date the work, while inspection tells you how the junction performs now.

## Hazardous materials follow the alteration timeline
Older coatings can contain lead. Pre-1990 additions and renovations may also introduce asbestos-containing products even though the original house predates those materials. Use [Lead Alert](https://www.agriculture.gov.au/sites/default/files/documents/lead-paint-fifth-edition.pdf) and the [national asbestos householders' guide](https://www.newaste.org.au/asbestos/assets/asbestos-guide-for-householders.pdf) before sanding, drilling, cutting or demolition. The age of the original façade is not enough to date every material behind it.

## Heritage status and physical condition are separate questions
A period appearance does not automatically mean a property is heritage-listed, and a heritage control does not tell you whether the building is in good condition. Check the planning and heritage controls that apply to the address, then assess the building fabric separately. In Victoria, the [Section 32 guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/reading-a-section-32) and [heritage-overlay guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/living-in-a-heritage-overlay) show how to read those planning layers.

Where a place is actually heritage-controlled, specialist conservation guidance can matter because repair materials and methods may need to preserve significant fabric. That is a scope and approval question, not a reason to defer ordinary water, structural or safety investigation.

## What should change the purchase decision?
**Turn period-home findings into next actions**

| Finding | Why it matters | Useful next action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unknown footing/restumping history with material floor distortion | The structural support and remaining scope are uncertain | Subfloor inspection and structural assessment where movement evidence warrants it |
| Persistent low-wall damp or salt damage | Source, masonry compatibility and concealed timber effects can alter scope | Moisture-pathway diagnosis before specifying injection, render, paint or repointing |
| Roof/chimney leakage history | Small junction defects can create widespread concealed moisture damage | Safe roof inspection and defined repair scope, then check affected internal fabric |
| Mixed or undocumented service upgrades | The visible switchboard or fixtures may not represent the whole installation | Licensed electrical/plumbing assessment focused on the actual installed systems |
| Evidence of termite activity or poor subfloor access | Extent, activity and future inspectability can be uncertain | Qualified pest inspection plus access/moisture correction plan |
| Renovated wet areas with moisture evidence | Concealed waterproofing and adjoining damage can expand the repair | Targeted moisture investigation and scope before relying on the renovation claim |
| Heritage control plus major planned alteration | Approval pathway and compatible repair method can affect design and cost | Confirm property-specific controls before committing to the renovation concept |

## A strong period home is an understood period home
The goal is not to make a century-old home behave as if it were built yesterday. It is to understand how the original fabric works, which later systems have been inserted into it, which repairs are compatible and where uncertainty could change the scope. A house with clear evidence of its footing work, roof, drainage, services, wet areas and repairs can be much easier to plan for than a younger house with unexplained defects.

Use [what your home needs by decade](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/what-your-home-needs-by-decade) for the shared era method, [the interwar guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/interwar-homes-1920s-40s) for the next construction period and [red flags by era](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/red-flags-by-era) when you need to compare several periods at once.

> Note: For a pre-1920s home, the best record is a layered one: how it stands, how it stays dry, what has been renewed, what remains old and which repairs changed the original fabric.

## Frequently asked questions
### What should I check in a pre-1920s home?
Identify the actual footing, floor, wall and roof systems; check subfloor clearance and moisture, drainage, low-wall damp and salts, roof and chimney junctions, timber/pest evidence, services, wet areas, later additions, hazardous materials and any heritage controls.

### How do I know if an old home needs restumping?
First confirm that it actually sits on stumps and identify their type. Then assess floor levels, movement, decay, drainage, timber condition and any earlier restumping or underpinning. Restumping is a property-specific scope, not an automatic requirement of age.

### Is rising damp common in period homes?
Low-wall damp is a common investigation question, but the pattern can also come from bridged damp-proofing, rain, plumbing, hard paving, garden moisture, condensation or historic salts. Diagnose the source and masonry before choosing a treatment.

### Why does mortar type matter in an old brick house?
Historic masonry may use softer lime-based mortars. Conservation guidance warns that incompatible hard cement repairs can redirect moisture and salt damage into surrounding masonry. Identify the existing materials before repointing or rendering.

### Does my period home have lead paint or asbestos?
Older coatings may contain lead, while later pre-1990 renovations can introduce asbestos-containing products. Treat both as material-identification questions before disturbance rather than assuming from the original build date.

### Can I add insulation to a period home?
Often yes, but the existing wiring, moisture behaviour, ventilation, roof-space access and hazardous materials need to be understood first. YourHome recommends an electrical safety assessment before insulation is added to an existing home.

### Can I renovate a heritage-listed period home?
Renovation is often possible, but the approval path and acceptable conservation methods depend on the property-specific heritage control. Confirm those controls before design while assessing physical defects separately.

### What makes a period home a sound purchase?
A sound purchase is one where the main uncertainties are understood: footings and subfloor, water and masonry, roof/chimneys, timber pests, services, wet areas, alterations, hazards and heritage constraints. The objective is not zero defects; it is a defensible scope and evidence trail.

## Method
We read the building from ground to roof: identify the structural and material system, follow moisture paths through subfloor and masonry, inspect roof/timber/pest interfaces, then separate every later service, wet-area and alteration timeline from the original shell.

## Limitations
Pre-1920s construction varies substantially across Australia. Heritage guidance can inform repair principles but planning controls and conservation requirements are property- and jurisdiction-specific. Diagnose moisture, structure, services and hazardous materials from property-specific records and physical evidence.

## Sources

- [Salt attack and rising damp: a guide to salt damp in historic and older buildings](https://cdn.environment.sa.gov.au/environment/docs/saltdamp_techguide.pdf) — Heritage agencies of NSW, Victoria and South Australia / Adelaide City Council; accessed 2026-09-07
- [Insulation](https://www.yourhome.gov.au/passive-design/insulation) — YourHome, Australian Government; accessed 2026-09-07
- [Lead Alert: the six step guide to painting your home](https://www.agriculture.gov.au/sites/default/files/documents/lead-paint-fifth-edition.pdf) — Australian Government; accessed 2026-07-19

guides.question: What does a postwar home (1950s–70s) need?
guides.title: Postwar homes (1950s–70s): what to expect and what they need
guides.summary: Postwar homes can be practical, adaptable buildings, but they often contain several generations of materials, services and renovation work. Read the shell first, then separate what is original from what has been replaced.
guides.answer: With a 1950s to 1970s home, first identify the actual wall, floor and footing system and what has changed since construction. Screen pre-1990 materials for possible asbestos before disturbance, establish the age and condition of wiring and plumbing, inspect roof-water disposal, drainage and footings, and read bathrooms and extensions by their own renovation dates. Termite risk, moisture and movement depend on the site and construction, not the decade alone.
guides.methodology: We separate the original shell, later alterations and current condition, then follow the highest-consequence systems: hazardous materials, water, footings, termites, wet areas and services.
guides.limitations: Confirm the age and condition of services, wet areas, footings, drainage, pest management and hazardous materials through records and physical evidence. Current code provisions are context, not a retrospective compliance test.
guides.researchNote: Postwar housing spans brick veneer, weatherboard, masonry and mixed systems with decades of later service and wet-area work. The reliable date-linked hazard screen is pre-1990 asbestos; the rest is established from the actual shell, drainage, termite/pest evidence, service history and present condition. See [YourHome's existing-house guidance](https://www.yourhome.gov.au/buy-build-renovate/buying-existing-house).

cluster.label: Read the building
cluster.blurb: Use age and construction as a starting hypothesis, then test it against evidence and physical inspection.

sections.heading: Opening
sections.markdown:
### A practical shell with decades of changes
- **Fabric:** Which shell is present: veneer, boards, masonry or mixed
- **Services:** When the wiring and plumbing were renewed, with proof
- **Hazards:** Anything pre-1990 gets screened before anyone drills into it

_The wiring in place sets the electrical question. Find its age and alteration history._

sections.heading: The houses that built the suburbs
sections.markdown:
Postwar expansion produced brick veneer, weatherboard, masonry and mixed construction across Australia, using slabs, stumps, piers and strip footings in different regions. Many of these homes have now accumulated half a century or more of bathroom renewals, extensions, service upgrades, window replacements, roof work and cosmetic renovation. The useful starting point is therefore **construction plus alteration history**, not decade alone.

A 1965 house can contain a 1965 frame, a 1988 bathroom, a 2004 extension, 2017 wiring work and a much newer hot-water system. Each layer carries its own questions. Your task is to identify which elements are original, which were renewed, and whether the evidence of that work is strong enough to budget from.

sections.heading: Start by identifying the shell
sections.markdown:
**Postwar construction clues that change the inspection**

| Element | What to establish | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| External walls | Brick veneer, weatherboard, masonry, fibre-cement or later recladding | The wall system changes how you read movement, cavities, moisture, maintenance and hidden framing. |
| Floor and footings | Raised timber floor, slab-on-ground, stumps, piers, strip footing or mixed additions | Movement, termite access, drainage and repair options differ materially between systems. |
| Roof | Tile, metal or mixed replacement; original versus later sections | Leaks often sit at flashings, valleys, gutters, penetrations and interfaces between old and new work. |
| Openings | Timber, steel or aluminium windows; later replacement glazing | Frame material, seals, flashings, drainage and condensation behaviour can differ by installation. |
| Alterations | Enclosed verandas, rear additions, wall removal, garages, decks and wet-area changes | The junction between original and later work is often where structure, drainage and waterproofing need the most evidence. |

If the house is brick veneer, use [brick veneer versus double brick](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/brick-veneer-vs-double-brick) to understand what the outer brick leaf does and what the timber frame behind it is doing. If it is weatherboard, use [the weatherboard guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/weatherboard-homes) to follow coatings, flashings, clearances and subfloor conditions.

sections.heading: Inspection priorities
sections.markdown:
### Asbestos: a high-priority pre-1990 screen

The [national householders' guide](https://www.newaste.org.au/asbestos/assets/asbestos-guide-for-householders.pdf) says homes built or renovated before 1990 may contain asbestos products. In postwar houses, suspect materials may be original or may come from later additions and refurbishments. Do not infer presence from appearance alone and do not disturb suspect material to 'check'. Identify it through the appropriate assessment pathway before drilling, sanding, cutting or demolition.

For a buyer, the practical question is not simply 'does this era contain asbestos?' It is **where might suspect material sit, will your planned work disturb it, and what evidence do you need before setting the renovation scope?** That distinction turns a generic red flag into a budget and sequencing decision.

### Wiring and switchboard: establish the installation, not the house age

A postwar house may have original circuits, partial upgrades, a later switchboard or extensive rewiring. Visual clues can tell you that work has changed, but a licensed electrician should assess the installation, alterations, protective devices, capacity and defects where electrical condition matters to the purchase or renovation. This becomes more important where the property now carries large air-conditioning loads, induction cooking, solar, batteries or electric-vehicle charging.

### Plumbing, hot water and drainage

Treat plumbing as another independent timeline. Ask what pipework has been replaced, whether drainage has been repaired or relined, where stormwater discharges and whether there is any history of leaks, blocked drains or ground movement associated with broken services. A new kitchen does not prove that buried drainage or the rest of the water service was renewed.

### Wet areas: date the room before you judge the system

A bathroom in a 1960s house may be original, 1980s, 2000s or nearly new. Look for swelling, staining, loose finishes, failed joints, cracked tiles, deteriorated sealants, poor drainage and dampness below or beside the room. The present evidence matters more than the decorative age. Where the wet area could materially affect the purchase, use appropriate moisture investigation and establish when the room was built or renewed.

Do not test an old bathroom against today's waterproofing rules as though modern requirements applied retrospectively. Current [NCC waterproofing guidance](https://ncc.abcb.gov.au/ncc-navigator/waterproofing-houses) is useful for understanding why wet areas depend on coordinated waterproof and water-resistant elements, penetrations, junctions and drainage; the compliance question for existing work depends on the rules and approvals relevant when that work was carried out.

### Roof, gutters and the path to ground

Follow water from the roof to the street or lawful discharge point. Look at roof covering, flashings, valleys, penetrations, gutters, downpipes, ponding, low ground levels and whether downpipes actually connect to functioning drainage. [YourHome](https://www.yourhome.gov.au/buy-build-renovate/repairs-and-maintenance) recommends regular gutter maintenance and early attention to leaks because roof and cavity-water problems can grow into larger building damage.

### Footings, drainage and movement

Postwar houses span raised floors and slab construction, often on sites where soil moisture varies significantly. Read cracks with their pattern, progression, associated distortion, footing type, plumbing leaks, trees and drainage. A crack repaired several times without a recorded cause is different evidence from diagnosed movement with completed drainage or footing work. Use [the crack guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/cracks-structural-or-cosmetic) and escalate progressive or consequential movement appropriately.

### Termites and timber concealed inside a practical shell

Postwar houses can contain substantial concealed timber even when the exterior is brick. Risk depends on region, moisture, subfloor ventilation and clearance, landscaping, slab edges and previous treatment. [YourHome's existing-home guidance](https://www.yourhome.gov.au/buy-build-renovate/buying-existing-house) recommends termite inspection before buying in termite-risk regions. Ask about previous activity, damage repairs, treatment, inspection frequency and whether later landscaping or additions have obscured inspection zones.

### Lead paint and layered finishes

Older coatings can contain lead, particularly in earlier layers. The [Australian Government Lead Alert](https://www.agriculture.gov.au/sites/default/files/documents/lead-paint-fifth-edition.pdf) is the right starting point before sanding, scraping or heat stripping. A freshly painted room does not tell you what remains beneath the new coating.

sections.heading: Comfort upgrades need to respect the existing building
sections.markdown: Many postwar homes have been progressively insulated, draught-sealed, reclad or fitted with replacement windows. These upgrades can be valuable, but the installed detail matters. [YourHome's insulation guidance](https://www.yourhome.gov.au/passive-design/insulation) highlights the need to manage electrical clearances and installation safety, while its [condensation guidance](https://www.yourhome.gov.au/passive-design/condensation) explains why ventilation, temperature, humidity and drying paths need to work together. Ask what is in the roof and walls, when it was installed and whether there is evidence of condensation, mould or disturbed insulation.

sections.heading: Renovations can be the most important era in the house
sections.markdown:
**Questions to ask about later work**

| Later work | Evidence worth finding | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Extension or wall removal | Plans, permits, engineering, builder details and completion evidence | Structure, drainage, roof junctions and load paths may have changed. |
| Bathroom/laundry renewal | Renovation date, invoices, waterproofing/inspection evidence where available and leak history | The wet-area age may be decades younger than the house, but present performance still needs checking. |
| Re-roofing | Material, date, flashing work, gutters/downpipes and any sarking/insulation changes | A new covering does not automatically mean every roof junction or rainwater issue was renewed. |
| Rewiring/solar/electrification | Electrical invoices, certificates where applicable, switchboard work and system specifications | Capacity and safety depend on the actual installation and later loads. |
| Recladding/window replacement | Product, date, flashings, membranes, permits where applicable and evidence of water ingress | Changing the envelope can alter drainage, ventilation and moisture behaviour. |

When opening walls or ceilings in a pre-1990 home, coordinate hazardous-material identification with service and structural planning before demolition. The broader sequence is in [planning a renovation](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/planning-a-renovation).

sections.heading: A buyer evidence stack for a postwar home
sections.markdown:
- **Construction:** confirm wall, floor, footing and roof systems rather than relying on the listing description.
- **Alterations:** establish dates and approvals for extensions, wall removal, wet areas, re-roofing, windows and major service work.
- **Hazard screen:** identify suspect pre-1990 materials before planned disturbance and consider older lead coatings before abrasive work.
- **Water:** trace roof water, stormwater, plumbing, wet areas, subfloor moisture and ground levels.
- **Movement:** record cracks, distortion, footing type, drainage, trees and whether the condition appears stable or progressive.
- **Pests:** obtain the latest timber-pest evidence and understand any treatment or management system.
- **Services:** use records and licensed inspection to establish electrical and plumbing condition where they affect safety, capacity or budget.

sections.heading: Worked example: new bathroom, older damage
sections.markdown:
**Illustrative reasoning example, not an inspected property.** A 1968 home has a bathroom renewed in 2019 and staining on the adjoining bedroom skirting. The renovation date makes an original-bathroom assumption inappropriate, but it does not explain the stain. Request the scope, ask when the mark appeared and arrange targeted inspection. A documented earlier leak followed by repair and no recurrence supports a different plan from continuing damp after use.

Keep the conclusions separate: the bathroom is reported as renewed; the stain is visible; the cause and current activity remain unconfirmed. If inspection establishes a local plumbing defect, the repair may be local. If concealed damage or failed waterproofing is established, the scope can expand. This is why the first budget should distinguish investigation from a conditional rebuild.

sections.heading: What good evidence looks like
sections.markdown:
A postwar home does not need to be 'fully renovated' to be a sound purchase. What matters is whether the major systems are understood. A documented older bathroom may be easier to budget than an undocumented new one. A weathered roof with a clear replacement plan may be easier to price than unexplained ceiling staining. The aim is not to remove every future cost; it is to turn uncertainty into a known condition, an evidence gap or a defined next inspection.

> Note: The strongest postwar-home record usually separates original fabric, later alterations and current condition. Keep those three columns distinct.

> Important: Have suspect asbestos-containing materials identified before work and use the removal pathway required in your state or territory. Do not create a sample by breaking, drilling or sanding suspect material.

guides.contentMarkdown:
# Postwar homes (1950s–70s): what to expect and what they need

With a 1950s to 1970s home, first identify the actual wall, floor and footing system and what has changed since construction. Screen pre-1990 materials for possible asbestos before disturbance, establish the age and condition of wiring and plumbing, inspect roof-water disposal, drainage and footings, and read bathrooms and extensions by their own renovation dates. Termite risk, moisture and movement depend on the site and construction, not the decade alone.

## Research note
Postwar housing spans brick veneer, weatherboard, masonry and mixed systems with decades of later service and wet-area work. The reliable date-linked hazard screen is pre-1990 asbestos; the rest is established from the actual shell, drainage, termite/pest evidence, service history and present condition. See [YourHome's existing-house guidance](https://www.yourhome.gov.au/buy-build-renovate/buying-existing-house).

## Opening
### A practical shell with decades of changes
- **Fabric:** Which shell is present: veneer, boards, masonry or mixed
- **Services:** When the wiring and plumbing were renewed, with proof
- **Hazards:** Anything pre-1990 gets screened before anyone drills into it

_The wiring in place sets the electrical question. Find its age and alteration history._

## The houses that built the suburbs
Postwar expansion produced brick veneer, weatherboard, masonry and mixed construction across Australia, using slabs, stumps, piers and strip footings in different regions. Many of these homes have now accumulated half a century or more of bathroom renewals, extensions, service upgrades, window replacements, roof work and cosmetic renovation. The useful starting point is therefore **construction plus alteration history**, not decade alone.

A 1965 house can contain a 1965 frame, a 1988 bathroom, a 2004 extension, 2017 wiring work and a much newer hot-water system. Each layer carries its own questions. Your task is to identify which elements are original, which were renewed, and whether the evidence of that work is strong enough to budget from.

## Start by identifying the shell
**Postwar construction clues that change the inspection**

| Element | What to establish | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| External walls | Brick veneer, weatherboard, masonry, fibre-cement or later recladding | The wall system changes how you read movement, cavities, moisture, maintenance and hidden framing. |
| Floor and footings | Raised timber floor, slab-on-ground, stumps, piers, strip footing or mixed additions | Movement, termite access, drainage and repair options differ materially between systems. |
| Roof | Tile, metal or mixed replacement; original versus later sections | Leaks often sit at flashings, valleys, gutters, penetrations and interfaces between old and new work. |
| Openings | Timber, steel or aluminium windows; later replacement glazing | Frame material, seals, flashings, drainage and condensation behaviour can differ by installation. |
| Alterations | Enclosed verandas, rear additions, wall removal, garages, decks and wet-area changes | The junction between original and later work is often where structure, drainage and waterproofing need the most evidence. |

If the house is brick veneer, use [brick veneer versus double brick](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/brick-veneer-vs-double-brick) to understand what the outer brick leaf does and what the timber frame behind it is doing. If it is weatherboard, use [the weatherboard guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/weatherboard-homes) to follow coatings, flashings, clearances and subfloor conditions.

## Inspection priorities
### Asbestos: a high-priority pre-1990 screen

The [national householders' guide](https://www.newaste.org.au/asbestos/assets/asbestos-guide-for-householders.pdf) says homes built or renovated before 1990 may contain asbestos products. In postwar houses, suspect materials may be original or may come from later additions and refurbishments. Do not infer presence from appearance alone and do not disturb suspect material to 'check'. Identify it through the appropriate assessment pathway before drilling, sanding, cutting or demolition.

For a buyer, the practical question is not simply 'does this era contain asbestos?' It is **where might suspect material sit, will your planned work disturb it, and what evidence do you need before setting the renovation scope?** That distinction turns a generic red flag into a budget and sequencing decision.

### Wiring and switchboard: establish the installation, not the house age

A postwar house may have original circuits, partial upgrades, a later switchboard or extensive rewiring. Visual clues can tell you that work has changed, but a licensed electrician should assess the installation, alterations, protective devices, capacity and defects where electrical condition matters to the purchase or renovation. This becomes more important where the property now carries large air-conditioning loads, induction cooking, solar, batteries or electric-vehicle charging.

### Plumbing, hot water and drainage

Treat plumbing as another independent timeline. Ask what pipework has been replaced, whether drainage has been repaired or relined, where stormwater discharges and whether there is any history of leaks, blocked drains or ground movement associated with broken services. A new kitchen does not prove that buried drainage or the rest of the water service was renewed.

### Wet areas: date the room before you judge the system

A bathroom in a 1960s house may be original, 1980s, 2000s or nearly new. Look for swelling, staining, loose finishes, failed joints, cracked tiles, deteriorated sealants, poor drainage and dampness below or beside the room. The present evidence matters more than the decorative age. Where the wet area could materially affect the purchase, use appropriate moisture investigation and establish when the room was built or renewed.

Do not test an old bathroom against today's waterproofing rules as though modern requirements applied retrospectively. Current [NCC waterproofing guidance](https://ncc.abcb.gov.au/ncc-navigator/waterproofing-houses) is useful for understanding why wet areas depend on coordinated waterproof and water-resistant elements, penetrations, junctions and drainage; the compliance question for existing work depends on the rules and approvals relevant when that work was carried out.

### Roof, gutters and the path to ground

Follow water from the roof to the street or lawful discharge point. Look at roof covering, flashings, valleys, penetrations, gutters, downpipes, ponding, low ground levels and whether downpipes actually connect to functioning drainage. [YourHome](https://www.yourhome.gov.au/buy-build-renovate/repairs-and-maintenance) recommends regular gutter maintenance and early attention to leaks because roof and cavity-water problems can grow into larger building damage.

### Footings, drainage and movement

Postwar houses span raised floors and slab construction, often on sites where soil moisture varies significantly. Read cracks with their pattern, progression, associated distortion, footing type, plumbing leaks, trees and drainage. A crack repaired several times without a recorded cause is different evidence from diagnosed movement with completed drainage or footing work. Use [the crack guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/cracks-structural-or-cosmetic) and escalate progressive or consequential movement appropriately.

### Termites and timber concealed inside a practical shell

Postwar houses can contain substantial concealed timber even when the exterior is brick. Risk depends on region, moisture, subfloor ventilation and clearance, landscaping, slab edges and previous treatment. [YourHome's existing-home guidance](https://www.yourhome.gov.au/buy-build-renovate/buying-existing-house) recommends termite inspection before buying in termite-risk regions. Ask about previous activity, damage repairs, treatment, inspection frequency and whether later landscaping or additions have obscured inspection zones.

### Lead paint and layered finishes

Older coatings can contain lead, particularly in earlier layers. The [Australian Government Lead Alert](https://www.agriculture.gov.au/sites/default/files/documents/lead-paint-fifth-edition.pdf) is the right starting point before sanding, scraping or heat stripping. A freshly painted room does not tell you what remains beneath the new coating.

## Comfort upgrades need to respect the existing building
Many postwar homes have been progressively insulated, draught-sealed, reclad or fitted with replacement windows. These upgrades can be valuable, but the installed detail matters. [YourHome's insulation guidance](https://www.yourhome.gov.au/passive-design/insulation) highlights the need to manage electrical clearances and installation safety, while its [condensation guidance](https://www.yourhome.gov.au/passive-design/condensation) explains why ventilation, temperature, humidity and drying paths need to work together. Ask what is in the roof and walls, when it was installed and whether there is evidence of condensation, mould or disturbed insulation.

## Renovations can be the most important era in the house
**Questions to ask about later work**

| Later work | Evidence worth finding | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Extension or wall removal | Plans, permits, engineering, builder details and completion evidence | Structure, drainage, roof junctions and load paths may have changed. |
| Bathroom/laundry renewal | Renovation date, invoices, waterproofing/inspection evidence where available and leak history | The wet-area age may be decades younger than the house, but present performance still needs checking. |
| Re-roofing | Material, date, flashing work, gutters/downpipes and any sarking/insulation changes | A new covering does not automatically mean every roof junction or rainwater issue was renewed. |
| Rewiring/solar/electrification | Electrical invoices, certificates where applicable, switchboard work and system specifications | Capacity and safety depend on the actual installation and later loads. |
| Recladding/window replacement | Product, date, flashings, membranes, permits where applicable and evidence of water ingress | Changing the envelope can alter drainage, ventilation and moisture behaviour. |

When opening walls or ceilings in a pre-1990 home, coordinate hazardous-material identification with service and structural planning before demolition. The broader sequence is in [planning a renovation](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/planning-a-renovation).

## A buyer evidence stack for a postwar home
- **Construction:** confirm wall, floor, footing and roof systems rather than relying on the listing description.
- **Alterations:** establish dates and approvals for extensions, wall removal, wet areas, re-roofing, windows and major service work.
- **Hazard screen:** identify suspect pre-1990 materials before planned disturbance and consider older lead coatings before abrasive work.
- **Water:** trace roof water, stormwater, plumbing, wet areas, subfloor moisture and ground levels.
- **Movement:** record cracks, distortion, footing type, drainage, trees and whether the condition appears stable or progressive.
- **Pests:** obtain the latest timber-pest evidence and understand any treatment or management system.
- **Services:** use records and licensed inspection to establish electrical and plumbing condition where they affect safety, capacity or budget.

## Worked example: new bathroom, older damage
**Illustrative reasoning example, not an inspected property.** A 1968 home has a bathroom renewed in 2019 and staining on the adjoining bedroom skirting. The renovation date makes an original-bathroom assumption inappropriate, but it does not explain the stain. Request the scope, ask when the mark appeared and arrange targeted inspection. A documented earlier leak followed by repair and no recurrence supports a different plan from continuing damp after use.

Keep the conclusions separate: the bathroom is reported as renewed; the stain is visible; the cause and current activity remain unconfirmed. If inspection establishes a local plumbing defect, the repair may be local. If concealed damage or failed waterproofing is established, the scope can expand. This is why the first budget should distinguish investigation from a conditional rebuild.

## What good evidence looks like
A postwar home does not need to be 'fully renovated' to be a sound purchase. What matters is whether the major systems are understood. A documented older bathroom may be easier to budget than an undocumented new one. A weathered roof with a clear replacement plan may be easier to price than unexplained ceiling staining. The aim is not to remove every future cost; it is to turn uncertainty into a known condition, an evidence gap or a defined next inspection.

> Note: The strongest postwar-home record usually separates original fabric, later alterations and current condition. Keep those three columns distinct.

> Important: Have suspect asbestos-containing materials identified before work and use the removal pathway required in your state or territory. Do not create a sample by breaking, drilling or sanding suspect material.

## Frequently asked questions
### What problems do 1950s–70s homes have?
Common inspection priorities include pre-1990 hazardous materials, wiring and switchboards, plumbing and drainage, wet areas, roof-water disposal, termite risk, footing movement and older coatings. The actual construction and alteration history matter more than the decade alone.

### Does my brick-veneer home from the 1960s have asbestos?
It may. Homes built or renovated before 1990 can contain asbestos products. Identify suspect materials before disturbance rather than assuming from appearance or house type.

### Do postwar homes need rewiring?
Not automatically. A licensed electrician should identify the actual installation, alterations, protective devices, defects and capacity before any upgrade scope is set.

### Why do bathrooms in postwar homes leak?
Water can escape through plumbing, junctions, drainage, screens, finishes or waterproofing. First establish when the room was built or renewed, then investigate current evidence rather than judging it from the age of the house.

### Is cracking in a brick-veneer home serious?
Read width, direction, location, associated distortion and change over time. Also check roof-water disposal, ground drainage, plumbing leaks, trees and the footing system. Progressive or consequential movement deserves professional assessment.

### Are termites only a timber-home problem?
No. Brick-veneer and other postwar homes can contain concealed timber framing. Termite risk depends on location, moisture, access, barriers and maintenance rather than the visible wall finish alone.

### Is a renovated 1960s house basically a modern house?
No. Renovation can replace some systems while leaving the original frame, footings, drainage, roof structure or concealed materials in place. Treat each major element by its own date and evidence.

### Are postwar homes a good buy?
They can be. The useful question is whether the shell, services, wet areas, drainage, pest risk, hazardous materials and alterations are understood well enough to price the next work realistically.

## Method
We separate the original shell, later alterations and current condition, then follow the highest-consequence systems: hazardous materials, water, footings, termites, wet areas and services.

## Limitations
Confirm the age and condition of services, wet areas, footings, drainage, pest management and hazardous materials through records and physical evidence. Current code provisions are context, not a retrospective compliance test.

## Sources
- [Asbestos: a guide for householders and the general public](https://www.newaste.org.au/asbestos/assets/asbestos-guide-for-householders.pdf) — Australian Government / enHealth; accessed 2026-07-19
- [Waterproofing in houses](https://ncc.abcb.gov.au/ncc-navigator/waterproofing-houses) — Australian Building Codes Board; accessed 2026-09-07
- [Repairs and maintenance](https://www.yourhome.gov.au/buy-build-renovate/repairs-and-maintenance) — YourHome, Australian Government; accessed 2026-07-19
- [Buying an existing house](https://www.yourhome.gov.au/buy-build-renovate/buying-existing-house) — YourHome, Australian Government; accessed 2026-09-07
- [Lead Alert: the six step guide to painting your home](https://www.agriculture.gov.au/sites/default/files/documents/lead-paint-fifth-edition.pdf) — Australian Government; accessed 2026-07-19

guides.question: What are the main strata risks for apartment owners?
guides.title: Strata risks: what every apartment owner should watch for
guides.summary: When you own an apartment, the roof, façade, lifts, fire systems and scheme finances become part of your home story too. The records show where future work and levies may come from.
guides.answer: Apartment risk lives across the lot, the shared building and the scheme that runs it. Read the maintenance plan beside the funds and liabilities, then follow the minutes for water, façade, fire, defect and legal issues. Work out who makes each decision and who pays. Recent problems may not have reached the minutes yet, so thin or delayed records deserve a question.
guides.methodology: An owner-action guide separating defect evidence, repair responsibility, authority, service continuity and contingent recovery. NSW examples are identified as jurisdiction-specific.
guides.limitations: General Australian strata guidance. Use the registered plan, scheme documents and state-specific professional advice.
guides.researchNote: [NSW's repair guidance](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/strata/living/repairs-and-maintenance) supplies the local process example. The action register separates technical findings, authority, funding and recovery; exact responsibilities require the scheme documents and applicable state rules.

cluster.label: Apartments and shared buildings
cluster.blurb: Read both purchases: your lot, and your share of the common property, records and future costs.

sections.heading: Opening
sections.markdown:
### Every shared problem has a decision and a bill
- **Issue:** The problem itself: a leak, a crack, a lift, a façade
- **Boundary:** Whose side of the plan it falls on
- **Response:** Who decides, who pays, and where that gets written down

_In a shared building, the committee is part of the structure._

sections.heading: Shared-building exposure
sections.markdown:
Apartment ownership connects a private lot to common property and collective decisions. The registered plan and state law establish the precise boundary. Shared systems, building defects, insurance, contracts and scheme finances can affect an owner even where the lot interior looks sound. Recent events, poor recordkeeping and inaccessible areas can leave gaps in the records.

For a Victorian property, [Consumer Affairs Victoria explains common-property responsibilities](https://www.consumer.vic.gov.au/housing/owners-corporations/buying-into-an-owners-corporation/what-is-an-owners-corporation) by reference to the plan of subdivision, including repair, fees, records and required insurance, with special rules for some schemes. For NSW, use the state's [levies, funds and insurance guidance](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/strata/living/levies-finances-insurance) alongside its repair guidance. Apply the relevant state's scheme rules when connecting a repair obligation to its funding.

sections.heading: The risks that land on owners
sections.markdown:
### Special levies from an underfunded reserve

A scheme may resolve an additional or special levy when available funds fall short of an approved need. Assess the fund beside the maintenance plan, the quotes, the contracts, the liabilities, the arrears and the levy schedule. Who ends up paying around a sale comes down to the contract and the state.

### Combustible cladding

Cladding risk depends on the installed system, building configuration and actual assessment, not an era label alone. Ask for any identification, fire-safety assessment, required action and completion evidence. Separate the cost of investigation, the rectification scope and its funding, and any current insurer conditions. An attractive reclad façade does not establish that every relevant finding has been closed.

### Builder defects

Original construction defects can involve waterproofing, fire separation, structure and services, and may remain unresolved beyond a building’s early years. Look for the technical findings and their status, not just a reference to a warranty or dispute. Minutes can help locate the issue, but omitted or recent findings may require further records.

### Waterproofing and balcony membranes

Water entry at a balcony can involve membranes, drainage, thresholds, joints or adjoining details. Identify the source and repair interfaces before assuming that resealing or a complete membrane replacement is the answer. Work may require access through multiple lots or common property; finishes, reinstatement and investigation can change the scope and cost.

### Underinsurance of the building

Scheme insurance obligations and the boundary between building, common-property, lot-owner and contents cover vary by jurisdiction, plan and policy. Review the current schedule, valuation basis, declared value, excesses, exclusions, claims and responsibility for owner improvements. The event and policy determine any coverage gap.

### A poorly run owners corporation

Thin minutes, high arrears, deferred decisions, missing close-out evidence or long-running disputes are investigation signals. Compare several reporting periods and trace material issues from proposal to resolution, funding, completion and warranty.

sections.heading: Buying in: check the scheme’s continuing obligations
sections.markdown: A buyer acquires the lot within the scheme's continuing physical, financial and governance position. The contract and state law determine treatment of existing levies and disclosure. Use the records to identify exposure and uncertainty, then have legal and technical advisers explain their effect. The companion checklist is [what to check before buying an apartment](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/buying-an-apartment-strata).

sections.heading: How to stay ahead of them
sections.markdown: Read financial statements, the maintenance-fund balance and minutes as they arrive. Compare the same signals year on year using [the owners-corporation records guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/reading-your-owners-corporation-report).

sections.heading: Start with the source, the boundary and the decision-maker
sections.markdown:
The room where damage appears does not settle who owns the failed component or must arrange the work. A stain inside a lot may originate at a shared roof, an adjoining bathroom or a private fitting. Establish the mechanism and read the registered plan, applicable by-laws and alterations records before allocating responsibility. [NSW's repair guidance](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/strata/living/repairs-and-maintenance) distinguishes owner and common-property repairs and directs owners to their manager or committee for common-property issues. Apply the process for your state and scheme.

**Turn a complaint into a decision that can be followed**

| Question | Useful record | Why it changes the response |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What is happening? | Location, dates, safe photographs and impact on use | Separates the symptom from a suspected cause |
| What has been established? | Relevant investigation, access limitations and scope | Shows whether the cause is known or still being tested |
| Who can act? | Plan, by-laws, delegated authority and written decision | Distinguishes reporting, authorising and carrying out work |
| What happens next? | Named action, responsible person and review point | Makes delay and incomplete follow-up visible |

Report recurrence under the same issue reference, with the new date and consequence. 'Same leak again' is less useful than identifying whether the location, weather and affected rooms match. If access to another lot is required, ask the authorised scheme representative to arrange it. Do not assume ownership gives you permission to enter another lot or alter common property.

sections.heading: Keep urgent protection and permanent repair separate
sections.markdown:
An immediate safety or damage-control response may be needed before a full cause investigation is possible. Use emergency services for immediate danger and follow the scheme's emergency contact arrangements. Record notifications and the attending professional's observations when safe. Whether an owner can commission work and recover the cost depends on the applicable process and circumstances; do not assume reimbursement.

Temporary protection should have a review point. A patch may reduce immediate water entry while the scheme obtains a diagnosis and permanent scope. It should not disappear from the action list because the next meeting is dry. Ask which condition would trigger escalation, who checks the temporary measure and what would establish that permanent work has addressed the original finding.

sections.heading: A recovery claim is not money available for repairs
sections.markdown:
A builder claim, insurer notification or legal proceeding can run alongside an unresolved building problem. Separate expected recovery from cash available and decisions actually authorised. Ask what the scheme will do if the claim is delayed, partly accepted or unsuccessful. Obtain appropriate advice about preserving evidence and rights while arranging necessary protection; neither waiting indefinitely nor destroying disputed evidence is a sound default.

Read repair cost, investigation fees, access costs, professional supervision and reinstatement as separate scope questions. A balcony quotation may exclude internal damage, temporary accommodation or work discovered when finishes are lifted. Compare the approved contract with the identified defect, not just the fund balance. The [records guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/reading-your-owners-corporation-report) explains how to reconcile plans, cash and commitments without treating receivables as money already in the bank.

sections.heading: Think about loss of service as well as a levy
sections.markdown:
A lift outage affects a person with limited mobility differently from an owner who can use stairs. Central hot water, fire systems, garage access and stormwater pumps can create shared dependencies even in a building with attractive interiors. Ask about competent servicing, recurring faults, replacement planning and arrangements for residents while essential work occurs. A service invoice alone does not show that every outstanding defect was rectified.

Small schemes may have fewer systems but also fewer owners to share a major cost and less administrative capacity. Large schemes can coordinate substantial work yet have more interfaces between managers, committees, contractors and residents. In either case, use a short issue register to connect the technical problem to an actual decision. When a repair remains unresolved, check your state authority's current escalation pathway; a routine meeting timetable does not determine the urgency of a safety issue.

sections.heading: Worked example: a leak waits for a builder claim
sections.markdown:
**Illustrative reasoning example, not an inspected property.** An owner reports ceiling staining after rain. Minutes say 'builder claim progressing', while two emergency patch invoices have been paid. There is no written permanent scope in the supplied records.

Treat the stain, attempted repairs and claim as three separate facts. The claim does not establish the leak's cause, successful recovery or a completed repair. Request the investigation, temporary-protection arrangements, plan-based responsibility assessment and the decision authorising further work.

If the investigation confirms a common-roof defect, ask how necessary work will be funded and managed while the recovery remains uncertain. If it identifies a private fitting instead, responsibility and scope need reassessment. Either finding is more useful than reading 'claim progressing' as evidence that the building problem is under control.

Keep conclusions at the level the evidence supports: observed, reported, inferred or confirmed. An unavailable document is a gap in the record; it does not prove the work was never done.

> Note: Track shared-building condition, decisions, funds and levies alongside the records for your lot.

> Important: Strata rules, terminology and owners’ rights vary by state: an owners corporation in Victoria, a strata scheme in New South Wales, a body corporate in Queensland. For a dispute, a levy challenge or a major decision, check the scheme in your state and consider strata-specialist or legal advice.

faqs.question: What are the strata risks for apartment buyers?
faqs.answer: Check shared defects, planned works, levies, insurance and governance. Records can reveal exposure but may omit recent or uninvestigated problems. The contract and applicable state law determine treatment of existing levies around settlement.

faqs.question: What are the biggest risks of owning an apartment?
faqs.answer: Mostly building-wide ones: a special levy from an underfunded maintenance fund, combustible cladding, builder defects, failed waterproofing, an underinsured building, and poor owners-corporation governance. Each can land a large, unplanned cost on you regardless of your own unit’s condition.

faqs.question: What is a special levy in strata?
faqs.answer: An additional contribution resolved under the applicable scheme process. Its purpose, amount, instalments and responsibility around a sale must be read from the resolution, state law, disclosure and contract.

faqs.question: How do I avoid a surprise strata levy?
faqs.answer: Read current plans, budgets, commitments and unresolved issues together. Ask how significant works will be funded. This improves preparation but cannot eliminate unforeseen defects or guarantee that an additional levy will not arise.

faqs.question: Is combustible cladding still a risk for apartment owners?
faqs.answer: It can be where the installed system and building circumstances create a risk. Obtain the actual assessment, rectification decisions and completion evidence; a construction decade alone does not establish the material or its safety.

faqs.question: What should I check about scheme insurance?
faqs.answer: Check the current policy, valuation basis, declared value, excesses, exclusions, claims and the boundary between scheme and lot-owner cover. Obligations and shortfalls depend on state law, the plan, policy and actual event.

faqs.question: How can I tell if my owners corporation is well run?
faqs.answer: Look for a current works plan, aligned funding, manageable arrears, clear minutes, appropriate insurance and closed-out disputes.

guides.contentMarkdown:
# Strata risks: what every apartment owner should watch for

Apartment risk lives across the lot, the shared building and the scheme that runs it. Read the maintenance plan beside the funds and liabilities, then follow the minutes for water, façade, fire, defect and legal issues. Work out who makes each decision and who pays. Recent problems may not have reached the minutes yet, so thin or delayed records deserve a question.

## Research note
[NSW's repair guidance](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/strata/living/repairs-and-maintenance) supplies the local process example. The action register separates technical findings, authority, funding and recovery; exact responsibilities require the scheme documents and applicable state rules.

## Opening
### Every shared problem has a decision and a bill
- **Issue:** The problem itself: a leak, a crack, a lift, a façade
- **Boundary:** Whose side of the plan it falls on
- **Response:** Who decides, who pays, and where that gets written down

_In a shared building, the committee is part of the structure._

## Shared-building exposure
Apartment ownership connects a private lot to common property and collective decisions. The registered plan and state law establish the precise boundary. Shared systems, building defects, insurance, contracts and scheme finances can affect an owner even where the lot interior looks sound. Recent events, poor recordkeeping and inaccessible areas can leave gaps in the records.

For a Victorian property, [Consumer Affairs Victoria explains common-property responsibilities](https://www.consumer.vic.gov.au/housing/owners-corporations/buying-into-an-owners-corporation/what-is-an-owners-corporation) by reference to the plan of subdivision, including repair, fees, records and required insurance, with special rules for some schemes. For NSW, use the state's [levies, funds and insurance guidance](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/strata/living/levies-finances-insurance) alongside its repair guidance. Apply the relevant state's scheme rules when connecting a repair obligation to its funding.

## The risks that land on owners
### Special levies from an underfunded reserve

A scheme may resolve an additional or special levy when available funds fall short of an approved need. Assess the fund beside the maintenance plan, the quotes, the contracts, the liabilities, the arrears and the levy schedule. Who ends up paying around a sale comes down to the contract and the state.

### Combustible cladding

Cladding risk depends on the installed system, building configuration and actual assessment, not an era label alone. Ask for any identification, fire-safety assessment, required action and completion evidence. Separate the cost of investigation, the rectification scope and its funding, and any current insurer conditions. An attractive reclad façade does not establish that every relevant finding has been closed.

### Builder defects

Original construction defects can involve waterproofing, fire separation, structure and services, and may remain unresolved beyond a building’s early years. Look for the technical findings and their status, not just a reference to a warranty or dispute. Minutes can help locate the issue, but omitted or recent findings may require further records.

### Waterproofing and balcony membranes

Water entry at a balcony can involve membranes, drainage, thresholds, joints or adjoining details. Identify the source and repair interfaces before assuming that resealing or a complete membrane replacement is the answer. Work may require access through multiple lots or common property; finishes, reinstatement and investigation can change the scope and cost.

### Underinsurance of the building

Scheme insurance obligations and the boundary between building, common-property, lot-owner and contents cover vary by jurisdiction, plan and policy. Review the current schedule, valuation basis, declared value, excesses, exclusions, claims and responsibility for owner improvements. The event and policy determine any coverage gap.

### A poorly run owners corporation

Thin minutes, high arrears, deferred decisions, missing close-out evidence or long-running disputes are investigation signals. Compare several reporting periods and trace material issues from proposal to resolution, funding, completion and warranty.

## Buying in: check the scheme’s continuing obligations
A buyer acquires the lot within the scheme's continuing physical, financial and governance position. The contract and state law determine treatment of existing levies and disclosure. Use the records to identify exposure and uncertainty, then have legal and technical advisers explain their effect. The companion checklist is [what to check before buying an apartment](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/buying-an-apartment-strata).

## How to stay ahead of them
Read financial statements, the maintenance-fund balance and minutes as they arrive. Compare the same signals year on year using [the owners-corporation records guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/reading-your-owners-corporation-report).

## Start with the source, the boundary and the decision-maker
The room where damage appears does not settle who owns the failed component or must arrange the work. A stain inside a lot may originate at a shared roof, an adjoining bathroom or a private fitting. Establish the mechanism and read the registered plan, applicable by-laws and alterations records before allocating responsibility. [NSW's repair guidance](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/strata/living/repairs-and-maintenance) distinguishes owner and common-property repairs and directs owners to their manager or committee for common-property issues. Apply the process for your state and scheme.

**Turn a complaint into a decision that can be followed**

| Question | Useful record | Why it changes the response |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What is happening? | Location, dates, safe photographs and impact on use | Separates the symptom from a suspected cause |
| What has been established? | Relevant investigation, access limitations and scope | Shows whether the cause is known or still being tested |
| Who can act? | Plan, by-laws, delegated authority and written decision | Distinguishes reporting, authorising and carrying out work |
| What happens next? | Named action, responsible person and review point | Makes delay and incomplete follow-up visible |

Report recurrence under the same issue reference, with the new date and consequence. 'Same leak again' is less useful than identifying whether the location, weather and affected rooms match. If access to another lot is required, ask the authorised scheme representative to arrange it. Do not assume ownership gives you permission to enter another lot or alter common property.

## Keep urgent protection and permanent repair separate
An immediate safety or damage-control response may be needed before a full cause investigation is possible. Use emergency services for immediate danger and follow the scheme's emergency contact arrangements. Record notifications and the attending professional's observations when safe. Whether an owner can commission work and recover the cost depends on the applicable process and circumstances; do not assume reimbursement.

Temporary protection should have a review point. A patch may reduce immediate water entry while the scheme obtains a diagnosis and permanent scope. It should not disappear from the action list because the next meeting is dry. Ask which condition would trigger escalation, who checks the temporary measure and what would establish that permanent work has addressed the original finding.

## A recovery claim is not money available for repairs
A builder claim, insurer notification or legal proceeding can run alongside an unresolved building problem. Separate expected recovery from cash available and decisions actually authorised. Ask what the scheme will do if the claim is delayed, partly accepted or unsuccessful. Obtain appropriate advice about preserving evidence and rights while arranging necessary protection; neither waiting indefinitely nor destroying disputed evidence is a sound default.

Read repair cost, investigation fees, access costs, professional supervision and reinstatement as separate scope questions. A balcony quotation may exclude internal damage, temporary accommodation or work discovered when finishes are lifted. Compare the approved contract with the identified defect, not just the fund balance. The [records guide](https://homechecker.com.au/guides/reading-your-owners-corporation-report) explains how to reconcile plans, cash and commitments without treating receivables as money already in the bank.

## Think about loss of service as well as a levy
A lift outage affects a person with limited mobility differently from an owner who can use stairs. Central hot water, fire systems, garage access and stormwater pumps can create shared dependencies even in a building with attractive interiors. Ask about competent servicing, recurring faults, replacement planning and arrangements for residents while essential work occurs. A service invoice alone does not show that every outstanding defect was rectified.

Small schemes may have fewer systems but also fewer owners to share a major cost and less administrative capacity. Large schemes can coordinate substantial work yet have more interfaces between managers, committees, contractors and residents. In either case, use a short issue register to connect the technical problem to an actual decision. When a repair remains unresolved, check your state authority's current escalation pathway; a routine meeting timetable does not determine the urgency of a safety issue.

## Worked example: a leak waits for a builder claim
**Illustrative reasoning example, not an inspected property.** An owner reports ceiling staining after rain. Minutes say 'builder claim progressing', while two emergency patch invoices have been paid. There is no written permanent scope in the supplied records.

Treat the stain, attempted repairs and claim as three separate facts. The claim does not establish the leak's cause, successful recovery or a completed repair. Request the investigation, temporary-protection arrangements, plan-based responsibility assessment and the decision authorising further work.

If the investigation confirms a common-roof defect, ask how necessary work will be funded and managed while the recovery remains uncertain. If it identifies a private fitting instead, responsibility and scope need reassessment. Either finding is more useful than reading 'claim progressing' as evidence that the building problem is under control.

Keep conclusions at the level the evidence supports: observed, reported, inferred or confirmed. An unavailable document is a gap in the record; it does not prove the work was never done.

> Note: Track shared-building condition, decisions, funds and levies alongside the records for your lot.

> Important: Strata rules, terminology and owners’ rights vary by state: an owners corporation in Victoria, a strata scheme in New South Wales, a body corporate in Queensland. For a dispute, a levy challenge or a major decision, check the scheme in your state and consider strata-specialist or legal advice.

## Frequently asked questions
### What are the strata risks for apartment buyers?
Check shared defects, planned works, levies, insurance and governance. Records can reveal exposure but may omit recent or uninvestigated problems. The contract and applicable state law determine treatment of existing levies around settlement.

### What are the biggest risks of owning an apartment?
Mostly building-wide ones: a special levy from an underfunded maintenance fund, combustible cladding, builder defects, failed waterproofing, an underinsured building, and poor owners-corporation governance. Each can land a large, unplanned cost on you regardless of your own unit’s condition.

### What is a special levy in strata?
An additional contribution resolved under the applicable scheme process. Its purpose, amount, instalments and responsibility around a sale must be read from the resolution, state law, disclosure and contract.

### How do I avoid a surprise strata levy?
Read current plans, budgets, commitments and unresolved issues together. Ask how significant works will be funded. This improves preparation but cannot eliminate unforeseen defects or guarantee that an additional levy will not arise.

### Is combustible cladding still a risk for apartment owners?
It can be where the installed system and building circumstances create a risk. Obtain the actual assessment, rectification decisions and completion evidence; a construction decade alone does not establish the material or its safety.

### What should I check about scheme insurance?
Check the current policy, valuation basis, declared value, excesses, exclusions, claims and the boundary between scheme and lot-owner cover. Obligations and shortfalls depend on state law, the plan, policy and actual event.

### How can I tell if my owners corporation is well run?
Look for a current works plan, aligned funding, manageable arrears, clear minutes, appropriate insurance and closed-out disputes.

### Does a builder claim mean the scheme can wait to repair?
A claim and a repair plan answer different questions. Ask how safety, ongoing damage, evidence preservation and funding are being handled while the claim is unresolved, with appropriate technical and legal advice.

### Can I arrange common-property repairs myself?
Check the scheme authority and current state process. Urgent circumstances may have specific provisions, but authority and reimbursement should not be assumed.

## Method
An owner-action guide separating defect evidence, repair responsibility, authority, service continuity and contingent recovery. NSW examples are identified as jurisdiction-specific.

## Limitations
General Australian strata guidance. Use the registered plan, scheme documents and state-specific professional advice.

## Sources
- [Strata repairs and maintenance](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/strata/living/repairs-and-maintenance) — NSW Government; accessed 2026-09-07
- [What is an owners corporation?](https://www.consumer.vic.gov.au/housing/owners-corporations/buying-into-an-owners-corporation/what-is-an-owners-corporation) — Consumer Affairs Victoria; accessed 2026-07-19
- [Your strata levies, finances and insurance](https://www.nsw.gov.au/housing-and-construction/strata/living/levies-finances-insurance) — NSW Government; accessed 2026-09-07
